EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Purpose
This Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) is prepared in accordance with the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to evaluate the potential environmental impacts associated with
the implementation of the Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project (State
Clearinghouse No. 2023080733). This document is prepared in conformance with CEQA (Public
Resources Code [PRC] § 21000, et seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines (California Code of Regulations
[CCR], Title 14 § 15000, et seq.).

The purpose of this Draft EIR is to inform decision-makers, representatives of affected and
responsible agencies, the public, and other interested parties of the potential environmental effects
that may result from implementation of the proposed project. This Draft EIR describes potential
impacts relating to a wide variety of environmental issues and methods by which these impacts can
be mitigated or avoided.

Project Summary
Project Location
The project site is located at 699 Gilman Street, as well as 1101, 1199–1231, 1201, and 1203 2nd
Street, in Berkeley, within the West Berkeley Plan area (Chapter 2, Project Description, Exhibit 2-2a).
Specifically, the project site is located within the Richmond, California Oakland West United States
Geological Survey (USGS) 7.5-minute Topographic Quadrangle Map Township 1S, Range 4W, Section
4 (Latitude 37o52’49.31” North; Longitude 122o18’21.01” West). The site is currently accessed from
Second Street and Gilman Street.

Most of the project site is within a transit priority area (TPA) (Chapter 2, Project Description, Exhibit
2-2b). A TPA is defined in California Public Resources Code Section 21099 as an area within 0.5 mile
of a major transit stop that is existing or planned.

Project Description
The proposed project would involve the replacement of the existing solid waste transfer station with
a proposed facility that is designed to enhance recycling and solid waste operations, address on-site
traffic flow, serve existing and future needs of the local community, and replace outdated buildings.
All existing buildings, concrete foundations, and other paved surfaces would be demolished and
removed from the project site. As part of the entitlement process, the proposed project would apply
for a lot line adjustment, and the six parcels would be merged into one parcel.

The proposed solid waste transfer facility would operate in accordance with the existing Solid Waste
Facility Permit (once revised to reflect the proposed lot line adjustment) and does not propose any
further increase of tonnage or expansion of hours of operation at the proposed facility beyond what



FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                         ES-1

is allowed under the current permit. Therefore, it is assumed that the number of employees at the

Table 2-4 provides details about the components for the proposed project. A site plan is provided in
Chapter 2, Project Description, Exhibit 2-9a; Exhibit 2-9b provides detail on the site plan with respect
to Codornices Creek. Chapter 2, Project Description, Exhibit 2-10 depicts the proposed circulation
through the site.

The proposed project would merge the six parcels into one; demolish the existing solid waste
transfer station and Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) on the project site, including buildings,
accessory structures, equipment, and paving; and construct new buildings, accessory structures,
equipment, and paving for a new solid waste transfer station facility and MRF. The existing
Codornices Creek landscaping (approximately 7,700 square feet) to the north of the existing fence
would remain.

The project proposes a two-building design with the transfer station building, truck scales, and
vehicle maintenance facility on the north portion of the site and the MRF building, City offices, and
public drop-off area on the south half of the site. Truck and trailer parking would be in the center of
the site, between the two main function areas. Bin repair and storage areas would be west of the
truck parking area, along the western property line. Also concentrated along the western property
line would be parking areas for the public and facility employees. The main truck entry would be at
the northwest corner of the project site.

Approximately 11,710 square feet (existing) of the northern portion of Second Street would be
repaved and redeveloped as the main truck entry, while maintaining public access to the driveway of
the adjacent property to the west and relocating the public vehicle turnaround area to south of its
existing location. This redevelopment would also include pedestrian walkways and replacement of
paving with ornamental species and transitional creek landscaping. This portion of Second Street
would remain as public right-of-way and would be an off-site improvement.

Project Objectives
The underlying purpose of the proposed project is to replace an outdated facility and optimize
existing infrastructure to meet the City’s Zero Waste and Climate Action Plan goals. The objectives of
the proposed project are to:

        • Provide new green infrastructure to meet the City’s Zero Waste climate goals. Support
             greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets per the City’s goals of becoming a fossil-
             fuel free city and achieving carbon neutrality by 2045.
        • Enhance operational efficiencies and model best practices in lower carbon emission
             operations.
        • Develop a facility that provides a maximum amount of space for the separation of materials,
             resulting in maximization of recovery and diversion of reusable and recyclable materials that
             would otherwise be transported to the landfill. including construction and demolition (C&D)
             waste.
        • Provide spaces for educational opportunities that will enhance the community’s effectiveness
             in a sustainable world.
        • Provide state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.

        • Integrate operations to provide customers with easy use and access for drop-off materials.


FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                           ES-3
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec00-03 Exec Summary.docx
                                                                     City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project

       • Incorporate design to facilitate future electrification of the collection fleet.

       • Improve on-site circulation and off-site circulation leading to the site entry.

       • Upgrade facilities to meet current seismic requirements.

       • Enhance existing open space by providing a publicly accessible walking path adjacent to
         Codornices Creek.
       • Contribute to the City’s open space through the addition of transitional creek landscaping.

       • Provide an enhanced facility layout that supports safe, efficient, and reliable long-term
         operation, including maintenance access, utility service, emergency response, and future
         infrastructure needs.


No Significant Unavoidable Adverse Impacts
The proposed project was analyzed for potentially significant impacts related to each of the
environmental topic areas discussed in Section 3.1, Aesthetics, through Section 3.15, Utilities and
Service Systems. The results of the analysis demonstrate that with identified mitigation the proposed
project would not result in any significant and unavoidable impacts.

Summary of Project Alternatives
As identified above, all impacts of the proposed project are less than significant or can be mitigated
to below a level of significance; therefore, the proposed project does not have any significant
unavoidable impacts. For discussion purposes, this Draft EIR presents a reasonable range of
potentially feasible alternatives to the proposed project for analysis and evaluation of their
comparative merits, pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6. Below is a summary of the
alternatives to the proposed project considered in Chapter 6, Alternatives to the Proposed Project.

Alternative 1–No Project, No Development Alternative
Under the No Project, No Development Alternative, the existing solid waste and recycling center
would not be redeveloped. Under this alternative, all buildings and paving on-site would remain and
the existing facility would remain in operation under current conditions. The proposed off-site
improvements would not occur, no transitional creek landscaping would be planted, and no pervious
pedestrian access path (referred to herein as Creek Walk) would be constructed (refer to Chapter 2,
Project Description, Exhibit 2-9a).

Alternative 2–One Building Alternative
This alternative would provide a singular large structure that would consolidate the functions of the
existing MRF, transfer station building, and equipment maintenance facility at the southern portion
of the project site and would locate truck parking and circulation areas at the northern portion of
the project site. An overall site plan is provided in Chapter 6, Alternatives to the Proposed Project,
Exhibit 6-1. This alternative would incorporate a transfer station building, dual-stream recyclables’
off-loading, sorting and baling area, and administrative offices. The proposed facility would include

EV charging infrastructure and solar panels, would be Leadership in Energy and Environmental
Design (LEED®) certified, and, similar to the proposed project, would also feature the Creek Walk.
This alternative would provide a creek buffer in order to protect the adjacent Codornices Creek.

Areas of Controversy
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15123(b), a summary section must address areas of
controversy known to the lead agency, including issues raised by agencies and the public, and it must
also address issues to be resolved, including the choice among alternatives and whether or how to
mitigate the significant effects.

A Notice of Preparation (NOP) for the proposed project was issued on August 31, 2023. The NOP
describing the original concept for the proposed project and issues to be addressed in the EIR was
distributed to the State Clearinghouse, responsible agencies, and other interested parties for a 30-
day public review period extending from August 31, 2023, through September 30, 2023. The NOP
identified the potential for significant impacts on the environment related to the following topical
areas:

        • Aesthetics                                                                                     • Hydrology and Water Quality
        • Air Quality                                                                                    • Land Use and Planning
        • Biological Resources                                                                           • Noise
        • Cultural Resources                                                                             • Public Services
        • Energy                                                                                         • Transportation
        • Geology and Soils                                                                              • Tribal Cultural Resources
        • Greenhouse Gas Emission                                                                        • Utilities and Service Systems
        • Hazards and Hazardous Materials


Potentially Controversial Issues
Below is a list of potentially controversial issues that may be raised during the public review and
hearing process of this Draft EIR:

        • Consistency with Zero Waste and Climate Action Plan Goals
        • Project design process
        • Hydrology and flooding impacts
        • Soil and groundwater quality
        • Sea level rise

It is also possible that evidence will be presented during the 45-day, statutory Draft EIR public review
period that may create disagreement. Decision-makers would consider this evidence during the
public hearing process.

Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                        Introduction




CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION
This Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) for the Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer
Stations Replacement Project (proposed project) has been prepared in accordance with—and
complies with—all criteria, standards, and procedures of the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA), as amended (Public Resources Code [PRC], § 21000, et seq.) and the CEQA Guidelines
(California Code of Regulations [CCR], Title 14, § 15000, et seq.). In accordance with California Public
Resources Code Section 21067, and Sections 15367 and 15050-15053 of the CEQA Guidelines, the
City of Berkeley (City) is the Lead Agency under whose authority this document has been prepared.
As an informational document, this Draft EIR is intended for use by the City and other public agency
decision-makers and members of the public in evaluating the potential environmental impacts of the
proposed project.

1.1 - Project Overview
The proposed project would merge six existing parcels into one; demolish the existing solid waste
transfer station and Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) on the project site, including buildings,
accessory structures, equipment, and paving; and replace the existing facility with new buildings,
accessory structures, equipment, and paving. Compared to the existing facilities and operations, the
new solid waste transfer station facility and MRF would include more sustainable operations and
would also improve circulation and access for the public and commercial operators.

The proposed project would preserve the riparian corridor along Codornices Creek, which is located
along the northern boundary of the project site (north of the existing fence line, see Chapter 2,
Project Description for additional details). The proposed project would remove the existing shrubs
and groundcover on the site (south of the existing fence line), while protecting trees that would not
conflict with proposed utilities, grading, stormwater treatment facilities, and architectural
improvements.

The project applicant proposes a two-building design with the transfer station building, truck scales,
and vehicle maintenance facility on the north portion of the site, and the MRF building, City offices,
and public drop-off area on the southern half of the site. Truck and trailer parking would be in the
center of the site, between the two main function areas. Bin repair and storage areas would be west
of the truck parking area, along the western property line. Also concentrated along the western
property line would be parking areas for the public and facility employees. The main truck entry
would be at the northwest corner of the project site.

Approximately 11,710 square feet (existing) of the northern portion of Second Street would be
repaved and redeveloped as the main truck entry, while maintaining public access to the driveway of
the adjacent property to the west and relocating the public vehicle turnaround area to south of its
existing location. This redevelopment would also include pedestrian walkways and replacement of
paving with ornamental and Creek landscape. This portion of Second Street would remain as public
right-of-way and would be an off-site improvement. Chapter 2, Project Description provides a
complete description of the proposed project.

1.2 - Environmental Review Process
An EIR is an informational document used by a lead agency (in this case, the City) when considering
approval of a project. The purpose of an EIR is to provide public agencies and members of the public
with detailed information regarding the environmental effects associated with implementing a
project. An EIR should analyze the environmental consequences of a project, identify ways to reduce
or avoid the project’s potential environmental effects, and identify alternatives to the project that
can avoid or reduce impacts. Pursuant to CEQA, State, and local government agencies must consider
the environmental consequences of projects over which they have discretionary authority. This EIR
provides information to be used in the planning and decision-making process. It is not the purpose
of an EIR to recommend approval or denial of a project.

Before approval of the proposed project, the City, as Lead Agency and the decision-making entity, is
required to certify that this EIR has been completed in compliance with CEQA, that the information
in the EIR has been considered, and that the EIR reflects the independent judgment of the City.
Pursuant to CEQA, decision-makers must balance the benefits of a project against its unavoidable
environmental consequences. If environmental impacts are identified as significant and unavoidable,
the City may still approve the project if it finds that social, economic, or other benefits outweigh the
unavoidable impacts. The City would then be required to state in writing the specific reasons for
approving the project, based on information in the EIR and other information sources in the
administrative record. This reasoning is called a “statement of overriding considerations” (PRC §
21081; CEQA Guidelines § 15093).

In addition, the City as Lead Agency must adopt a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program
(MMRP) describing the measures that were made a condition of project approval to avoid or
mitigate significant effects on the environment (PRC § 21081.6; CEQA Guidelines § 15097). The
MMRP is adopted at the time of project approval and is designed to ensure compliance with the
project description and EIR mitigation measures during and after project implementation. If the City
decides to approve the proposed project, it would be responsible for verifying that the MMRP for
this project is implemented. The EIR will be used primarily by the City during approval of future
discretionary actions and permits.

1.3 - Purpose and Legal Authority
1.3.1 - Purpose
This Draft EIR provides a project-level analysis of the environmental effects of the proposed project.
The environmental impacts of the proposed project are analyzed in the Draft EIR to the degree of
specificity appropriate, in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15146. This document addresses
the potentially significant adverse environmental impacts that may be associated with the planning,
construction, or operation of the proposed project. It also identifies appropriate and feasible
mitigation measures and alternatives that may be adopted to significantly reduce or avoid these
impacts.

CEQA requires that an EIR contain, at a minimum, certain specific components. These components
are contained in this Draft EIR and include:

        • Significant Unavoidable Adverse Impacts (if any)
        • Alternatives to the Proposed Project
        • Growth-Inducing Impacts
        • Effects Found not to be Significant
        • Areas of Known Controversy


1.3.2 - Lead Agency Determination
The City of Berkeley is designated as the Lead Agency for the proposed project. CEQA Guidelines
Section 15367 defines the lead agency as “. . . the public agency, which has the principal
responsibility for carrying out or approving a project.” Other public agencies may use this Draft EIR in
the decision-making or permit process and consider the information in this Draft EIR along with
other information that may be presented during the CEQA process.

This Draft EIR was prepared by FirstCarbon Solutions (FCS), an environmental consultant. Prior to public
review, it was extensively reviewed and evaluated by the City. This Draft EIR reflects the independent
judgment and analysis of the City of Berkeley as required by CEQA. Lists of organizations and persons
consulted and the report preparation personnel is provided in Chapter 7 of this EIR.

1.4 - Notice of Preparation and Public Scoping Process
In accordance with Sections 15063 and 15082 of the CEQA Guidelines, the City, as Lead Agency, sent
a Notice of Preparation (NOP) to responsible and trustee agencies and interested entities and
individuals on August 31, 2023, thus beginning the formal CEQA scoping process. The purpose of the
scoping process is to allow the public and government agencies to provide input on the scope of the
EIR. The scoping period began on August 31, 2023, and ended on September 30, 2023, representing
the statutory 30-day public review period. Five comment letters were received in response to the
NOP during the public review period. Two comments were received after the close of the 30-day
public scoping period, which ended on September 30, 2023. The City, as Lead Agency, has agreed to
accept the additional two letters and consider them as part of the preparation of this Draft EIR. The
NOP and comment letters are provided in Appendix A.

Pursuant to Section 15083 of the CEQA Guidelines, the NOP announced that the City would hold a
public scoping meeting on September 14, 2023 starting at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Standard Time (PST) via a
videoconference platform and in-person. At the meeting, attendees were given an opportunity to
provide comments and express concerns about the potential effects of the proposed project; one
public comment and three comments from zoning adjustment board members related to the EIR
were made during the public scoping meeting.

             topics that are addressed within Chapter 3 are as follows:
             - Section 3.1—Aesthetics: Addresses the potential visual impacts of redevelopment of the site
               and the overall increase in illumination (light and glare) produced by the proposed project.
             - Section 3.2—Air Quality: Addresses potential air quality impacts associated with project
               implementation and emissions of criteria pollutants. In addition, the section also evaluates
               project emissions of toxic air contaminants.
             - Section 3.3—Biological Resources: Addresses potential impacts on habitat, vegetation, and
               wildlife; the potential degradation or elimination of important habitat; and impacts on
               listed, proposed, and candidate threatened and endangered species.
             - Section 3.4—Cultural Resources: Addresses potential impacts on historical resources,
               archaeological resources, paleontological resources, and burial sites.
             - Section 3.5—Energy: Addresses potential project impacts related to energy usage.
             - Section 3.6—Geology and Soils: Addresses potential impacts the proposed project may
               have on soils and assesses the effects of project development in relation to geologic and
               seismic conditions. Also addresses potential impacts related to paleontological or unique
               geologic resources.
             - Section 3.7—Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Addresses potential project emissions of
               greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
             - Section 3.8—Hazards and Hazardous Materials: Addresses potential for presence of
               hazardous materials or conditions on the project site and in the vicinity of the project site
               that may have the potential to create a significant hazard to the public or the environment.
             - Section 3.9—Hydrology and Water Quality: Addresses the potential impacts of the
               proposed project on local hydrological conditions, including drainage areas, and changes in
               the flow rates, as well as the proposed project’s potential impacts to water quality, erosion,
               and groundwater supplies.
             - Section 3.10—Land Use and Planning: Addresses the potential land use impacts associated
               with division of an established community and consistency with relevant land use plans,
               policies and regulations adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental
               impact.
             - Section 3.11—Noise: Addresses potential noise impacts during construction and at project
               buildout from mobile and stationary sources. The section also addresses the impact of noise
               generation on neighboring uses.
             - Section 3.12—Public Services: Addresses potential impacts of the proposed project upon
               public services, including fire protection, law enforcement, schools, libraries, parks, and
               recreational facilities in terms of the need to provide new or physically alter facilities in
               order to maintain acceptable service ratios, response times, or other performance
               objectives.
             - Section 3.13—Transportation: Addresses potential impacts related to the local and regional
               roadway system with respect to Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) and public transportation,
               bicycle, and pedestrian access.

CHAPTER 2: PROJECT DESCRIPTION

2.1 - Overview
The City of Berkeley Public Works Department, Zero Waste Division (herein referred to as Zero Waste
Division or the project applicant) is proposing the Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station
Replacement Project (proposed project) on a 7.48-acre site in the City of Berkeley (City), Alameda
County (County). The City of Berkeley Public Works Department is the applicant, and the City of
Berkeley Planning Department serves as the Lead Agency for environmental review pursuant to the
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The proposed project is intended to replace the
current, outdated solid waste and recycling center with a modern, state-of-the-art facility.

The project site is located at 669 Gilman Street and at 1101, 1199–1231, 1201, and 1203 Second
Street and consists of six separate parcels (Assessor Parcel Numbers 60-2382-3-3, 60-2382-1-2, 60-
2382-3-1, 60-2362-1-9 and 60-2362-1-11, 60-2362-1-8, and 60-2362-1-10) with three separate City
contracted vendors (Ecology Center, Community Conservation Center, and Urban Ore) providing
collection or sorting operations. The project site is designated “M (Manufacturing)” by the City of
Berkeley General Plan (General Plan). The site is zoned “M (Manufacturing)” and is within the West
Berkeley Specific Plan (West Berkeley Plan) planning area.

The proposed project includes construction of two new buildings on the project site (one for the
proposed transfer station and vehicle maintenance activities and one for Materials Recovery Facility
[MRF] activities). The drop-off area would be reconfigured from existing conditions to include more
areas for unloading. The vehicle maintenance facility would be located directly south of the transfer
station building.

The proposed project would include demolition and removal of all existing structures and buildings,
concrete foundations, and other paved surfaces on the project site. The proposed project would also
remove the existing shrubs and groundcovers on the site (south of the existing fence line) while
protecting trees that would not be in conflict with proposed utilities, grading, stormwater treatment
facilities, and architectural improvements.

The purpose of this Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) is to identify potential
environmental impacts associated with construction and operation of the proposed project. This
section provides the proposed project location and setting, project objectives, project
characteristics, and construction phasing. It also describes the intended uses of the Draft EIR by
agencies with permitting and approval authority over the proposed project, as well as required
permits and approvals.

2.2 - Project Background
The City constructed and began operation of the existing solid waste transfer station in 1983.
Although it was originally conceived as a transfer station attached to a waste-to-energy incinerator,
the attached waste-to-energy incinerator was never constructed, and since 1983, the existing solid


FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                  2-1
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
                                                                            City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Project Description                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


waste transfer station currently operates only as a transfer station building and a separate recycling
center. After more than 35 years of operation, the transfer station and its operational facilities have
exceeded their service life and need replacement. In addition, the existing solid waste transfer
station and recyclable collection and sorting consists of three separate operations that are not
integrated. A new integrated facility to accept solid waste and recyclables is proposed to reach the
City’s stated Zero Waste Goal of sending zero waste to landfills. 1,2 The City is in the process of
preparing the Zero Waste Strategic Plan, which launched in January 2023, and will establish an
overarching framework and roadmap for reaching this goal. 3

On July 23, 2020, the City of Berkeley Zoning Adjustments Board approved Use Permit Modification
No. ZP2019-0077 and adopted an associated Initial Study/Negative Declaration (IS/ND) (State
Clearinghouse [SCH] No. 2020060134) 4 to increase the tonnage at the facility from 560 to 620 tons
per day. The Use Permit also expanded operating hours but did not change the availability hours for
general public access to the existing solid waste transfer station.

The City filed a Solid Waste Facility Permit (SWFP) application with the California Department of
Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) on January 11, 2021, to increase capacity at the
existing solid waste transfer station to 620 tons per day and change the hours of operation, as
provided in detail below. CalRecycle approved the SWFP on July 2, 2021 (Solid Waste Information
System [SWIS] No. 01-AC-0029).

2.3 - Project Location and Setting
2.3.1 - Location
Regional Location
The City is located in northern Alameda County. The City is bordered by the City of Albany and the
unincorporated Kensington neighborhood to the north, East Bay Regional Park District lands to the
east, North Oakland and Emeryville to the south, and Interstate 80 (I-80)/I-580 and the San Francisco
Bay to the west (Exhibit 2-1). The City covers 17.66 square miles. Major roadway networks, including
I-580, I-80, State Route (SR) 13, and SR-123 provide regional access to the City and surrounding areas.
The San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge provides a connection between Alameda and San Francisco
counties. The Richmond-San Rafael Bridge (I-580), which accommodates two westbound lanes on
the upper level and two to three eastbound lanes on the lower level, provides a connection between
Contra Costa and Alameda Counties and Marin County.

located within the Richmond, California United States Geological Survey (USGS) Oakland West 7.5-
minute Topographic Quadrangle Map Township 1S, Range 4W, Section 4 (Latitude 37o52’49.31”
North; Longitude 122o18’21.01” West). The site is currently accessed from Second Street and Gilman
Street.

Surrounding Land Uses
The project site is in an urbanized area surrounded primarily by industrial, commercial, and retail
uses. The site includes a stretch of Codornices Creek (Creek). The centerline of the Creek meanders
from 2.5 to 14 feet south of the site’s northern boundary, and the site also includes the southern
edge of the Creek’s riparian corridor. The Creek is part of the Codornices Watershed. 5 A Target store
with associated parking is to the north of the site, across Codornices Creek.

To the east of the project site is the Union Pacific Railroad/Amtrak right-of-way and tracks with an at-
grade crossing at Gilman Street, commercial 6 and industrial buildings (1- to 2-story), and Harrison
House Emergency Shelter.

Harrison Park (also known as Gabe Catalfo Fields) and the Berkeley Skate Park are east of the rail
lines. Both sites are actively used by the public.

To the west of the project site is Second Street, a self storage facility, an auto-body shop, industrial
and warehouse buildings (1- to 3-story), and an equipment rental agency. Just beyond the storage
facility and auto-body shop are Eastshore Highway and I-80/I-580. To the south of the project site is
Gilman Street, as well as industrial and retail buildings, including a building that was the former
Pacific Steel Castings (across Gilman Street to the south). I-80/I-580 is located approximately 400
feet west of the project site, and San Francisco Bay is located approximately 0.25 mile west of the
site.

2.3.2 - Existing Facilities and Operations
The solid waste transfer station is open to the public, receives on average 400-plus customers per
day, and is permitted by a CalRecycle SWFP to receive 620 tons per day of materials, including
refuse, green waste or plant debris and food waste, construction and demolition materials (SWIS No.
01-AC-0029), and miscellaneous recyclable materials. Table 2-1 provides a breakdown of materials
processed between 2017 and 2025. As shown in Table 2-1, the MRF currently accepts approximately
40–45 tons of recyclable material per day.

parcel provided an access bridge over Codornices Creek that was removed between 1990 and 2006.
The City is exploring various options, including acquiring the parcel from Target via purchase or
lease. For the purposes of the Draft EIR, the proposed project addresses the acquisition and
development of this parcel.

The project site is relatively flat (approximately 6 to 13 feet above mean sea level) with a slight
gradient descending toward the west. The project site is developed and is occupied by the existing
solid waste transfer station, which was originally constructed in 1983; a Compressed Natural Gas
(CNG) fueling station operated by Trillium, Inc., which is fenced and separated from the existing
transfer station operations; the MRF; and ancillary buildings to support both the solid waste transfer
station and MRF operations. Aside from the existing building footprints, the site is almost completely
paved with asphalt.

Scale House
The existing scale house is a prefabricated modular building, 32 feet by 10 feet (320 square feet) in
size, and consists of two rooms and a restroom. The weighmaster room has a large front window to
observe the tipping floor so vehicles can be directed to the proper area for unloading. Sliding doors
at each side provide weighmasters access to the entering and exiting vehicles. The building is
elevated on a curbed concrete foundation to prevent trucks from driving too close to the building
when they are weighed in and out. There are two 70-foot scales for inbound vehicles (one for non-
tare weight vehicles and one scale for collection trucks with registered scale house tare weights) and
one 70-foot scale for outbound vehicles.

Transfer Station and Tipping Floor Building
The existing transfer station and tipping floor building (existing transfer station) is a pre-engineered
metal building (PEMB) with metal roof deck and metal siding. A top load tunnel is located at the west
end of the building. The existing tipping floor is constructed with reinforced concrete slab-on-grade.
The existing transfer station building consists of an uncovered concrete apron on the north and east
sides and a covered building with metal frame structure, metal sides, and metal roof. The east side
apron area is for vehicle maneuvering into the covered tipping floor area, and the north side is for
the staging of construction and demolition (C&D) debris awaiting transport to a third-party
contracted sorting facility. The roofed area is 150 feet by 155 feet and the interior floor dimensions
are 140 feet by 150 feet.

Vehicle access to the tipping floor is provided for unloading both third-party vehicles and City
collection trucks. The dumping pit is located in the southwest corner of the building and is bordered
on two sides by converging pushwalls and on the back by a steel splash plate to minimize debris
spillage as the front-end wheel loader pushes the waste into the pit and the waiting transfer trailer. A
digital read-out indicates to the wheel loader operator the weights of the loads on the trailer and
truck axles. The building’s tipping floor is equipped with misters to suppress dust.

Storage Shed
The existing storage shed is a PEMB with a metal roof and siding along three sides (the west side is
open). The floor is constructed with reinforced concrete slab-on-grade. It is isolated from the main
facility and is generally used for storage of cathode ray tubes, fluorescent bulbs, and batteries. Used
oil, cylinders, and other prohibited wastes are stored on pallets and in drums or other storage
containers in the hazardous materials lockers (described in more detail below).

Construction and Demolition Debris Handling Area
The area immediately north of the existing transfer station building is used for unloading,
segregating, and temporary storage of C&D debris awaiting transfer to a processing facility for
sorting and recovery. These materials include, but are not limited to, clean wood, painted wood,
concrete, drywall, dirt, plastic, toilets, and bathtubs.

Recycling Materials Container/Areas
These are additional areas or containers located south of the existing transfer station building and
used for segregation and temporary storage of scrap metal, tires, mattresses, and carpet. Additional
or fewer containers or areas for other diverted materials are included on the site as needed.

Administration Buildings
Administration Building 1
The existing Administration Building 1 is a modular building with metal roof and metal siding. It
consists of six private offices, a common office area, an employee lunchroom/large assembly room,
and restrooms. The existing Administration Building 1 houses the office of the Solid Waste and
Recycling Operations Manager and operations supervisory and clerical staff.




FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-27
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
                                                                            City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Project Description                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


Administration Building 2 (AirCo Building)
The existing Administration Building 2 (AirCo Building) consists of three areas: (1) Solid Waste &
Recycling and Recycling Program managers, field representatives, safety officer, and environmental
compliance offices; (2) container shop and office; and (3) canopy area. Bins and carts are repaired in
the canopy area, which is covered to protect employees and their tools from the weather; 220-volt
ac power is supplied for welding equipment. The office and shops are constructed with pre-cast wall
panels, steel girders, wood purlins, and plywood diaphragm. The canopy is a PEMB. The floor is
reinforced concrete slab-on-grade.

Equipment Maintenance Building
The existing equipment maintenance building includes two side-by-side PEMBs with reinforced
concrete slab-on-grade. There are four maintenance bays. Two bays provide drive-through capability
for oversized vehicles, and two are open on the south end of the building, each with high overhead
clearance. This is sufficient to provide a dry working area for the transfer trailer rigs and other
equipment. Additionally, there is an office, break room, restrooms, and a parts storage room on the
second level.

Fuel Station
An island is located in the transfer trailer queueing and maintenance area. Previously, there were
two manifold fiberglass underground storage tanks (USTs) which each contained a 10,000-gallon
diesel tank. The USTs are permanently closed as of November 14, 2025, 10 and were removed in
December 2025 along with the associated underground pipes, nozzles, and dispenser.

Truck and Bin Wash Rack
The existing wash rack consists of a curbed concrete slab 70 feet long by 18 feet wide, and the
corners slope down to a grate-covered drain. On both 70-foot sides of the pad, 8-foot-high catwalks
run the entire length, enabling personnel to wash all areas of their vehicles from ground level or
from the elevated catwalk. There are two independent high-pressure washers installed below the
catwalk (one for each side), incorporating a cleaning wand on approximately 50 feet of heavy-duty
rubber hose; stowing brackets for the cleaning wands are mounted on the catwalks. Detergent
addition capability is contained within the units.

Used Oil Recycling Depot
The existing used oil recycling depot is a wood-framed canopy. The floor is constructed with
reinforced concrete slab-on-grade. A 1,000-gallon, double-walled, aboveground UL-rated tank is
installed just north of the scale house. It is intended for private citizens who service their own
personal vehicles and other engine-operated equipment. No commercial companies’ used oil is
accepted. The tank is enclosed in a secondary concrete containment; a safety drain valve system
provides additional physical protection for the depot.

Hazardous Materials Storage
The existing prefabricated hazardous materials storage locker is located next to the existing used oil
recycling depot. The building incorporates standard security and fire protection measures; eye/face
wash unit; dry chemical suppression system; explosion proof lighting, secondary containment, and
explosion relief construction. It is used to store illegally disposed of hazardous materials that are
pulled from the tipping floor. The facility is permitted and inspected under the City of Berkeley
Hazardous Material Business Plan.

Materials Recovery Facility
The existing MRF is a PEMB with metal roof and siding on three sides. The floor is constructed with
reinforced concrete slab-on-grade. The existing MRF is where recyclable materials are collected from
the residential and commercial sectors and are sorted by materials type, baled, and shipped off-site
to be recycled into products to be used again. The MRF is operated by Community Conservations
Centers, Inc. under a contract with the City.

Ecology Center
The existing Ecology Center provides residential curbside collection services and provides parking for
their eight collection trucks that collect residential curbside materials under contract to the City. The
Ecology Center is sited on City-owned land and office space is provided within a double wide
modular building with wood siding.

Buyback Center
The existing Buyback Center is a modular building with wood siding. This is where the general public
can come to exchange California Redemption Value (CRV) containers such as cans, glass bottles and
jars, and plastic bottles for their monetary value. The Buyback Center is operated by Community
Conservations Centers, Inc. under contract with the City.

Electrical Power and Telephone Lines
Electrical power and telephone lines are located on overhead poles. An overhead line crosses the
site parallel to Harrison Street in an east/west direction (at the existing scale house).

Stormwater Infrastructure
Any storm drain debris or non-industrial liquid sludge materials that are delivered to the existing
solid waste transfer station are off-loaded separately from solid wastes into the dewatering area
located in the northeast corner of the roofed section of the existing transfer station building. The
storm debris water drains to a trench drain that conveys it to the existing solid waste transfer
station’s sewer system. The remaining material is off-loaded into the municipal solid waste for
landfilling. The debris is allowed to gravity drain until the material is dry enough to mix into the solid
waste in the existing transfer station building.

Existing Operations
Information in this section is based, in part, on the Processing Report, 11 the City of Berkeley Transfer
Station Solid Waste Facilities Permit Revision Project Initial Study/Negative Declaration (IS/ND), 12
and the Feasibility Study, which are provided in Appendix B. The City-owned facility opened in 1983
and was operated by Browning Ferris Industries, Inc. (BFI) from 1983-1985 under contract with the
City. The project applicant has operated the facility since August 1, 1985. The recycling operation was
added to the facility in the late 1980s.

The existing solid waste transfer station complex is managed by the project applicant, which employs
over 90 people and utilizes 83 vehicles, including long haul tractor/transfer trailers and the City’s
collection fleet.

The project applicant provides residents (23,000-plus customers) and businesses (4,500-plus
customers) in Berkeley with (1) residential and commercial refuse and compost collection service
and (2) commercial collection recycling program which collects recyclables from commercial
establishments throughout the City (including multi-family housing with 10 or more units as well as
businesses). Together, the programs collect refuse, recyclables, and green/food waste materials.

The facility provides operations yards and buildings for the following: (1) Ecology Center, which
operates the City’s residential curbside collection recycling program for single- and multi-family
housing (up to nine units) and 2) the Community Conservation Centers, Inc. (CCC), which operates
the City’s “Berkeley Recycling” and includes public drop-off of recyclables, CRV, a universal waste
material drop-off center, and a MRF to sort and market all recyclables delivered to the facility as part
of the City’s and Ecology Center’s curbside recycling collection program. Reuse salvage collection is
operated by and currently contracted with Urban Ore, which operates a salvage and diversion
program for reusable goods delivered to the floor of the existing transfer station building.

Exhibit 2-6 depicts the flow of materials for the transfer station. The following provides details about
the transfer station, the Ecology Center and the MRF, by address:

Existing Hours of Operation
Transfer Station-Public
The current CalRecycle permit allows for general public access from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. seven
days a week. However, the existing solid waste transfer station is open to the public to drop-off
waste materials 6 days a week (Monday through Saturday) from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The facility
operates every day except Sundays, July 4, Thanksgiving Day (fourth Thursday of November),
Christmas Day (December 25), and New Year’s Day (January 1).

Transfer Station-Commercial Haulers
The on-site operation and off-site hauling of materials hours are Monday through Friday from 3:00
a.m. to 9:30 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday (if needed) from 3:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

2.3.3 - Existing Land Use Designation and Zoning
Land Use Designations
The General Plan designates the site as “M (Manufacturing)” which is intended to maintain and
preserve areas of the City for manufacturing and industrial uses (Exhibit 2-7a). 13

The West Berkeley Plan designates the site as Manufacturing (Exhibit 2-7b). 14 This land use is largely
west of the railroad tracks and allows intensive, manufacturing uses as well as light industrial uses. 15
It does not allow residential, live-work, retail, or office uses and is meant to be a protected
manufacturing district. 16

Zoning
The site is located within the Manufacturing (M) zoning district and is not part of any zoning overlays
(Exhibit 2-8). 17 Within these areas there is a maximum floor area ratio (FAR) of 2 and a maximum
building height of 45 feet. The purpose of the M zoning district is to implement the West Berkeley
Plan’s Manufacturing designation and to encourage development of a general manufacturing district
for the full range of manufacturers, including larger scale materials processing manufacturers
sometimes known as heavy manufacturers; encourage the development of a manufacturing district
dedicated to manufacturing and industrial uses; and support the development of industrial
businesses which contribute to the maintenance and improvement of the environment. Some
allowable uses include those such as light manufacturing, dry cleaning, warehouse, warehouse-
based non-store retail, recycled materials processing, art/craft studio, commercial uses, and
contractor uses. The proposed project would not change the site’s land use designation or zoning.

2.4 - Project Objectives
The underlying purpose of the proposed project is to replace an outdated facility and optimize
existing infrastructure to meet the City’s Zero Waste and Climate Action Plan goals. The objectives of
the proposed project are to:

        • Provide new green infrastructure to meet the City’s Zero Waste and climate goals. Support
             greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets per the City’s goals of becoming a fossil-
             fuel free city and achieving carbon neutrality by 2045.
        • Enhance operational efficiencies and model best practices in lower carbon emission
             operations.
        • Develop a facility that provides a maximum amount of space for the separation of materials,
             resulting in maximization of recovery and diversion of reusable and recyclable materials that
             would otherwise be transported to the landfill including C&D waste.
        • Provide spaces for educational opportunities that will enhance the community’s effectiveness
             in a sustainable world.
        • Provide state-of-the-art, well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities.

        • Integrate operations to provide customers with easy use and access for drop-off materials.

        • Incorporate design to facilitate future electrification of the collection fleet.

        • Improve on-site circulation and off-site circulation leading to the site entry.

        • Upgrade facilities to meet current seismic requirements.

        • Enhancing existing open space by providing a publicly accessible walking path adjacent to
             Codornices Creek.
        • Contribute to the City’s open space through the addition of transitional creek landscaping.

        • Provide an enhanced facility layout that supports safe, efficient, and reliable long-term
             operation, including maintenance access, utility service, emergency response, and future
             infrastructure needs.


2.5 - Project Characteristics
The proposed project would involve the replacement of the existing solid waste transfer station with
a proposed facility that is designed to enhance recycling and solid waste operations, address on-site
traffic flow, serve existing and future needs of the local community, and replace outdated buildings.
All existing buildings, concrete foundations, and other paved surfaces would be demolished and
removed from the project site. The proposed project would also remove the existing shrubs and
groundcovers on the site while protecting trees that would not conflict with proposed utilities, grading,
stormwater treatment facilities, and architectural improvements. As part of the permitting process,
the proposed project would apply for a lot line adjustment and the six parcels would be merged into
one parcel.



FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-41
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx

It is conservatively assumed that the proposed project would include removing 40,000 cubic yards of
soil and filling 1,500 cubic yards of soil. A total net of 38,500 cubic yards of soil would be exported from
the project site.

The current SWFP is assigned to APNs 60-2362-1-9, 60-2362-11, 60-2382-1-2, and 60-2382-3-3 and
covers the existing 4.68-acre transfer station operation (Exhibit 2-4). The Zero Waste Division is
coordinating with CalRecycle and the Local Enforcement Agency (LEA) to update permit records to
reflect the proposed parcel merger. The SWFP would continue to apply to the existing transfer
station operations and associated permitted area.

Based on consultation with the LEA, the proposed Materials Recovery Facility (MRF), which would be
constructed as a separate facility, would operate separately from the permitted transfer station and
would not be incorporated into the SWFP. Accordingly, the existing SWFP would remain limited to
the current transfer station operations and associated permitted area and would not be expanded to
include the proposed MRF. The MRF would be described as part of the overall facility operations but
would not be subject to regulation under the existing SWFP.

The proposed solid waste transfer facility would operate in accordance with the current SWFP (once
revised to reflect the proposed lot line adjustment) and does not propose any further increase of
tonnage or expansion of hours of operation at the proposed facility beyond what is allowed under
the current permit.

The hours of operation for the MRF would not change. Following the implementation of the
proposed project, the City does not anticipate any increase in volume of materials, although given
efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed MRF would be capable of processing an
average of 80–130 tons of recyclable material per day (an increase of up to 85 tons per day). The
increase in capacity relates to the enhancement of the facility with components such as laser sorters,
magnets to separate metals, and fans to separate paper, all of which would allow for more efficient
processing. As the enhanced processing relates entirely to mechanical components, the increase in
potential throughput would not require any increase in employees.

The City and Zero Waste Division will continue to promote diversion of waste materials in
accordance with local and State Law such that an increased amount of material coming into the
project site is expected to be processed at the MRF rather than the transfer station portion of the
facility. Accordingly, the number of vehicle trips entering the facility to deliver material generated
within the City is not expected to increase substantially.

The increase related to diversion of existing throughput from the transfer station to the MRF is not
expected to reach the maximum throughput capacity of 130 tons per day, even looking out into the
future. Nevertheless, this analysis conservatively assumes the maximum increase in order to study a
worst-case scenario (referred to as the “future maximum operating capacity”).

Given the expected total increase in capacity of 85 tons per day, and the anticipated use of
commercial trucks for delivery of materials at a rate of 7 tons per truck, the future maximum
operating capacity would result in an estimated 12 trips per day above existing conditions if the

facility were to operate at its maximum future capacity of 130 tons per day. Since the site operates

about 1.5 additional trucks per hour, which would be within the daily fluctuation in truck traffic
during typical operations at the site and on the adjacent streets. Therefore, the additional trucks

Overview–Project Description
Information in this section is based, in part, on the Feasibility Study. 18 Minor updates to the detailed
project plans included in the Feasibility Study are included in Appendix B.

A site plan is provided in Exhibit 2-9a; Exhibit 2-9b provides detail on the site plan with respect to the
Creek. Exhibit 2-10 depicts the proposed circulation through the site. Table 2-4 provides details
about the components for the proposed project.

The proposed project would merge the six parcels into one; demolish the existing solid waste
transfer station and MRF on the project site, including buildings, accessory structures, equipment,
and paving; and construct new buildings, accessory structures, equipment, and paving for a new
solid waste transfer station facility and MRF. The proposed project would remove the existing shrubs
and groundcover on the site while protecting trees that would not conflict with proposed utilities,
grading, stormwater treatment facilities, and architectural improvements. As discussed in greater
detail in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, preliminarily, all trees within the riparian corridor (14
trees) would be preserved while trees located outside of the riparian corridor (46 trees) would be
removed. The existing Codornices Creek landscaping (approximately 7,700 square feet) to the north
of the existing fence would remain.

The project proposes a two-building design with the transfer station building, truck scales, and
vehicle maintenance facility on the north portion of the site and the MRF building, City offices, and
public drop-off area on the south half of the site. Truck and trailer parking would be in the center of
the site, between the two main function areas. Bin repair and storage areas would be west of the
truck parking area, along the western property line. Also concentrated along the western property
line would be parking areas for the public and facility employees. The main truck entry would be at
the northwest corner of the project site.

Approximately 11,710 square feet (existing) of the northern portion of Second Street would be
repaved and redeveloped as the main truck entry while maintaining public access to the driveway of
the adjacent property to the west and relocating the public vehicle turnaround area south of its
existing location; see Section 2.5.3, Circulation and Access, for additional detail. This redevelopment
would also include pedestrian walkways and replacement of paving with ornamental species and
transitional creek landscaping. This portion of Second Street would remain as a public right-of-way
and would be an off-site improvement.
