Public Buyback and Drop-off Center (Public Recycling Center)
The proposed Public Recycling Center (including the public CRV buyback area and the free recycle
drop-off area) would anchor the southern portion of the site. The Gilman Street frontage would be
shared with the proposed MRF structure, and the Public Recycling Center would be located adjacent
to the western side of the MRF facing Second Street. The public entrance would be located along
Second Street in the southwestern portion of the project site. The Public Recycling Center is planned
as a one-way drive with parking on the right and bins on the left. Once parked, customers would
have access to both the free recycle drop-off, the public buyback area, and the cashier.


FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-51
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
                                                                            City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Project Description                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


The Public Recycling Center would provide covered parking spaces with steel-framed canopies
embedded with photovoltaic (PV) glass that would provide weather protection. These canopies
would include large signage for easy identification for type of material collected; these signs would
be movable to provide flexibility for reorganizing the bin areas.

The Public Recycling Center would be fenced. The project applicant anticipates that security fencing
would be a combination of masonry walls and decorative fencing that would be fabricated from
recycled construction materials (e.g., steel rebar, angle, and sheeting by local artisans). However,
fencing materials are unknown at this time.

Public Buyback Area
The public CRV buyback area would provide an area for customers to turn in their buyback items; it
would be located on the south end of the free recycling drop-off area. A cashier would be located at
the center of this area for transactions and Zero Waste Division staff would be available to answer
questions.

Free Recycle Drop-off Area
The free recycle drop-off area would be located at a center island, would be canopied, and would
include bins and/or carts for the collection of paper, plastic, glass, metals, clothing/textiles, and
books. This line of bins and/or carts would have a staff aisle behind the bins for carting and
forklifting collected materials to the sorting area parallel to the proposed MRF building.

Universal Waste Drop-off Area
The universal waste drop-off area would be located adjacent to the cashier operations office at the
south end of the site, adjacent to the one-way (right turn) exit to Gilman Street; it would accept
limited quantities of oils, paints, batteries, e-waste, and fluorescent tubes. It would be within direct
line of site of the cashier operations office and information kiosk.

Walk-in Service
Pedestrian access would be provided through an entrance at the northeast corner of the Gilman and
Second Street intersection. This entrance would be opened during business hours and connect
directly to the cashier and public buyback area. Security fencing would be a combination of masonry
walls and decorative fencing that could be fabricated from recycled construction materials (e.g., steel
rebar).

Return Circulation
Exiting the free recycle drop-off area to westbound Gilman Street, customers would have an
opportunity to turn right (north) on Second Street to return to the Public Recycling Center or
continue to the public scale main entry at the north end of Second Street. Customers with other
materials such as bulky items (e.g., furniture, appliances, mattresses, carpet, tires, etc.), C&D
materials, yard waste, or refuse would also proceed directly down Second Street to the main entry
gate at the end of the street.




2-52                                                                                                                                                                     FirstCarbon Solutions
                      https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


Information Kiosk
The information kiosk would be located at the entrance to the Public Recycling Center, which is
where most of the customer activities would take place. It would be a small gatehouse structure and
would provide a waystation for addressing customer questions, and it would provide customers with
a variety of information including: (1) rates and how to use the facility, (2) recycling tips to better
prepare the user for their next visit, and (3) community recycling events.

Materials Recovery Facility
The proposed MRF would be a fully enclosed 35,000-square-foot structure dedicated to the
processing of recyclables and the temporary staging of recovered materials for shipping to
commodity markets. This building would have multiple large overhead doors facing the east side of
the facility providing access to recyclables collection trucks. Recyclable collection trucks would weigh
in at the RFID scale located near the doors. The trucks would be able to maneuver to this RFID scale
several times as needed. The trucks would unload in three tip floor areas: (1) paper (fiber), (2)
containers (bottles and cans), and (3) clean cardboard and commerical mixed paper. A front-end
wheel loader would move the material to three separate infeed conveyors for paper, containers, or
direct to a baler.

The southern portion of the MRF would have four bunkers for glass (green, brown, clear, and three-
color mix). A forklift aisle would provide access to the bunker for removal of the glass. This area of
the building would have a temporary staging area for baled materials which would open to a two-
bay shipping dock. Adjacent to this area on the west wall would be a 12-foot by 14-foot overhead
door that would provide access to the public buyback and free recycle drop-off areas where
collected items could be consolidated.

The west wall of the MRF would have overhead doors, which would provide interor areas for the
collection of smaller bins and totes from the free recycle drop-off area as needed. These doors
would also serve as maintenace access for service of the equipment and removal of equipment
components when needed.

Transfer Station
The proposed 45,500-square-foot transfer station building would be a separate and fully enclosed
space providing a large open floor area for the varied types of material arriving and would provide
multiple opportunities for the separation of materials for reuse. The floor area would have a large
tipping floor space that would include nine interior bays which could be organized based on need.
Overhead doors would be 18 feet wide by 25 feet high with fast roll up and down doors with
proximity sensors to control air flows and odor migration and any fugitive dust. The proximity
sensors would open a door when a vehicle approaches and, as such, would control the air flow
because doors would remain closed until needed to access the transfer station.

In addition to assistance from floor staff such as a “spotter,” public access would be enhanced with
large wayfinding graphics (e.g., numbered stations color coded for direction). The south bays would
be used by commercial collection trucks as needed and could be separated from the public with
movable vehicle barriers. The public tipping floor area would be on the northern half of the building

FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-53
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
                                                                            City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Project Description                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


approximately 150 feet deep (east–west direction) by 125 feet long (north–south direction). On low-
to-moderate volume days, this depth could provide sufficient interior maneuvering area for cars and
pickups with only two (as opposed to four) doors for access. After unloading, customers would
return to the north side and the two exit scales at the proposed scale house to complete the
transaction. An additional area at the north side of the floor area would provide space for material
separation or staging for loadout or shipping (approximately 60 feet deep by 40 feet long).

When commercial collection trucks are not active (e.g., weekend vs. weekday schedules), self-haul
customers could use the additional access doors and tip floor area at the south end of the building.
The commercial side of the transfer station floor at the south end of the structure would have an
area of approximately 150 feet deep (east–west direction) by 100 feet long. The receiving floor
would be designed to accommodate delivery of materials from various types of collection vehicles,
including front end, side, and rear-end loaders and roll-off trucks.

Bulky Item Drop-off Area
The first bay at the north end of the floor area is a dedicated area for the public to unload larger
items such as appliances, mattresses, carpet, tires, etc. This area would have direct access to a two-
bay loading dock area. This interior area would also offer space for roll-off boxes or shipping
containers which could be picked up when loaded.

Salvage Items
At the main entry public scale house, a customer may offer (or the scale operator may identify)
salvageable items. With direction from the scale operator, the customer would proceed to the first
station at the north end of the proposed transfer station building where salvage reusable items
would be collected and stored in transportable boxes or placed directly into a trailer.

Loadout/Transfer Areas
Tractor trailer trucks would remove refuse and transport it to the landfill. These trucks would access
the site at “staff-only” driveway at Second Street across from the Harrison Street intersection. Once
on-site, a transfer truck and trailer would use one of the two loadout positions at the west side of
the Transfer Station. The transfer of material from the tipping floor to a trailer for delivery to an off-
site facility(ies) would be accomplished by a wheel loader lifting the material into the trailer that
would be located in a reduced-depth loadout tunnel. The grade of the loadout tunnel floor would be
approximately 4 feet to 8 feet below the tipping floor grade. The trailer would be under a three-
sided steel backboard hopper to conduct material into the trailer. The trailer would be subsequently
tarped prior to leaving the site. Trucks would leave the site via the Second Street driveways and use
Harrison Street to I-80/I-580.

The tip floor would have a zoned misting system which would control dust in active areas of material
consolidation and loading.

Bin Repair Facility
Located to the south of the proposed vehicle maintenance building, this canopied area would
provide weather protection for bin repair activities. The bin repair facility would also have storage

2-54                                                                                                                                                                     FirstCarbon Solutions
                      https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


capacity and would have a 10-foot-tall security wall that would screen the facility from the public in
the queue line for the main scales.

Main Public Entry and Scale Facility
The proposed scale facility would be located at the north end of the site, which would provide
optimal queueing capacity. At the main gate, a digital display is proposed that could provide wait
time information, which may encourage customers to try another time, thereby leveling out
demand.

The proposed scale house would provide counter space for two weighmaster staff for inbound and
outbound traffic. A separate staff support structure would be within 30 feet of the scale house,
located within the north side of the proposed transfer station building. Two 70-foot scales at
inbound lanes and two 70-foot scales at outbound lanes would be installed in pits level with the
adjacent road surface grade. Stop/go signals would be placed in front of the scales in both
directions. Rates and rules signage would be placed in the median on the approach.

Vehicle Maintenance Facility, Truck Wash, and Truck Parking
The proposed vehicle maintenance facility would provide six 20-foot-wide by 50-foot-deep truck
service bays with 22-foot height clearance.

Interior lighting would be high bay light-emitting diode (LED)-style light fixtures. Translucent wall
panels over each door would provide daylighting. Equipment inside the facility would include
pneumatic wrenches, tire changing equipment, floor-mounted lifts, jib cranes, carbon monoxide
systems, diagnostic equipment, etc.

A lobby stair and elevator would provide access to the second floor, which would include
administrative offices, staff restrooms, and lockers. A through-floor lift is proposed for supplying the
service bays with larger items such as tires, etc. The second level would also include a compressor
room to serve pneumatic systems at ground level service bays. This room would have floor vibration
isolation and exterior wall sound control louvers.

Truck Parking
The truck parking area, adjacent and to the south of the proposed vehicle maintenance facility,
would provide 44 spaces for collection-type trucks and nine spaces for semi-tractor trailer trucks.
The garbage truck fleet parking would be serviced by electric charging stations in compliance with
the most up-to-date regulations. The fueling area, with separate stations for renewable diesel and
CNG, would be located on the east side of the truck parking area.

Truck Wash
A truck wash structure would be located at the east side of the proposed vehicle maintenance
facility. The truck wash area would have a single 25-foot by 80-foot bay for larger trucks (65-foot
semi-tractor trailer trucks) and would be accessed from the north end of the structure.




FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-55
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
                                                                            City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Project Description                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


Administrative/Employee Support Area
A 3-story structure would be located at the north end of the proposed MRF structure, providing
consolidated office and staff support for the City and City contractors. Administrative office space
would be provided for two City contractors on the second floor. Each suite would have matched
spaces, including two enclosed offices, four workstations, one receptionist, a meeting/breakroom
and copy area, and a visitor wait area. On the ground floor, the City contractors would have separate
staff support accommodations that would include restroom/locker areas as well as break rooms that
could be used for informal training activities.

Employee parking would be provided along Second Street, in the same general location as existing
parking.

Parking
Vehicle Parking
Parking is not included as an environmental issue under California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Guidelines. However, a parking supply analysis during operation is provided in the Transportation
Analysis prepared by Fehr & Peers.

Based on the analysis provided in the Transportation Analysis, the maximum observed existing
parking demand at the site is 24 vehicles. The proposed project would provide 21 public spaces for
customers in a parking lot at the southwest corner of the project site and 14 employee spaces in a
parking lot just north of the customer parking lot (see Exhibit 2-9a).

Municipal Code Section 23.322.030(C)(3)(a) provides that the Zoning Officer or Zoning Adjustment
Board shall determine required parking for categories shown in Table 23.206-1, Allowed Uses in
Manufacturing Districts, “based on the amount of traffic generated by the use and the number of
spaces required [by] other similar uses.” As described in the Transportation Analysis, the maximum
observed existing parking demand at the site is 24 vehicles, which is below the proposed 35 parking
spaces. Since the employment and activity levels after completion of the proposed project are
expected to remain similar to existing conditions, the parking demand at the site is expected to
remain similar to existing conditions, and, therefore, the proposed 35 spaces would be able to
accommodate the parking demand at the site once the proposed project is completed.

Bicycle Parking
Municipal Code Section 23.322-10 090(A)(1)) requires one bicycle parking space per 2,000 square
feet of new floor area for nonresidential buildings, and the bicycle parking can be either long-term or
short-term. Therefore, the number of spaces proposed would meet the bicycle parking
requirements.

2.5.1 - Phasing and Construction
For the purposes of this EIR, the construction of the proposed project was modeled to account for a
construction schedule of 15 months and was based on information available at the time of the



2-56                                                                                                                                                                     FirstCarbon Solutions
                      https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


analysis. Construction is proposed to be in eight phases, each including several activities. 19 Note that
while modeling is based on 15 months, actual construction is estimated to be completed in 5 years.
Final sequencing is subject to review by the City’s contracted Construction Manager and
collaboration with the selected General Contractor. It is anticipated that the existing solid waste
transfer facility would be operational during construction and that solid waste would be handled and
stored on-site during construction.

The proposed MRF footprint overlays the existing MRF, which would require the City to divert
material to other processing facilities for an estimated 15 months. The 15-month modeling period
reflects the assumed duration of the most intensive construction and diversion activities and was
used to evaluate a conservative worst-case scenario. The anticipated 5-year construction schedule
reflects the broader phased implementation period needed to maintain facility operations during
construction; therefore, it is longer than the period modeled for peak construction-related impacts.

Because the proposed project would require the City to divert materials to other processing facilities
during construction, the proposed project includes preparation of a diversion plan that would
maintain uninterrupted collection and processing services for Berkeley customers and ensure that
materials continue to be managed at appropriately permitted facilities throughout the construction
period to the greatest extent feasible. Potential operational strategies during construction may
include a combination of phased construction, temporary on-site operations, temporary relocation
of specific activities within the property, and diversion of materials to permitted regional processing
and disposal facilities. Although diversion of all materials is unlikely for the entire construction
period, to be conservative the analysis in the Draft EIR assumes full diversion of all materials for the
15-month construction period.

Facilities with sufficient capacity that are available to accept diverted materials are identified in
Section 3.15, Utilities and Service Systems. These include the Davis Street Transfer Station in San
Leandro (approximately 16 miles from the project site) and the Golden Bear Transfer Station in
Richmond (approximately 10 miles from the project site) which are the nearest facilities currently
accepting municipal solid waste (MSW) and compostable materials. For public drop-off of recyclable
materials, the closest facility is located in El Cerrito (approximately 4.6 miles from the project site).
The specific facilities utilized, material streams diverted, and duration of any diversions will depend
on the final construction phasing plan, contractor requirements, facility availability, and regulatory
considerations. Once the proposed project is in the design phase, the Zero Waste Division will issue a
Request for Proposals (RFP) to processing facilities in the area to solicit proposals for receiving
materials during the construction of the proposed project (see further discussion in Section 3.15,
Utilities and Service Systems).

Upon completion of construction, operations would return to the Berkeley Transfer Station. No
permanent changes to waste generation, fleet size, service area, employment, or collection
frequency are proposed.

2.5.2 - Codornices Creek
The centerline of the Creek meanders from 2.5 to 14 feet south of the site’s northern boundary, and
the site also includes the southern edge of the Creek’s riparian corridor (Exhibit 2-3). In accordance
with the City of Berkeley Creek Ordinance (Creek Ordinance) Section 17.08.053 of the City’s
Municipal Code, as part of a natural environment restoration strategy, the proposed project would
maintain a minimum 30-foot buffer from the centerline of the Creek. The buffer area would be
delineated with a berm located along the northerly curb of the scale facility and planted with native
grasses and shrubs consistent with what currently exists within the Creek. Because the proposed
project includes a setback in compliance with the Creek Ordinance that would be graded at or below
the existing site grade, the overbank storage volume would be improved compared to existing
conditions. The plantings here would feature native riparian species, such as willow, sedges, etc. The
buffer would be modestly sloped up away from the Creek flowline.

The nearest paving would be approximately 37 feet south of the centerline of the Creek, and the
landscaping to be provided to the south of the existing fence would be approximately 11 feet from
the centerline of the Creek at its nearest point (Exhibit 2-9b).

Sharing the main public entry would be a pervious pedestrian access path (referred to herein as
Creek Walk) that would have a low wall separating the walkway from the vehicle lane, which would
be approximately 46 feet south of the centerline of the Creek at its nearest point (Exhibits 2-9a and
2-9b). The Creek Walk would be made of permeable pavement and would be approximately 5 feet
wide and 95 feet long. The Creek Walk would lead to a small respite (seating) area at the site’s
northwestern corner that would be approximately 20-feet long with a 22-foot, 7-inch wide northern
end and a 12-foot, 3-inch wide southern end that would feature an information podium display on
Bay Area watershed.

Additional information about the Creek and potential environmental impacts is provided in Section
3.3, Biological Resources.

Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


2.5.3 - Circulation and Access
Vehicle
Second Street would serve as the main point of ingress and egress for the site. The one-way (south
to north) direction of Second Street on the southern portion between Gilman Street and Harrison
Street would provide some basic rules for accessing the site.

The types of public and commercial traffic accessing the site are not anticipated to change from
existing conditions.

Site access and roadways would be designed for self-haul vehicles with trailers, residential and
commercial collection trucks, roll-off trucks, and transfer vehicles, as applicable to the various parts
of the site. The following criteria would be met for roadways and maneuvering areas:

        • Turning radius for self-haul vehicles with trailer would be 24 feet
        • Turning radius for residential and commercial collection truck would be 42 feet
        • Turning radius for transfer vehicles would be 72–75 feet

No dead-end drive lanes are proposed, in order to maintain loop access lanes for fire and emergency
equipment. Exhibit 2-10 depicts the proposed circulation.

Emergency Vehicle Access
As shown in Exhibit 2-12, emergency access would be provided to the project site at the northwest
corner of the project site, through a grass paved fire access. 20 Only emergency vehicles would utilize
the grass paved fire access. From the grass paved fire access, emergency vehicles would turn left into
the northernmost lane of the scale facility. This lane would be designated for Fire and City vehicles
only and members of the public would be required to use other lanes in the scale facility. Emergency
vehicles would turn right to continue along the eastern edge of the project site and turn around in
the trailer parking area. Emergency vehicles would exit the project site via either of the motion-
sensor entrance gates at the southeast corner of the project site along Gilman Street or at the south
end of the project site at Second Street and Harrison Street.

Passenger Vehicles
Second Street is currently a one-way street (south to north) from Gilman Street to the Harrison
Street intersection to the north. This intersection is approximately the midpoint of the site in the
north–south direction. The north remainder of Second Street (Harrison Street north) is two-way and
primarily provides access to the Public Storage property on the west, in addition to the project site
on the east side.

Passenger vehicles would access the parking facilities described above on Second Street and exit
either through Second Street to Harrison Street and I-80/I-580 or use the Gilman Street driveway
east of Second Street. The Gilman Street driveway would be limited to right-out only and vehicles
exiting the driveway and wishing to travel eastbound on Gilman Street would turn right onto

20   Grass pavers are an alternative to asphalt, concrete, and traditional pavers. They are made of concrete or recycled plastic with open
     cells to allow grass to grow through them.


FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                                                 2-77

westbound Gilman Street and navigate through the east roundabout (see description of roundabout
as part of the I-80/Gilman Street Interchange Project [Interchange Project], below) to access
eastbound Gilman Street. Refer to Section 3.14, Transportation, and Exhibit 2-10 for additional
information.

Trucks
Most trucks would enter and exit the site through the two northmost driveways on Second Street at
either the north end of the Second Street cul-de-sac to access the scales or opposite Harrison Street
to access the rest of the site.

Collection trucks would use the Gilman Street driveway west of the railroad tracks to enter and exit
the site, which the proposed project would widen. Transfer trucks accessing the MRF in the
southeast corner of the site would enter the site on Second Street at the driveway opposite Harrison
Street and circulate through the site to reach the MRF; they would leave the site through either the
Gilman Street driveway just west of the railroad tracks or turnaround in the MRF loading area and
circulate through the site and exit through the driveway on Second Street opposite Harrison Street.
Left-turns out of the project driveway on Gilman Street west of the railroad tracks would be
prohibited. Trucks exiting this driveway and wishing to travel eastbound on Gilman Street would turn
right onto westbound Gilman Street and navigate through the east roundabout to access eastbound
Gilman Street.

Off-site Roadway Improvements
There would be 0.50-acre of asphalt paving for roadway improvements along Second Street and
Gilman Street (see Exhibit 2-3). This asphalt paving would occur within areas that are currently
paved. Construction emissions associated with these off-site roadway improvements are included in
the air quality, energy, and GHG calculations for the proposed project (see Section 3.2, Air Quality;
Section 3.5, Energy; and Section 3.7, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, for additional information).

Interstate 80/Gilman Street Interchange Project (Interchange Project)
The California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) completed the construction of two
roundabouts at the intersections of Gilman Street and I-80/I-580 ramps in 2025 (see Section 3.13
Transportation, Exhibit 3.13-1). The roundabouts replaced stop sign-controlled intersections on the I-
80 northbound and southbound off-ramps, West Frontage Road, and Eastshore Highway.

The project site continues to have two driveways on Gilman Street. The median on Gilman Street
west of the railroad tracks includes a break opposite of the existing site driveway on Gilman Street
west of the railroad tracks to allow left-turns from eastbound Gilman Street into the project
driveway.

Section 3.13, Transportation, discusses the Interchange Project and how it relates to the proposed
project in more detail.

Union Pacific Railroad/Amtrak
The Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR)/Amtrak right-of-way defines the eastern edge of the site. This
corridor through West Berkeley is a critical part of the region’s freight and passenger rail network. As
part of the Interchange Project, a center barrier was constructed on the west side of the tracks
preventing turns from the site to the eastbound side of Gilman Street (toward the Berkeley Hills)
(see Figure ES-4 of the Feasibility Study (Appendix B). Access to and from the project site was
planned with this in mind. The proposed access for vehicles, primarily collection trucks, traveling
westbound on Gilman Street may be delayed by the at-grade crossing when a train is passing (the
gates are down an average of 30–40 seconds). The driveway is designed for one-way access for
multiple trucks to efficiently clear the Gilman Street right-of-way as well as the at-grade crossing.

2.5.4 - Design, Landscaping, and Lighting
Architectural Design and Building Height
Structures would be completed in a uniform gray metal panel cladding that would reflect the
neighboring buildings and be consistent with the existing design and the neighborhood. An alternate
shade of gray, as well as a bold “dark red cedar” accent color, would be used to highlight different
functions of the structures. All buildings would be less than 45 feet tall (exclusive of roof equipment).

Recovered materials would be incorporated into site construction features where feasible. This
would include the use of recovered demolition slab concrete for low landscape walls. Decorative
fencing made from recycled rebar and construction steel are proposed based on the availability of
local artisans for fabrication.

The hardscape, particularly at key public pedestrian access points, would stress accessibility and
stormwater permeability but also offer varied paving materials and patterns for an organically
inspired design. Vertical sculpture and available decorative surfaces using recycled materials would
be used to demonstrate reuse possibilities.

Visual simulations are provided in Section 3.1, Aesthetics.

Landscaping
Project landscaping would comply with the Model Water Efficient Landscape Ordinance, 21 with the
East Bay Municipal Utility District (EMBUD) Water Efficiency Review: Section 31 Regulations, 22 and
with the applicable requirements of the Bay-Friendly Basics Landscape Checklist, 23 including
enhanced street frontages with low-maintenance plants to assure the landscape installation’s
success over time. Planting would be drought-tolerant and native to minimize maintenance needs

once the plantings are fully established. The landscape plan, including the proposed transitional
Creek landscape palette, is provided in Exhibit 2-13.

Site Lighting
Exterior lighting will be provided by a combination of pole-mounted and building-mounted LED-type
fixtures, which would minimize light trespass beyond the site boundary. These fixtures would be
activated by light sensor (with manual overrides) and would provide a minimum of 0.5-foot candles.

Interior lighting would be energy-efficient LED luminaires. Interior staff areas will have occupancy
sensors.

2.5.5 - Ventilation/HVAC/Odor Control
As a fully enclosed building, the proposed transfer station building would have code-compliant
mechanical ventilation. The ventilation system would be based on a negative air flow approach with
fresh air drawn in through openings (e.g., wall louvers) and pulled to the roof-mounted exhaust fans
with Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value (MERV) 8 filtration media. The filtered air will be
discharged vertically. 24 Multiple variable drive exhaust fans (10,000–20,000 cubic feet per minute
each) would provide approximately four air changes per hour.

The tipping floor area off-loading zone would have an overhead misting system which would mitigate
airborne dust from wheel loader activity. The misting system would also have an integrated odor
neutralizer.

All mechanical ventilation and heating and cooling would be electric systems. (Combustion systems
will not be used.)

Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) for conditioned workspaces would be based on an
electric heat pump unit approach.

2.5.6 - Infrastructure Improvements
Because the proposed project is replacing an outdated facility, it is assumed that utility service
connections for domestic water, storm drainage, sanitary sewer, telephone, and data would be of
similar if not greater capacity, as well as more efficient. Construction of such utilities would utilize
current technology and materials, and it would be designed and installed pursuant to current codes
and regulations. New connections to the public right-of-way would follow requirements from the
respective utility. Adequate offsets from easement boundaries and utility lines would be followed
based on utility company requirements.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT
THIS PAGE INTENTIONALLY LEFT BLANK
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


The proposed project would meet the City’s design requirements, including relevant criteria for
water and sewer design and service connections, surface water drainage, clearing and grading,
building, zoning, transportation and street frontage, right-of-way, and fire protection. Fire
suppression will be supported by on-site hydrants with locations as approved by the local fire
authority. Additional information with respect to proposed tie-in locations, etc., are provided in
Section 3.14, Utilities and Services Systems, in this Draft EIR.

Domestic Water
Similar to current conditions, the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) would supply the
proposed project with potable water. The project site is currently served by a 10-inch water pipeline
in Second Street. Therefore, the project site is within EBMUD’s existing service area near existing
facilities already served by EBMUD, and no expansion of EBMUD facilities is anticipated to be needed
to serve the project. 25 Final design of operational conveyance features would be confirmed as part of
the site-specific project review pursuant to applicable EBMUD standards and requirements. 26

Stormwater Drainage and Sanitary Sewer
Surface water controls would be installed in accordance with National Pollutant Discharge
Elimination System (NPDES) and Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) drainage
requirements. The project site would be graded to direct flows to the east and west, with a bioswale
at the east property boundary and smaller landscaped bioswales at the west boundary.

The proposed project would adhere to Best Management Practices (BMPs) required as part of the
NPDES permitting process implemented by the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control
Board (San Francisco Bay RWQCB), such as pervious pavement, rainwater harvest and reuse, and
compost amended soils where feasible. Additional flow control measures would include an
underground detention basin. Media filter treatment vaults would have a vault filter chamber for
treating runoff prior to exiting the vault. Although detailed stormwater routing has not yet been
designed for post-project conditions, the proposed site drainage is expected to remain generally the
same and is not expected to include any rerouting of current drainage patterns. Peak flow and runoff
volume is expected to decrease under post-project conditions. Additional information with respect
to stormwater drainage is provided in Sections 3.14, Utilities, and Service Systems and 3.9,
Hydrology and Water Quality.

Wastewater from the proposed project would be conveyed to EBMUD’s Main Wastewater Treatment
Plant via the 48-inch diameter wastewater pipeline in Second Street in compliance with applicable
requirements and standards established by the San Francisco Bay RWQCB and under applicable laws
and regulations. EBMUD has confirmed that no expansion of EBMUD facilities is anticipated to be
needed to serve the proposed project. 27 Final design of operational conveyance features would be
confirmed as part of the site-specific project review pursuant to applicable EBMUD standards and

Power
Buildings would be equipped with smart energy meters to measure, monitor, record, and display
energy consumption data for each energy source and end use category to enable efficient energy
management.

The overall building design would promote daylighting to reduce use of artificial lighting. Highly
efficient LED interior and exterior lighting fixtures would include manual and automated lighting
controls and a smart energy metering system.

Power distribution would be provided by a new pad-mounted transformer and main service
entrance switchboard with primary distribution, equipment, and conductors provided by Pacific Gas
and Electric Company (PG&E).

2.5.7 - Waste Reduction and Recycling Features
With landfills as a GHG generator, reducing the volume of both inorganic and organic material that is
transported from the existing solid waste transfer station to the landfill along with the associated
vehicle emissions is fundamental to the purpose of the proposed project and its ability to reduce
that volume. Key programming elements which would contribute to that reduction are as follows:

       • Enhanced options for customers to separate materials at drop-off

       • Larger proposed transfer station building floor area for separation of off-loaded bulky and
         organic materials and enhanced recovery
       • Improved recovery volume from improved MRF processing equipment technology

       • Improved quality of recovered materials from proposed MRF equipment technology

       • Enhanced public education with respect to waste reduction, reuse, recycling, and composting
         via on-site information kiosks

2.5.8 - Environmental Strategies/Sustainability Features
Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design
The proposed project would be built to Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED®) Gold
certification standards.

Energy
None of the new proposed buildings would include natural gas plumbing or hookups. The proposed
project has targeted a net zero energy approach, maximizing use of renewable energy strategies,
including solar.




2-86                                                                                                                                                                     FirstCarbon Solutions
                      https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec02-00 Project Description.docx
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                               Project Description


All buildings on-site would be equipped with smart energy meters to measure, monitor, record, and
display energy consumption data for each energy source and end use category to enable efficient
energy management.

Solar Energy
The proposed project is designed for extensive presence of PVs with approximately 38,500 square
feet of PV equipment at roof level. This would produce enough energy to power the proposed
project, with the exception of the electric vehicle (EV) charging stations. The potential exists that the
MRF’s peak operating periods would require additional energy that would exceed the proposed PV
system. PV panels would be placed on the roof with support framing that would assure optimal
positioning. Although this system could power the proposed project (with the exception of the EV
charging stations), extended use of the high-demand processing equipment would require on-site
battery systems. PVs would also be embedded in the canopy structures used in the proposed Public
Recycling Center to produce power while also providing shade and shelter features from a typical
canopy structure.

At the southwest portion of the MRF, two solar panels would be raised above the roof, which would
be 43-feet, 6-inches tall at its highest point, in order to showcase the use of solar energy at the
facility.

Electric Charging Stations for Staff Vehicles and Truck Parking Areas
For employee cars and trucks, garbage truck fleet parking, and semi-trailer parking, EV charging
technology will be provided in compliance with the most up-to-date State and local regulations.

Water Conservation
Rainwater harvesting would be used on-site to capture sufficient quantities of rooftop rainwater and
store for nonpotable uses such as landscape irrigation and wash down of operational area paving.
Uses of this water would be localized so each tank system (cistern) would have some minor filtration
and an integrated solar-powered pump. Cisterns are assumed to be no larger than 2,500-gallon
capacity. Rainwater exceeding the cisterns capacity would be directed to the stormwater conveyance
system. Low water usage fixtures will be used for all public and staff restrooms.

Recycled Materials
Steel used for structure beams, columns, and exterior wall cladding would have a high percentage of
recycled steel content, as defined by LEED® certification requirements. Deconstruction of existing
site structures and infrastructure would generate large quantities of materials. Items that have
potential reuse/resale would be quantified accordingly for third-party resellers and/or stored off-
site. This would include process equipment, modulars, etc. Demolition concrete would be processed
for use as site base gravel and new concrete slabs and flatwork (as complies with design
specifications). Demolition slab concrete would be sorted for select piecework for rubble masonry
low landscape walls.

CHAPTER 3: ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ANALYSIS
This chapter sets forth the physical and regulatory environmental setting and addresses environmental
impacts of the proposed project with respect to 15 environmental resource areas. The discussions of
the environmental setting describe present physical conditions, or baseline conditions, in the vicinity of
the project site. The baseline used for analyses of environmental impacts under the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) reflects the conditions present at the time the Notice of Preparation
(NOP) for this Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) was published. Potential impacts of the
proposed project are compared against the existing baseline conditions for each environmental
resource.

Issues Addressed in this Draft EIR
The following environmental issues are addressed in Chapter 3:

              • Aesthetics                                                                             • Hydrology and Water Quality
              • Air Quality                                                                            • Land Use and Planning
              • Biological Resources                                                                   • Noise
              • Cultural Resources                                                                     • Public Services
              • Energy                                                                                 • Transportation
              • Geology and Soils                                                                      • Tribal Cultural Resources
              • Greenhouse Gas Emissions                                                               • Utilities and Service Systems
              • Hazards and Hazardous Materials



Format of the Environmental Analysis
Each resource area analyzed in this Chapter includes the subsections summarized below.

Introduction
This subsection summarizes what will be discussed in the respective environmental topic section,
states what informational documents are used as the basis for the section, and indicates what
related comments, if any, were received during the Draft EIR public scoping period.

Environmental Setting
This subsection describes existing, baseline physical conditions of the project site and surroundings
(e.g., existing land uses, transportation conditions, noise environment) with respect to each resource
topic at the time the NOP was issued. Conditions are described in sufficient detail and breadth to
allow a general understanding of environmental impacts of the proposed project.

Regulatory Framework
This subsection describes relevant federal, State, regional (if applicable), and local regulatory
requirements that are directly applicable to the environmental topic being analyzed.

Impacts and Mitigation Measures
This subsection evaluates potential for the proposed project to result in direct and indirect adverse
impacts on the existing physical environment, with consideration of both short-term and long-term
impacts. The analysis covers construction and operation of the proposed project. The City of
Berkeley (City) is utilizing Appendix G of the State CEQA Guidelines as thresholds of significance for
this project. Where applicable, the analysis also applies topic-specific thresholds, standards, plans,
policies, or technical guidance adopted or relied upon by the City or other responsible agencies and
supported by substantial evidence in the record. The significance thresholds for environmental
impacts are defined at the beginning of this subsection, and the discussion of the approach to the
analysis explains how significance thresholds have been applied to evaluate impacts of the proposed
project.

Indirect impacts are discussed only for those resources for which they have potential to occur (e.g.,
cultural resources, air quality, and biological resources). Both project-level and cumulative impacts
are analyzed. Project-level impacts could result from actions related to implementation of the
proposed project. Cumulative impacts could result from implementation of the proposed project in
combination with other cumulative projects in the study area. As discussed in “Cumulative Impacts,”
below, the projects listed in Table 3-1, in conjunction with the proposed project, are considered the
cumulative scenario for analysis of cumulative impacts.

Impacts are analyzed and the respective assessment and findings are included in this Draft EIR,
applying the following levels of significance:

        • No impact. A conclusion of no impact is reached if no potential exists for impacts or if the
             environmental resource does not occur in the vicinity of the project site.
        • Less than significant impact. This determination applies if the impact does not exceed the
             defined significance criteria or would be eliminated or reduced to a less than significant level
             through compliance with existing local, State, and federal laws and regulations. No mitigation
             is required for impacts determined to be less than significant.
        • Less than significant impact with mitigation. This determination applies if the proposed
             project would result in a significant impact, exceeding the established significance criteria, but
             feasible mitigation is available that would reduce the impact to a less than significant level.
        • Significant and unavoidable impact. This determination applies if the proposed project would
             result in an adverse impact that exceeds the established significance criteria and no feasible
             mitigation is available to reduce the impact to a less than significant level. Therefore, the
             residual impact would be significant and unavoidable.
        • Significant and unavoidable impact with mitigation. This determination applies if the
             proposed project would result in an adverse impact that exceeds the established significance
             criteria, and, although feasible mitigation might lessen the impact, the residual impact would
             be significant, and, therefore, the impact would be unavoidable.

Impacts are defined based on the City’s applicable significance criteria identified for each resource
topic and on substantial evidence in the record, including technical studies, regulatory standards,
existing environmental conditions, and the characteristics of the proposed project. Where
applicable, Best Management Practices (BMPs), project design features, standard permit conditions,
or other project requirements are incorporated into the proposed project and considered in
determining whether an impact would be significant. Context is related to the uniqueness of a
resource; intensity refers to severity of the impact. Where applicable, BMPs, project design features,
or both, are incorporated into the proposed project to limit potential for a significant impact. Where
necessary, mitigation measures are identified for significant impacts to limit the degree or lower the
magnitude of the impact; rectify the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected
environment; or compensate for the impact by replacing or providing substitute resources or
environments. These impacts conclude with a finding of less than significant impact with mitigation.
Where no mitigation measures are necessary, relevant impacts are concluded to be less than
significant or to have no impact.

As part of the impact analysis, mitigation measures are identified, where feasible, for impacts
considered significant or potentially significant consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4,
which states that an EIR “shall describe feasible measures which could minimize significant adverse
impacts.” CEQA requires that mitigation measures have an essential nexus and be roughly
proportional to the significant impact identified in the EIR. Mitigation measures identified in this
Draft EIR, and adopted by the City, will be incorporated into the project approvals, as applicable, and
implemented by the City, its contractors, and/or other responsible parties identified in the
Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4,
mitigation measures are not required for environmental impacts that are found not to be significant.

Cumulative Impacts
The discussion of cumulative impacts in this subsection analyzes cumulative impacts of the proposed
project, taken together with other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future projects
producing related impacts. The goal of this analysis is to determine whether overall long-term
impacts of all such projects would be cumulatively significant and to determine whether the
proposed project itself would cause a “cumulatively considerable” incremental contribution to any
such cumulatively significant impacts. To determine whether the overall long-term impacts of all
such projects would be cumulatively significant, the analysis generally considers the following:

        • The area in which impacts of the proposed project would be experienced;

        • The impacts of the proposed project that are expected in the area;

        • Other past, proposed, and reasonably foreseeable projects that have had or are expected to
             have impacts in the same area;
        • The impacts or expected impacts of these other projects; and

        • The overall impact that can be expected if the individual impacts from each project are
             allowed to accumulate.

“Cumulative impacts” refers to two or more individual impacts that, when considered together, are
considerable, or that compound or increase other environmental impacts (CEQA Guidelines §
15355). Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor but collectively significant impacts
taking place over time. If the analysis determines that potential exists for the proposed project,
taken together with other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future projects, to result in a
significant or adverse cumulative impact, the analysis then determines whether the proposed
project’s incremental contribution to any significant cumulative impact is itself significant (i.e.,
“cumulatively considerable”). Both conditions must apply for the proposed project’s cumulative
effects to rise to the level of significance. Conversely, if either the cumulative condition is not
significant, or if the proposed project’s incremental contribution is not cumulatively considerable,
then the proposed project’s cumulative impact is less than significant.

The cumulative impact analysis for each individual resource topic is presented in each resource
section immediately after the description of direct project impacts and identified mitigation
measures.

3-1 shows the locations of the cumulative projects.

3.1 - Aesthetics
3.1.1 - Introduction
This section describes the existing aesthetics, light, and glare conditions on the project site and
project site vicinity, relevant regulatory framework, and potential effects from project
implementation on visual resources and the site and its surroundings. Descriptions and analysis in
this section are based, in part, on-site reconnaissance and photo inventory, visual simulations
prepared specifically for the proposed project, as well as the City of Berkeley General Plan (General
Plan), West Berkeley Plan, and the Berkeley Municipal Code (Municipal Code). No comments related
to Aesthetics were received on the Notice of Preparation (NOP).

3.1.2 - Environmental Setting
Visual Character
Visual character in the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) context is an impartial
description of the defining physical features, landscape patterns, and distinctive physical qualities
within a landscape. Visual character is informed by the composition of land, vegetation, water, and
structure and their relationship (or dominance) to one another and by prominent elements of form,
line, color, and texture that combine to define the composition of views. Visual character-defining
resources and features within a landscape may derive from notable landforms, vegetation, land uses,
building design and façade treatments, transportation facilities, overhead utility structures and
lighting, historic structures or districts, or panoramic open space.

City of Berkeley
The City of Berkeley (City) is located between the San Francisco Bay shoreline (west) and the
Berkeley Hills (east). The Berkeley Hills form the eastern backdrop of the City. The City has a variety
of natural resources and open space areas including lush landscaping, urban vegetation, abundant
street trees, waterfront habitat along the shoreline, and wooded areas in the hills. Urban creeks,
which descend from the hills to the San Francisco Bay, run throughout the City. While most of the
creeks in the flatter, western portion of the City are contained within underground drain culverts,
many segments are still exposed aboveground, including large segments of Codornices Creek. 1

The City has a diversity of buildings, most of which were constructed between 1875 and 1940.
Nearly all of the land within the City is developed and residential uses and streets occupy most of
the City’s land area. 2

West Berkeley is adjacent to the San Francisco Bay and Interstate 80 (I-80)/I-580 and also contains
the Union Pacific Railroad (UPRR) line, which generally parallels I-80/I-580 and is located
approximately 400 to 800 feet to the east. West Berkeley’s built environment has a wide range of
building and site types from massive “heavy” industries (generally to the west) to single-family

     Environmental Management Element.
2    City of Berkeley Department of Planning and Development. 2001. City of Berkeley General Plan: A Guide for Public Decision-Making,
     Urban Design and Preservation Element.

houses on small lots (generally to the east), most of which were built in the 1870s to the 1990s.
West Berkeley contains industrial architecture, historic Victorian homes, and urbane new
commercial buildings, as well as highway-oriented “strips.” A few parks are located throughout West
Berkeley. 3

Project Site
The project site is developed and is occupied by the existing solid waste transfer station, the Trillium
Inc.-operated Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) fueling station, and recycling center. The surrounding
area consists of industrial, commercial, and retail uses. Additionally, a portion of the Codornices
Creek riparian corridor is directly north of the project site, and Harrison Park and Berkeley Skate Park
are east of the project site beyond the UPRR/Amtrak right-of-way.

Scenic Resources
Scenic resources typically involve prominent, unique, and identifiable natural features in the
environment (e.g., trees, rock outcroppings, islands, ridgelines, channels of water, and aesthetically
appealing open space) and cultural features or resources (e.g., regional or architecturally distinctive
buildings, or structures that serve as a focal point of interest).

City of Berkeley
The West Berkeley Plan and the General Plan do not identify scenic resources. However, the City
includes a number of policies to improve the City’s entry corridors. The West Berkeley Plan states
that entry corridors “are areas of transition, places which communities use to highlight their
identity” that “serve as the entrances into Berkeley.” 4 The West Berkeley Plan identifies Gilman
Street as an industrial entry corridor into West Berkeley. The West Berkeley Plan states that Gilman
Street could be improved as an entry corridor by “ . . . strengthen[ing] the ‘street wall’ of buildings,”
by having industrial buildings “turn their faces’ to Gilman Street,” and by creating “ . . . greater
design uniformity—similar setbacks, heights, landscaping, etc.” 5

Project Site
While not specified as a scenic resource, Gilman Street is identified as an industrial entry corridor
adjacent to the southern boundary of the project site.

Views
Views may be generally described as panoramic vistas of a large geographic area, for which the field
of view can be wide and extend into the distance. Vantage points provide an orientation from
publicly accessible locations. Examples of distinctive views include urban skylines, valleys, mountain
ranges, or large bodies of water.

City of Berkeley
Neither the General Plan nor West Berkeley Plan designate scenic vistas or views. However, views of
the San Francisco Bay and the San Francisco skyline are visible from the eastern portion of the City at

Project Site
The San Francisco Bay and other views are not visible from the project site or its vicinity because of
obstruction by intervening development including I-80/I-580. While there are no officially designated
or eligible State Scenic Highways within the City, a portion of I-80 that is approximately 0.2 mile from
the northern boundary of the project site is eligible for designation as a State Scenic Highway. The
closest officially designated State Scenic Highway is a portion of I-580 located at the intersection of
SR-24 and I-580 approximately 4.7 miles south of the project site. Exhibit 3.1-1 depicts officially
designated and eligible State Scenic Highways near the project site. 7

FirstCarbon Solutions (FCS) conducted field visits on February 8, 2022, and September 7, 2023, at the

character of the area. Exhibit 3.1-2 identifies and describes specific viewpoint locations near the
project site that provide a representative cross section of visual images and information about the
existing aesthetic conditions of the immediate surrounding area. These locations represent publicly
accessible views that may be visible to a variety of observers in the area, ranging from motorists
traveling along Gilman Street to people recreating at Harrison Park. As summarized in Table 3.1-1
and as depicted in Exhibit 3.1-2, there are various publicly accessible locations in the project vicinity
with views toward and/or through the project site. Exhibit 3.1-3 through Exhibit 3.1-8 demonstrate
six existing views from the identified viewpoints.

Light and Glare
In the context of CEQA Guidelines, light is nighttime illumination that stimulates sight and makes things
visible, and glare is difficulty seeing in the presence of bright light such as direct or reflected sunlight.

Project Vicinity
The primary sources of nighttime light in the surrounding area are from vehicle headlights traveling
along Gilman Street and other surrounding roadways including I-80/I-580. There are also streetlights
and buildings with outdoor lighting in the project vicinity.

Project Site
Interior lighting from buildings, lamps on the exterior of buildings along Gilman Street, streetlights
along Second Street, truck lights, and passenger vehicle lights associated with the existing facility are
the existing sources of light and glare on the project site.

3.1.3 - Regulatory Framework
State
California Scenic Highway Program
The California Scenic Highway Program is intended to preserve and protect State Scenic Highway
corridors from change that would diminish aesthetic value of highway lands. A highway may be
designated scenic depending upon how much of the natural landscape can be seen by travelers,
scenic quality of the landscape, and the extent to which development intrudes upon travelers’
enjoyment of the view. A scenic corridor is land generally adjacent to and visible from the highway
and is identified using a motorist’s line of vision. The corridor protection program seeks to encourage
quality development that does not degrade scenic value of corridors. Minimum requirements for
scenic corridor protection include:

        • Regulation of land use and density of development
        • Detailed land and site planning
        • Control of outdoor advertising (including a ban on billboards)
        • Careful attention to and control of earthmoving and landscaping
        • Careful attention to design and appearance of structures and equipment

Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations Building Energy Efficiency Standards
California Building Standards Code (CBC) (CCR Title 24)—including Title 24, Part 6—includes Section
132 of the Building Energy Efficiency Standards, which regulates lighting characteristics, such as
maximum power and brightness, shielding, and sensor controls to turn lighting on and off. Different
lighting standards are set by classifying areas by lighting zone. The classification is based on
population figures of the 2010 Census. Areas can be designated as LZ0 (undeveloped), LZ1 (rural),
LZ2 (urban cluster), or LZ3 (urban). Lighting requirements for dark and rural areas are stricter to
protect the areas from the introduction of new sources of light pollution and light trespass.

Physical Form Element

                                 should generally be placed along the front property line to strengthen the urban

                                 these corridors, while parking should be placed at the side or rear of the lot. Signage
                                 and façade design (of features such as doors and windows) should be urban instead
                                 of suburban in character, providing visual interest while remaining appropriate to
                                 the use(s) of the building.

3.1.4 - Project Impacts and Mitigation Measures
Significance Criteria
The City is utilizing the questions in Appendix G of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Guidelines to establish thresholds of significance for the proposed project. Accordingly, the proposed
project would have a potentially significant impact if the project would:

                a) Have a substantial adverse effect on a scenic vista.
                b) Substantially damage scenic resources, including, but not limited to, trees, rock
                   outcroppings, and historic building within a State Scenic Highway.
                c) If the project is in an urbanized area, would the project conflict with applicable zoning
                   and other regulations governing scenic quality.
                d) Create a new source of substantial light or glare which would adversely affect day or
                   nighttime views in the area.

Approach to Analysis
This analysis provides a discussion of the visual impacts associated with the proposed project and its
potential impacts on the project site and the vicinity. Several variables affect the degree of visibility,
visual contrast, and ultimately the determination as to project impacts: (1) scale and size of facilities,
(2) viewer types and activities, (3) distance and viewing angle, and (4) influences of adjacent scenery or
land uses. Viewer response and sensitivity vary depending on viewer attitudes and expectations.
Viewer sensitivity is distinguished among project viewers in identified scenic corridors and from
publicly accessible recreational and plaza areas. Recreational areas and scenic corridors are considered
to have relatively high sensitivity. Because Gilman Street is considered an entry corridor to the City by
the West Berkeley Plan, it is considered to have relatively high sensitivity.

FCS evaluated potential project impacts on aesthetics, light, and glare through site reconnaissance
and review of applicable plans and policies. FCS personnel visited the project site in March 2021 and
conducted field visits on February 8, 2022, and September 7, 2023, at the project site and its
surrounding area to observe and document site conditions through photographs, notes, aerial
photographs, topographical and street maps, and project plans and elevations to identify
surrounding land uses and to evaluate potential impacts from project development. The General
Plan, the Municipal Code and West Berkeley Plan were reviewed to determine applicable policies
and design requirements for the project, and project plans were reviewed to determine compliance
with the applicable requirements of the General Plan, Municipal Code, and the West Berkeley Plan.

Light and Glare
The analysis of light and glare impacts in this section focuses on the nature and magnitude of
changes in light and glare conditions of the project site and surrounding area. If light and glare
conditions of the proposed project and the existing environment are similar, then the visual
compatibility would be high. If light and glare conditions of the proposed project would strongly
contrast with existing light and glare or applicable General Plan or West Berkeley Plan policies and
guidelines and/or any applicable Municipal Code requirements, then light and glare compatibility

Impact Evaluation
Scenic Vistas
Impact AES-1:                  The proposed project would not have a substantial adverse effect on a scenic
                               vista.

Construction
A significant impact would occur if the project construction would have a substantial adverse effect on
a scenic vista. 8 Neither the General Plan nor the West Berkeley Plan defines or identifies scenic vistas;
therefore, there would be no impact to scenic vistas.

However, the West Berkeley Plan defines and identifies entry corridors into the City as “areas of
transition, places which communities use to highlight their identity.” Accordingly, for informational
purposes, this EIR provides an evaluation of the proposed project’s relationship to the industrial entry
corridor. The West Berkeley Plan states that entry corridors set the tone of the City and define the
City’s image and character. The West Berkeley Plan identifies Gilman Street as an industrial entry
corridor into West Berkeley, and attempts to identify ways to improve it while recognizing its
ongoing function as an industrial corridor.

Construction of the proposed project would be visible from the industrial entry corridor for
individuals in vehicles traveling along Gilman Street and pedestrians walking on the sidewalk in the
east/west direction. Project construction would result in construction vehicles entering and exiting
the site; however, construction vehicles would be similar in nature to the existing vehicles that
access the site and would not materially alter the image or character of the industrial entry corridor
for pedestrians or individuals in automobiles looking north toward the site as they travel along
Gilman Street. Construction of the proposed project would not result in a substantial impact to
publicly accessible views of the industrial entry corridor as defined in the West Berkeley Plan. There
would be no impact.

Operation
A significant impact would occur if project operation would have a substantial adverse effect on a
scenic vista as defined and identified in the West Berkeley Plan or the General Plan. Neither the
General Plan nor the West Berkeley Plan defines or identifies scenic vistas; therefore, there would be
no impact to scenic vistas.

The West Berkeley Plan defines and identifies entry corridors into the City, stating that entry corridors
set the tone of the City and define the City’s image and character. The West Berkeley Plan identifies
Gilman Street as an industrial entry corridor into West Berkeley. The project site is just north of the
industrial entry corridor.


8   A scenic vista is defined as a viewpoint that provides expansive views of a highly valued landscape for the benefit of the general public.

Scenic Highways
Impact AES-2:                The proposed project would not substantially damage scenic resources, including,
                             but not limited to, trees, rock outcroppings, and historic buildings within a State
                             Scenic Highway.

A significant impact would occur if project operation would substantially damage scenic resources as
seen from a designated State Scenic Highway. While there are no officially designated or eligible
State Scenic Highways within the City, a portion of I-80 that is approximately 0.2 mile north of the
project site is eligible for designation as a State Scenic Highway. The closest officially designated
State Scenic Highway is I-580 at the intersection of I-580 and SR-24, approximately 4.7 miles south of
the project site. 9 Exhibit 3.1-1 depicts officially designated and eligible State Scenic Highways near
the project site. The project site is not visible from these portions of I-80 and I-580 because of
intervening development. In addition, there are no scenic resources designated by the West Berkeley
Plan or the General Plan located on the project site. Given the absence of scenic highways proximate
to the project site, the lack of designated scenic resources (i.e., ridgelines, hillsides, rock
outcroppings) on the project site, and the presence of intervening development between the project
site and the nearest scenic highways, the proposed project would not adversely affect views from a
State Scenic Highway during operation. Thus, there would be no impact.

Level of Significance
No impact.

Consistency with Regulations
Impact AES-3:                The proposed project is within an urbanized area. The proposed project would not
                             conflict with applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic quality.

The proposed project is in an urbanized area and therefore, impacts to scenic quality are analyzed in
terms of compatibility with applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic quality.

Zoning
The site is located within the Manufacturing (M) zoning district pursuant to the Zoning Code and is
not part of any zoning overlays (Exhibit 2-8). 11 The purpose of the M zoning district is to implement
the West Berkeley Plan’s designation and to encourage development of a general manufacturing
district. Like the M land use designation, the M zoning district allows for a maximum FAR of 2.0, a
maximum building height of 45 feet, and a maximum lot coverage of 100 percent. There are no
minimum setback requirements.

Analysis
The proposed project would not change the land use designation or the zoning. The proposed
buildings would have a maximum height of 45 feet and the FAR would be below the maximum FAR
of 2. The City’s Zoning Code requires that projects in the M zoning district are designed in such a
manner to be supportive of the industrial character of the district, which requires landscaping,
materials, façade treatments, and other features to be physically compatible with the district.
Proposed landscaping would include enhanced street frontages with low-maintenance plants to
assure the landscape installation’s success over time (Exhibit 2-13). Structures would be completed
in a uniform gray metal panel cladding that would reflect the neighboring buildings and be
consistent with the existing design in the neighborhood (eclectic with an old industrial past). An
alternate shade of gray as well as a bold “dark red cedar” accent color would be used to highlight
different functions of the structures. These landscaping and design features would be supportive of
the district’s existing industrial character.

The proposed development would be required to adhere to standards and guidelines for
development identified in the Zoning Code related to building height, massing, setbacks, and site
planning including the requirement that construction of 40,000 square feet or more requires a Use
Permit and a public hearing. The proposed project would also be required to adhere to Policies UD-9
(tree replacement), UD-16 (design and scale fits context), UD-17 (design elements to the
surrounding area), UD-22 (regulating new construction and alterations to ensure good design), UD-
23 (required design review), UD-24 (compatible with area character), UD-25 (façades and exterior
features add interest), and UD-29 (signs contribute aesthetically) of the General Plan as well as to
Goal 3 (visually improve entry corridors) and Policies 3.2 (design of buildings along entry corridors),
3.3 (landscaping and screening), 3.4 (lighting to enhance entry corridors), and 3.5 (high quality
signage), Goal 5 (cohesive, sensitive design) and Policies 5.1 (scale and placement), 5.2 (reinforce
existing street and development patterns), and 5.3 (compatible with existing development), and
Goal 9 (green space) and Policies 9.1 (tree planting) and 9.10 (improve visual character from the
Freeway) of the Physical Form Element of the West Berkeley Plan, among other applicable standards
and guidelines set forth by the City. UD-23 specifically requires that the proposed project undergo
design review, which would ensure consistency and visual compatibility with surrounding existing
and planned uses. Therefore, impacts related to consistency with applicable scenic quality
regulations would be less than significant.

Level of Significance
Less than significant impact.
