Impact Evaluation
Substantial Noise Increase in Excess of Standards
Impact NOI-1:               The proposed project could generate a substantial temporary or permanent
                            increase in ambient noise levels in the vicinity of the project in excess of standards
                            established in the local general plan or noise ordinance, or applicable standards of
                            other agencies.

Construction
Construction-related Traffic Noise
Noise impacts from construction activities associated with the proposed project would be a function
of the noise generated by construction equipment, equipment location, sensitivity of nearby land
uses, and the timing and duration of the construction activities. One type of short-term noise impact
that could occur during proposed project construction would result from the increase in traffic flow
on local streets associated with the transport of workers, equipment, and materials to and from the
project site. The transport of workers and construction equipment and materials to the project site
would incrementally increase noise levels on access roads leading to the site. Because workers and
construction equipment would use existing routes, noise from passing trucks would be similar to
existing vehicle-generated noise on these local roadways.

According to the Air Quality, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, and Energy Analysis Report prepared by FCS
for the proposed project, the phase of construction that would generate the highest number of trips
would be the grading phase, which would generate 82 total daily trips on average. 5 Documented
traffic counts from 2019 for peak-hour traffic volumes provided by Fehr & Peers were as follows: 67
vehicles per hour on Second Street, 1,417 on Gilman Street, and 638 vehicles per hour on Eastshore
Highway, north of Gilman Street. Therefore, on a daily or hourly average, these construction-related
trips would not double daily or hourly trips on any road segment in the project vicinity. For this
reason, short-term intermittent noise from construction trips would not be expected to result in a
perceptible increase in hourly or daily average traffic noise levels in the project vicinity. Thus, short-
term construction-related noise impacts associated with the transportation of workers and
equipment to the project site would be less than significant.

Potential noise impacts during construction related to the temporary diversion of materials to other
nearby, existing transfer stations would only result from traffic related to the short-term changes to
haul routes. However, these diverted trips are existing trips and would be of such a small
concentration that, even if they all went to the same facility, they would not result in a doubling of

    Transfer Station Replacement Project.

existing traffic volumes on access roadways to an alternate facility and would thus not result in a

Construction Equipment Operational Noise
The second type of short-term noise impact is related to noise generated during construction on the
project site. Construction is completed in discrete steps, each of which has its own mix of equipment
and, consequently, its own noise characteristics. These various sequential phases would change the
character of the noise generated on the site and, therefore, the noise levels surrounding the site as
construction progresses. Despite the variety in the type and size of construction equipment,
similarities in the dominant noise sources and patterns of operation allow construction-related noise
ranges to be categorized by work phase. Table 3.11-2 lists typical construction equipment noise
levels based on a distance of 50 feet between the equipment and a noise receptor. Typical operating
cycles for these types of construction equipment may involve 1 or 2 minutes of full power operation
followed by 3 or 4 minutes at lower power settings. Impact equipment such as pile drivers are not
expected to be used during construction of this project.

The site preparation phase, which includes excavation and grading of the site, tends to generate the
highest noise levels because the noisiest construction equipment is earthmoving equipment.
Earthmoving equipment includes excavating machinery and compacting equipment, such as
bulldozers, draglines, backhoes, front loaders, roller compactors, scrapers, and graders. Typical
operating cycles for these types of construction equipment may involve 1 or 2 minutes of full power
operation followed by 3 or 4 minutes at lower power settings.

Construction of the proposed project is expected to require the use of scrapers, bulldozers, water
trucks, haul trucks, and pickup trucks. Based on the information provided in Table 3.11-2, the
maximum noise level generated by each scraper is assumed to be 85 dBA Lmax at 50 feet from this
equipment. Each bulldozer would also generate 85 dBA Lmax at 50 feet. The maximum noise level
generated by graders is approximately 85 dBA Lmax at 50 feet. The effect on sensitive receptors is
evaluated below.

The closest sensitive receptor to the project site is the Harrison House, an 80-bed shelter facility,
east of the project site on Harrison Street. To provide a conservative analysis, construction noise
impacts to this nearest sensitive receptor are compared to the City’s thresholds for Multiple-Family
Residential District (R-3) type residential land uses. The façade of this facility would be located
approximately 180 feet from the nearest construction footprint where heavy construction
equipment would operate during project construction. At this distance, and assuming multiple
pieces of heavy equipment operating simultaneously on the project site, reasonable worst-case
hourly average noise levels would range up to 63 dBA Leq. These noise levels would not exceed the
City’s weekday threshold of 65 dBA Leq(h) for R-3 residential receptors; however, they could exceed the
weekend threshold of 55 dBA Leq(h) for R-3 residential receptors. Therefore, construction noise would
result in a potentially adverse impact. It should be noted that construction activities located 500 feet
or further from this nearest sensitive receptor would not result in exceedances of the City’s weekend
threshold of 55 dBA Leq(h) for R-3 residential receptors. The calculation sheets for this analysis are
included in Appendix I.

According to the Municipal Code Section 13.40.070, noise from construction activities should comply
with the established maximum allowable noise performance standards to the extent that the activities
occur during the permissible hours for construction and all technically and economically feasible noise
reduction measures are incorporated. Construction impacts at residential land uses, although
permitted and exempted during the construction hours specified by the City, would exceed the
suggested maximum noise levels for stationary sources as established by the City, and mitigation would
be required to reduce this potential impact to less than significant.

Implementation of Mitigation Measure (MM) NOI-1, which restricts the construction activities within
500-feet of off-site sensitive receptors to weekdays only or requires implementation of a temporary
sound wall to reduce noise impacts, would preclude the proposed project from exceeding the City’s
weekend threshold and would reduce construction noise impacts on off-site sensitive receptors to
less than significant. If the option of use of a temporary sound wall is selected, the sound wall shall
be a minimum of 8-feet high and shall have a minimum Sound Transmission Class (STC) rating of STC-
15. The sound wall would ensure that worst-case construction noise levels would be reduced to
below the City’s weekend threshold of 55 dBA for receiving R-3 land uses (63 dBA - 15 dBA = 48
dBA).

Implementation of this noise reduction measure would eliminate potential exceedances of the City’s
more restrictive weekend noise threshold of 55 dBA Leq(h) for R-3 residential zone receptors in the
project vicinity. Therefore, implementation of MM NOI-1 would reduce construction noise impacts
to less than significant.

Operation
Mobile Source Operational Noise Impacts
As described in the methodology section above, an increase of 4 dBA or more above existing traffic
noise levels would be considered a substantial permanent increase in traffic noise levels for the
purpose of this analysis.

As explained in the project-specific Transportation Analysis prepared by Fehr & Peers, 6 the proposed
project would not increase passenger vehicle trips, but the future maximum operating capacity
would result in an estimated 12 trucks per day above existing conditions if the facility were to
operate at its maximum future capacity of 130 tons per day. Since the site operates from 8:00 a.m.
to 4:30 p.m. on typical days, this corresponds to about 1.5 additional trucks per hour.

Documented traffic counts from 2019 for peak-hour traffic volumes provided by Fehr & Peers were
as follows: 67 vehicles per hour on Second Street, 1,417 on Gilman Street, and 638 vehicles per hour
on Eastshore Highway, north of Gilman Street. Therefore, an increase of 12 trucks per day would not
double existing hourly or daily trips on local roadways accessing the project site. Thus, impacts from
project-related traffic noise levels would not result in a substantial permanent increase in traffic
noise levels in excess of applicable standards, and the impact would be less than significant.

Stationary Source Operational Noise Impacts
The proposed project would generate noise from truck unloading activities at exterior drop-off areas
and parking lot activities, which includes people conversing, doors shutting, engine startup, and
slow-moving vehicles; from new exterior mechanical equipment sources; and from rooftop
ventilation systems. Potential impacts from these noise sources are discussed below.

Truck Loadout Activities
Proposed on-site operations would remain relatively similar to existing operations, with primary
changes being changes in circulation; in addition, most unloading and sorting operations would now
occur inside the Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) and inside the transfer station building. The fact
that the proposed project would result in these operations occurring within fully enclosed structures
would result in lower operational noise levels as measured at off-site receptors in the project vicinity.

The loudest activity that would still occur outdoors would be the truck loadout activity located at the
loading bays on the north side of the proposed transfer station building. The transfer of material from
the tipping floor to a trailer for delivery to an off-site facility would be accomplished by a wheel
loader lifting the material into the trailer that would be located in a reduced depth loadout tunnel.
The grade of the loadout tunnel floor would be approximately 4 feet to 8 feet below the tipping floor
grade. The trailer would be under a three-sided steel backboard hopper to conduct material into the
trailer. Typical noise levels from this type of truck loading activity range from 70 dBA to 80 dBA Lmax
as measured at 50 feet.

The nearest noise-sensitive receptor to this proposed truck loadout area is the aforementioned
Harrison House, which is approximately 390 feet from the closest proposed loading dock. Because of
distance attenuation, and assuming minimal shielding that would be provided by the loadout tunnel
walls and building façade, noise levels from truck unloading activities would attenuate to below 30 dBA
Lmax at this nearest sensitive receptor land use. The calculation sheets for this analysis are included in
Appendix I.

In addition, noise levels from project-related truck loading and unloading activities would not exceed
the documented existing ambient noise levels identified in the existing noise levels discussion above.

The noise levels from truck loading would not exceed the daytime (55 dBA Lmax) noise performance
standards at this nearest sensitive receptor. These operations would not occur during nighttime
hours and would therefore not exceed the City’s nighttime noise performance standards. Again,
these types of activities are similar to existing on-site activities. Therefore, noise levels from truck
unloading activities would not generate a substantial temporary or permanent increase in ambient
noise levels in the project vicinity and impacts would be less than significant.

Parking Lot Activities
Typical parking lot activities include people conversing, doors shutting, and vehicles idling, which
generate noise levels ranging from approximately 60 dBA to 70 dBA Lmax at 50 feet. These activities
are expected to occur sporadically throughout the day as visitors and staff arrive and leave the
parking lot areas at the project site.

Mechanical Equipment Operations
Overall, on-site operations would remain the same with implementation of the proposed project.
However, a new noise source associated with implementation of the proposed project would be
mechanical ventilation equipment operation. As a fully enclosed building, the proposed transfer
station building would have code-compliant mechanical ventilation.

Commercially available air ventilation equipment, of the size anticipated to be needed for this
facility, are rated as producing noise levels of up to 80 dBA Leq at approximately 5 feet from the fan.
At the time of this analysis, the exact location of these proposed fans has not been determined. The
nearest noise-sensitive receptor is the Harrison House. The nearest sensitive receptor property line
would be located over 175 feet from the nearest building façade where these fans could be installed.
At this distance the operational noise levels from this equipment would attenuate to be below 32
dBA Leq. These noise levels would not exceed the City’s daytime and evening noise performance
standards of 55 dBA Leq from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. and 45 dBA Leq from 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.

In addition, noise levels from project-related mechanical equipment operations would not exceed
documented existing ambient noise levels identified in the existing noise levels discussion above.

Therefore, noise levels from mechanical equipment operations would not generate a substantial
temporary or permanent increase in ambient noise levels in the project vicinity and impacts would
be less than significant.

Mitigation Measures
MM NOI-1      The project applicant shall ensure that the operation of noise-producing
              construction activities on the project site that would be located within 500 feet of
              off-site noise-sensitive land uses shall meet the following requirements:

                                 • Construction equipment shall be well maintained and used judiciously to be as
                                      quiet as practical.
                                 • All internal combustion engine-driven equipment shall be equipped with mufflers,
                                   which are in good condition and appropriate for the equipment.
                                 • Utilize “quiet” models of air compressors and other stationary noise sources
                                   where technology exists. Select hydraulically or electrically powered equipment
                                   and avoid pneumatically powered equipment where feasible.
                                 • Locate stationary noise-generating equipment as far as possible from sensitive
                                   receptors to the east of the project site. Construct temporary noise barriers or
                                   partial enclosures to acoustically shield such equipment where feasible.
                                 • Prohibit unnecessary idling of internal combustion engines. Construction
                                   equipment that would not be used for more than 5 minutes shall be turned off
                                   completely.
                                 • Route construction-related traffic along major roadways and away from sensitive
                                   receptors where feasible.
                                 • Limit all demolition or site preparation or foundation construction activities to
                                   weekdays only (no weekends or legal holidays); alternatively, a variance may be
                                   approved by the Environmental Health Division, pursuant to Municipal Code
                                   Section 13.40.70.
                                      Or
                                 • Prior to initiation of demolition or site preparation activities, the project applicant

Groundborne Vibration/Noise Levels
Impact NOI-2:                            The proposed project would not result in generation of excessive groundborne
                                         vibration or groundborne noise levels.

This section analyzes both construction and operational groundborne vibration and noise impacts.
Groundborne vibrations consist of rapidly fluctuating motions within the ground that have an


FirstCarbon Solutions                                                                                                                                                     3.11-21
https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec03-11 Noise.docx
                                                              City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Noise                                                                                                                               Draft EIR


average motion of zero. Vibrating objects in contact with the ground radiate vibration waves through
various soil and rock strata to the foundations of nearby buildings. Groundborne noise is generated
when vibrating building components radiate sound, or noise generated by groundborne vibration. In
general, if groundborne vibration levels do not exceed levels considered to be perceptible, then
groundborne noise levels would not be perceptible in most interior environments. Therefore, this
analysis focuses on determining exceedances of groundborne vibration levels.

Pursuant to Section 13.40.070 of the Municipal Code, a significant impact would occur if
implementation of the proposed project would cause vibration that annoys or disturbs at least two
or more reasonable persons of normal sensitiveness who reside in separate residences (including
apartments and condominiums) at or beyond the property boundary of the source, if on private
property, or at least 150 feet (46 meters) from the source, if on a public space or public right-of-way.

Construction
The City has not established vibration standards for temporary construction activities. Therefore, the
FTA’s vibration impact criteria are utilized for the purpose of this analysis. The FTA has established
industry-accepted standards for vibration impact criteria and impact assessment. These guidelines
are summarized in Table 3.11-4.

Of the variety of equipment used during construction, the large vibratory rollers that are anticipated
to be used in the site preparation phase of construction would produce the greatest groundborne
vibration levels. Large vibratory rollers produce groundborne vibration levels ranging up to 0.201
inch per second (in/sec) PPV at 25 feet from the operating equipment.

The nearest off-site structure to the project construction footprint is the Public Storage commercial
building located west of the project site on Second Street. The façade of this closest structure would
be located approximately 60 feet from the construction footprint where the heaviest construction
equipment would potentially operate. At this distance, groundborne vibration levels would range up
to 0.05 in/sec PPV from operation of the types of equipment that would produce the highest
vibration levels. This is well below the FTA’s Construction Vibration Impact Criteria of 0.2 in/sec PPV
for this type of structure, a building of non-engineered timber and masonry construction. Therefore,
project construction activities would not generate groundborne vibration or groundborne noise levels
in excess of established standards, and the impact to off-site receptors from short-term groundborne
vibration associated with construction would be less than significant.

Operation
Implementation of the proposed project would not include any new permanent sources that would
expose persons in the project vicinity to groundborne vibration levels that could be perceptible
without instruments beyond the boundary line of the project property. The only major source of
groundborne vibration in the project vicinity is railroad activity along the UPRR rail line located east
of the project site. Implementation of the proposed project would not introduce any new permanent
sources of groundborne vibration to the project site vicinity and would not increase existing off-site
railroad activity. Therefore, the proposed project would not generate groundborne vibration or
groundborne noise levels in excess of established standards and there would be no impact related to
operational groundborne vibration.

Excessive Noise Levels from Airport Activity
Impact NOI-3:                            The proposed project is not located within the vicinity of a private airstrip or an
                                         airport land use plan and would not expose people residing or working in the
                                         project area to excessive noise levels.

A significant impact would occur if the proposed project would expose people residing or working in
the project area to excessive noise levels for a project located in the vicinity of a private airstrip or an
airport land use plan or, where such a plan has not been adopted, within 2 miles of a public airport
or public use airport.

The project site is not located within the vicinity of a private airstrip. The nearest public airport to
the project site is the Oakland International Airport, located approximately 11.4 miles south of the
project site. The project site is located outside of the 65 dBA CNEL airport noise contours. While
aircraft noise is occasionally audible on the project site from aircraft flyovers, aircraft noise
associated with airport activity would not expose people working near the project site to excessive
noise levels. Therefore, implementation of the proposed project would not expose persons residing
or working in the project vicinity to noise levels from airport activity that would be in excess of
normally acceptable standards for the proposed land use development, and no impact would occur.

Level of Significance
No impact.

3.11.5 - Cumulative Impacts
Because of the localized nature of noise and vibration impacts, the geographic scope for the
cumulative analysis for noise and vibration impacts is limited to areas within 1,000 feet of the
project site boundary for on-site noise sources. There is only one project on the cumulative projects
list that is within 1,000 feet of the project site, Cumulative Project 34, I-80/Gilman Street
Interchange Improvement Project (Interchange Project).

This analysis first evaluates whether the impacts of cumulative development could result in a
cumulatively significant noise or vibration impact. If there is a cumulative significant impact, this
analysis then considers whether the incremental contribution of the impacts associated with the
implementation of the proposed project would be cumulatively considerable. Both conditions must
apply for the project’s cumulative effects to rise to the level of significance.

Construction Noise
As explained above, the geographic scope of the cumulative noise analysis is the project vicinity,
including surrounding sensitive receptors. Noise impacts tend to be localized; therefore, the area
surrounding the project site (approximately 1,000 feet) would be the area most affected by
cumulative development. Cumulative development would be required to comply with all applicable
construction hour requirements and would be anticipated to incorporate appropriate Best

Management Practices (BMPs) to help reduce construction noise. Additionally, cumulative

requirements in the General Plan and Municipal Code, which would ensure that noise impacts are
less than significant.

As also described above, the only project on the cumulative projects list that is within 1,000 feet of
the project site is the Interchange Project. However, that project was completed in April 2025 and

Because there is not a cumulative significant construction noise impact to existing or planned land

Therefore, the proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative impact related to
construction noise.

Operational Traffic Noise
A significant cumulative impact would occur if there is an identified cumulative traffic noise impact
in the project vicinity, and if the proposed project would result in an incremental contribution to an
identified cumulative traffic noise impact.

The Interstate 80/Gilman Street Interchange Improvement Project is the only project on the
cumulative projects list that is within 1,000 feet of the project site. Completed in 2025, the project
consisted of improvements to the existing interchange facility to improve traffic flow and enhance
safety; it did not result in any increase in traffic volumes. Potential cumulative noise levels at
operation resulting from this project would not combine to result in any noise increase at the
nearest sensitive receptors in the project vicinity compared to the existing conditions or what has
already been identified for the proposed project-only impacts. Moreover, the proposed project
would replace an existing facility.

As explained above, the proposed project would not increase passenger vehicle trips, but the future
maximum operating capacity would result in an estimated 12 trucks per day above existing
conditions if the facility were to operate at its maximum future capacity of 130 tons per day, which
would not result in a measurable increase in traffic noise levels in the project vicinity and would not
contribute to any cumulative traffic noise impact condition. Therefore, the proposed project would
result in a less than significant cumulative impact related to traffic noise.

Construction Vibration
The geographic scope of the cumulative construction vibration analysis is the project vicinity,
including surrounding sensitive receptors. Construction vibration impacts are very localized;
therefore, the area surrounding the project site (approximately 100 feet) would be the area most
affected by proposed project construction activities.

There are no cumulative projects within 100 feet of the project site; therefore, there is no potential
for the project to contribute to a cumulative construction-related groundborne vibration impact in
the project vicinity. Therefore, the proposed project’s contribution to this already less than
significant cumulative impact would not be cumulatively considerable.

Operational Vibration

considerable contribution to vibration conditions in the project vicinity would result from
introduction of past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future permanent sources of groundborne
vibration in the project site vicinity.

The only major source of groundborne vibration in the project vicinity is the existing UPRR along the
rail line located east of the project site. Implementation of the proposed project would not include
any new permanent sources that would expose persons in the project vicinity to groundborne
vibration levels that could be perceptible without instruments beyond the boundary line of the
project property and would not increase existing off-site railroad activity.

3.12 - Public Services
3.12.1 - Introduction
This section describes the existing conditions related to public services in the City of Berkeley (City)
and the project site and vicinity, as well as the relevant regulatory framework. This section also
evaluates the potential impacts related to public services that could result from project
implementation. Information in this section is based, in part, on information obtained from the City
of Berkeley General Plan (General Plan), the City of Berkeley website, the Berkeley Fire Department
(BFD), and the Berkeley Police Department (BPD).

3.12.2 - Environmental Setting
Fire Protection and Emergency Medical Services
City of Berkeley
The BFD provides fire and emergency services to residents of the City including firefighting and
rescue, fire prevention and training, and emergency medical services.

The BFD has seven fire stations. Table 3.12-1 provides the station address and apparatus assigned to
each station. 1 BFD also includes a Division of Training, Fire Administration, Fire Warehouse, and
Water Rescue Berkeley Marina. Fire prevention programs operated by the BFD include high fire
danger patrols, fire fuel/vegetation management (administered through the City's Public Works
Department), and inspection of parcels. The BFD also manages training programs for its staff and
teaches the Citizens Emergency Response Training (CERT) classes.

City of Berkeley
The BPD provides services intended to protect life and property, prevent crime, arrest criminal

Support, and Administrative. There has been an average of 370 calls for service per year, between

Schools
City of Berkeley
The Berkeley Unified School District (BUSD) serves the entire City. The BUSD operates 35 schools
serving grades K-12. There are 17 early childhood education locations, 12 elementary schools, three
middle schools, one high school, and one adult school.

The University of California Berkeley occupies a 1,250-acre central campus in the east central portion
of the City. The University is the largest landowner and employer in the City, and is a world-
renowned center of education, research, and culture. There is also a considerable number of private
schools (private secondary schools, private colleges and universities, and private special education
schools) in the City.

Project Site
The project site is within the BUSD. The nearest school is Ocean View Elementary School,
approximately 0.35 mile northeast of the site. The Berkeley Adult School is approximately one mile
southeast of the site.

Parks
City of Berkeley
The City maintains 53 parks available for City resident and employee use totaling approximately 302
acres. 3 These facilities include parks, mini-parks, gardens, tot lots, dog parks, swim centers, school
playgrounds, trails, paths, and Marina facilities.

Project Site
Harrison Park (also known as Gabe Catalfo Fields), located at 1100 Fourth Street is immediately east
of the Union Pacific Railroad/Amtrak right-of-way, approximately 105 feet east of the project site.
Berkeley Skate Park is located at 711 Harrison Street, approximately 485 feet east of the project site.

Libraries
City of Berkeley
The Berkeley Public Library has been providing public library services to the Berkeley community
since 1893. The library operates a Central Library, four branch libraries, and a Tool Lending Library.

Project Site
The West Branch Library of the Berkeley Public Library system, the branch nearest the project site, is
located at 1125 University Avenue approximately 1 mile southeast of the project site.

3.12.3 - Regulatory Framework
State
California Building Code
The State of California provides a minimum standard for building design through the California
Building Standards Code (CBC), which is in Part 2 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations. It is
generally adopted on a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction basis, subject to further modification based on
local conditions. Commercial and residential buildings are plan-checked by local, City, and County
building officials for compliance with the CBC. Typical fire safety requirements of the CBC include:
the installation of sprinklers in all high-rise buildings; the establishment of fire-resistant standards for
fire doors, building materials, and particular types of construction; and the clearance of debris and
vegetation within a prescribed distance from occupied structures in wildfire hazard areas.

California Fire Code
The California Fire Code incorporates, by adoption, the International Fire Code of the International
Code Council, with California amendments. This is the official Fire Code for the State and all political
subdivisions. It is in Part 9 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations. The California Fire Code is
revised and published every three years by the California Building Standards Commission.

California Health and Safety Code
California Health and Safety Code, Sections 13100–13135, establish the following policies related to
fire protection:

Section 13100.1 The functions of the office of the State Fire Marshall, including the California
                Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE), shall be to foster, promote,
                and develop strategies to protect life and property against fire and panic.

Section 13104.6 The Fire Marshall has the authority to require fire hazards to be removed in
                accordance with the law relating to removal or public nuisances on tax-deeded
                property.

California Senate Bill 50
Senate Bill (SB) 50 (funded by Proposition 1A, approved in 1998) limits the power of cities and
counties to require mitigation of school facilities impacts as a condition of approving new
development and provides instead for a standardized developer fee. SB 50 generally provides for a
50/50 State and local school facilities funding match. SB 50 also provides for three levels of statutory
impact fees. The application level depends on whether State funding is available, whether the school
district is eligible for State funding and whether the school district meets certain additional criteria
involving bonding capacity, year-round school, and percentage of movable classrooms in use.

SB 50 added the following language to Government Code Section 65996:

     (b) The provisions of this chapter are hereby deemed to provide full and complete school
         facilities mitigation and, notwithstanding Section 65858, or Division 13 (commencing with
         Section 21000) of the Public Resources Code, or any other provision of State or local law, a

Mitigation Fee Act
The Mitigation Fee Act requires any local agency establishing, increasing, or imposing an impact fee
as a condition of development to identify the purpose of the fee and the use to which the fee is to
be put. The agency must also demonstrate a reasonable relationship between the fee and the
purpose for which it is charged, and between the fee and the type of development project on which
it is to be levied.

Impact Evaluation
Need for New or Altered Fire Protection Facilities
Impact PUB-1:                             The proposed project would not result in substantial adverse physical impacts
                                          associated with the provision of new or physically altered governmental facilities,
                                          or need for new or physically altered governmental facilities, the construction of
                                          which could cause significant environmental impacts, in order to maintain
                                          acceptable service ratios, response times or other performance objectives for fire
                                          protection.

Construction
During project construction, the proposed project would be required to comply with all applicable
provisions of the then applicable California Building Standards Code (CBC), which the City has
adopted via the Berkeley Municipal Code (Municipal Code) Chapter 19.28, and the California Fire
Code, adopted via the Municipal Code Chapter 19.48. In compliance with the California Fire Code
and Part 9 of the CBC, the proposed project would be required to follow fire safety standards related
to provision of fire apparatus access and acquisition of building permits during construction.
Specifically, CBC Section 105.7.17 requires plans be submitted and a permit approved to install,
improve, modify, or remove public or private roadways, driveways, and bridges for which Fire
Department access is required by the Fire Code; this would ensure adequate driveway/entry turning
radius, height clearance, and fire hydrant access for fire trucks and engines at the project site during
construction. In addition, CBC Section 105.7.18 requires plans be submitted to the Fire Code official
for all land developments or for the construction, alteration, or renovation of a building within the
jurisdiction where a building permit is required; this would ensure that construction and alteration
would not obstruct BFD from delivering adequate levels of fire protection services during
construction.

While construction workers would be required, it is expected they would be from the local labor
force and would not move to the area for this project, given the temporary construction period, and
would not increase population such that additional fire protection facilities would be required during
construction.

Thus adherence to the CBC and the California Fire Code would ensure that project construction
would not create the need for new or altered fire protection facilities to maintain acceptable service
ratios, response times, or other objectives of fire protection. Therefore, construction impacts related
to fire protection would be less than significant.

Operation
The proposed project is intended to replace the current, outdated solid waste transfer station and
recycling center with a modern, state-of-the-art facility and does not involve the development of
new housing or habitable residences. Therefore, the proposed project would not result in direct
population growth.

Following the implementation of the proposed project, the City does not anticipate any increase in
volume of materials, although given efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed
Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) would be capable of processing an average of 80-130 tons of
recyclable material per day (an increase of up to 85 tons per day). The increase in capacity relates to
the enhancement of the facility with components such as laser sorters, magnets to separate metals,
and fans to separate paper, all of which would allow for more efficient processing. As the enhanced
processing relates entirely to mechanical components, the increase in potential throughput would
not require any increase in employees and would not result in indirect population growth.

Historically, the BFD has been called to the site for minor on-site incidents contained within a small
area approximately once every two years, and the facility maintains on-site fire suppression
equipment. 4 The types of materials brought to the site would be similar to the materials currently
brought to the site and would not substantially increase calls for service.

As part of operation, the proposed project would be required to comply with applicable provisions of
the Berkeley Municipal Code, the CBC, and the California Fire Code. Specifically, the proposed
project would be required to follow standards for fire safety such as fire flow requirements for
buildings, fire hydrant location and distribution criteria, automated sprinkler systems, and fire-
resistant building materials. Operation of the facility includes specific health and safety procedures
intended to minimize the potential for fires and accidents, and these procedures would continue to
be implemented with the proposed project.

Given that the BFD currently serves the project site, and calls for service would not substantially
increase due to operation of the proposed project, the proposed project would not adversely affect
response times or increase use of existing fire protection or emergency medical response facilities
such that substantial physical deterioration, alteration, or expansion would be required, thereby

Construction
The BPD is headquartered at 2100 Martin Luther King Junior Way, approximately 1.8 miles southeast

officers who are consistently patrolling the area. During construction, the proposed project would
implement appropriate security measures such as provision of adequate lighting, fences, and gates
around the construction area to prohibit access to unauthorized persons other than construction
personnel.

project is not expected to result in an increase in population such that additional police protection
facilities would be required.

The BPD noted that the proposed project would not require BPD to obtain additional personnel or
equipment to continue to provide the same level of service at the project site. 5 Project construction
would not create the need for new or altered police protection facilities, and impacts would be less
than significant.

3.12.5 - Cumulative Impacts
The geographical scope of the cumulative public services analysis is the development listed in Table
3-1 (Refer to Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis), which consists predominantly of
commercial, residential, and light industrial development.

Cumulative development would result in an increase in demand for public services including fire
protection and emergency services, police protection, schools, libraries, park, and other public
facilities. The cumulative projects would be in an already-urbanized area with ready access to the
foregoing public facilities that are well-established. Moreover, it is reasonable to assume that service
providers would regularly review the needs of their users within their respective service areas and
plan accordingly from a capital improvement as well as operation and maintenance perspective, and
that such master planning efforts would help to ensure sufficient availability of public services for
the growth in population associated with cumulative development. In addition, consistent with
applicable policies and plans, it is reasonable to assume that service providers would identify
whether and to what extent a specific proposal triggered the need for additional staffing or facilities.
Cumulative projects would be required to pay applicable development impact and in lieu fees, and
any new or expanded facilities that are built to provide public services would be required to obtain
the necessary approvals and complete any required environmental review pursuant to CEQA. The
foregoing would ensure there would be less than significant cumulative impacts in this regard.

As explained above, the proposed project would not require any increase in employees. Therefore,
the proposed project would not result in an adverse impact related to public services. Moreover, the
foregoing would further ensure that the proposed project, which would be near ample public
services with capacity to serve its residents and other users, would not make a cumulatively
considerable contribution to this already less than significant cumulative impact. Therefore, the
proposed project, in conjunction with other cumulative projects, would result in a less than
significant cumulative impact related to sensitive natural communities and associated riparian
habitat.

Level of Cumulative Significance
Less than significant impact.

3.13 - Transportation
3.13.1 - Introduction
This section describes existing conditions related to transportation in the study area and the relevant
regulatory framework. This section also evaluates the potential effects related to transportation that
could result from implementation of the Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement
Project (proposed project). Information in this section is based, in part, on the project-specific City of
Berkeley Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project-Transportation Analysis
(Transportation Analysis) 1 (included as Appendix J).

3.13.2 - Existing Conditions
The project site is currently accessed through nine driveways on Second Street and two driveways on
Gilman Street. Because Second Street is a one-way street northbound between Gilman Street and
Harrison Street, with a cul-de-sac north of Harrison Street, most vehicles enter the site through
Second Street and exit through Harrison Street and the Eastshore Highway.

The following describes the existing roadways that provide access to the project site and vicinity.

Roadway Facilities
State
Interstate 80/I-580
Interstate 80 (I-80) and Interstate 580 (I-580) are a merged section of both interstates to the west of
the project site from approximately the City of Richmond to the City of Emeryville. I-80 is a primary
east–west transcontinental freeway that serves drivers and goods movements between the San
Francscio Bay Area, Northern California, ports and transshipment facilities, transcontinental highway
newtworks, the Midwest, Canada, and the eastern United States. Near the project site, I-80/I-580 is a
10-lane freeway with a maximum speed limit of 65 miles per hour (mph).

Arterial Roads
Gilman Street
Gilman Street connects to I-80/I-580 to the west and runs eastward into the City of Berkeley (City).
Gilman Street has two lanes in each direction west of Third Street and one lane in each direction
with on-street parking east of Third Street. The curb-to-curb distance east and west of Third Street
are 50 feet. The current speed limit is 25 mph.

Collector Roads
Eastshore Highway
Eastshore Highway runs parallel to the eastern side of I-80/I-580 to the west of the project site.
Eastshore Highway is an access road to commercial businesses and other collector streets near the

driveway on Gilman Street west of the railroad tracks to allow left-turns from westbound Gilman

Existing Public Transit Service and Facilities
Bus
The two closest bus stops to the project site are approximately 0.2 miles to the east at Sixth Street,
providing service eastbound and westbound on Gilman Street. The stops are served by AC Transit
Line 12, connecting northwest Berkeley to the Oakland Amtrak at Jack London Square. 2 Additional
AC Transit bus stops are located further east on Gilman Street and San Pablo Avenue.

The East Bay Paratransit Service area boundary includes the City of Berkeley and the project site.3

Rail
The Berkeley Amtrak Station is located at 700 University Avenue, approximately 0.8 mile south of the
project site. The Union Pacific Railroad/Amtrak right-of-way and tracks are located directly east of
the project site and include an at-grade crossing at Gilman Street.

Bicycle Facilities
The California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) Highway Design Manual and National
Association of City Transportation Officials Urban Bikeway Design Guide define four major types of
bicycle facilities: 4

        • Class I: Multiuse Path—These paths provide a completely separate right-of-way and are
             designated for the exclusive use of bicycles and pedestrians with vehicle cross-flow minimized.
        • Class II: Bicycle Lane—These bicycle lanes provide a restricted right-of-way and are designated
             for the use of bicycles for one-way travel with a striped lane on a street or highway. These
             bicycle lanes are generally a minimum of 5 feet wide, and vehicle/pedestrian cross-flow is
             permitted.
        • Class III: Bicycle Route with Sharrows—These bikeways provide right-of-way designated by
             signs or pavement markings for shared use with motor vehicles. These bikeways include
             sharrows or “shared-lane markings” to highlight the presence of bicyclists.
        • Class IV: Buffered Bicycle Lanes—These bicycle lanes consist of a physically separate lane for
             increased comfort and protection of bicyclists. These bicycle lanes can be physically separated
             by a barrier, such as planters or on-street parking, grade-separated from the roadway, or a
             painted buffer area. These can also be called cycle-tracks and can allow for one-way or two-
             way bicycle travel.

Vehicle Miles Traveled
In approving Senate Bill (SB) 743 in 2018, the California State Legislature directed the California
Governor’s Office of Planning and Research (OPR) to develop guidelines for assessing transportation
impacts based on Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT). In response to SB 743, the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) and its implementing guidelines (CEQA Guidelines) were significantly amended
regarding the methods by which lead agencies are to evaluate a project’s transportation impacts for
purposes of CEQA review. As described in CEQA Guidelines Section 15064.3(a):

           Generally, vehicle miles traveled is the most appropriate measure of transportation
           impacts. For the purposes of this section, “vehicle miles traveled” refers to the
           amount and distance of automobile travel attributable to a project. Other relevant
           considerations may include the effects of the project on transit and non-motorized
           travel. Except as provided in subdivision (b)(2) below (regarding roadway capacity), a
           project’s effect on automobile delay shall not constitute a significant environmental
           impact.

This section of the CEQA Guidelines continues to set forth the criteria for analyzing transportation
impacts. On June 29, 2020, the City adopted VMT thresholds of significance and local criteria for
VMT analysis in City of Berkeley VMT Criteria and Thresholds (Thresholds). 6

In its Technical Advisory on Evaluating Transportation Impacts in CEQA (OPR Technical Advisory), the
OPR recommendations suggest that a VMT reduction target of 15 percent below baseline levels is
consistent with the achievement of the State’s climate goals. The City is relying upon the evidence
and data presented by OPR in its recommendations for VMT thresholds, and is applying the
following significance thresholds within Berkeley:

      • A residential project’s VMT impact is considered less than significant if its Household VMT per
         Capita is at least 15 percent below the regional average Household VMT per Capita.
      • An employment-generating project’s VMT impact is considered less than significant if its
         Home- Work VMT per Worker is at least 15 percent below the regional average Home-Work
         VMT per Worker.

Land use projects that meet at least one of the following screening criteria are presumed to cause a
less than significant VMT impact and would not require further CEQA analysis:

        • Transit Priority Area: Projects located within 0.5 mile walkshed around major transit stops 7
             (i.e., the Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) stations and the Amtrak station) or within a 0.25 mile
             walkshed around high-quality transit corridors. 8 Maps that depict the transit priority area
             (TPA) within Berkeley are included in the Thresholds.
        • Low Income Housing: Low-income housing units typically generate less VMT than market-rate
             units of similar sizes and can contribute to improving jobs-housing balance. As such, projects
             that contain 100 percent restricted units affordable to Low-Income Households and Very Low-
             Income Households, as defined in Berkeley Municipal Code 22.20.065, are presumed not to
             require transportation VMT analysis for CEQA, as long as the projects do not include more
             parking supply than the project’s estimated demand.
        • Small Projects: Projects defined as generating 836 daily VMT or less. Based on recent data
             from the California Household Travel Survey, this level of VMT would equate to 20 units of
             residential use or up to 10,000 square feet of nonresidential use. 9
        • Locally Serving Public Facility: Locally serving public facilities generally encompass
             government, civic, cultural, health, and infrastructure uses which contribute to and support
             community needs and mostly generate trips within the local area. Locally serving public
             facilities include, but are not limited to, public schools, passive parks (parks designed for use in
             an informal way and typically less developed), libraries, community centers, police stations,
             fire stations, and public utilities.
        • Projects in Low VMT Areas: Projects that are located in low VMT areas and that have
             characteristics similar to other uses already located in those areas can be presumed to
             generate VMT at similar rates. The low VMT areas in Berkeley are defined based on the results
             of the Alameda County Transportation Commission (Alameda CTC) model, and maps of these
             areas are attached to this Thresholds:
             - Residential projects will be screened out if located in an area that has household VMT per
               capita that is 15 percent lower than the baseline regional average.
             - Office and industrial projects will be screened out if located in an area that has home-work
               VMT per worker that is 15 percent lower than the baseline regional average.

3.13.3 - Regulatory Framework
State
Assembly Bill 1358
Assembly Bill (AB) 1358, also known as the California Complete Streets Act of 2008, requires cities
and counties to include “Complete Streets” policies in their general plans. These policies address the
safe accommodation of all users, including bicyclists, pedestrians, motorists, public transit vehicles
and riders, children, the elderly, and the disabled. These policies can apply to new streets as well as
the redesign of corridors.

Senate Bill 375
SB 375 provides guidance regarding reducing emissions from cars and light trucks. There are four
major components to SB 375. First, SB 375 requires regional greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets.
These targets must be updated every 8 years in conjunction with the revision schedule of the
housing and transportation elements of local general plans. Second, Metropolitan Planning
Organizations (MPOs) are required to create a Sustainable Communities Strategy (SCS) that provides
a plan for meeting regional targets. Third, SB 375 requires housing elements and transportation
plans to be synchronized on 8-year schedules. Finally, MPOs must use transportation and air
emissions modeling techniques that are consistent with the guidelines prepared by the California
Transportation Commission. The applicable SCS for the nine-county Bay Area Region is Plan Bay Area
2050+, which was officially adopted in March 2026. The Association of Bay Area Governments
(ABAG) Executive Board approved the plan on March 19, 2026, followed by the unanimous adoption
by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (MTC) on March 25, 2026.

California Department of Transportation
Caltrans builds, operates, and maintains the State Highway System, including the Interstate Highway
System. Caltrans’s mission is to improve mobility Statewide. Caltrans operates under strategic goals
to provide a safe transportation system, optimize throughput, and ensure reliable travel times,
improve the delivery of State highway projects, provide transportation choices, and improve and

enhance the State’s investments and resources. Caltrans controls the planning of the State Highway
System and accessibility to the system. Caltrans requires encroachment permits from agencies or
new development before any construction work may be undertaken within the State’s right-of-way.
For projects that would impact traffic flow and levels of service on State highways, Caltrans would
review measures to mitigate the traffic impacts.

Caltrans Construction and Safety Requirements
On May 20, 2020, Caltrans adopted the Transportation Impact Study Guide (TISG), 10 which updated
guidance to Caltrans Districts, lead agencies, tribal governments, developers, and consultants to
codify changes to Caltrans’s review process for transportation analysis of land use projects and plans
to comply with updated CEQA Guidelines. The guidance is not binding, rather it is intended to be
used as an informational and reference document. The TISG does not include VMT calculation
methodologies, metrics, or significance criteria, but does provide guidance based primarily on the
OPR Technical Advisory.

Caltrans also issued the Transportation Analysis Framework (TAF) in September 2020, 11 which details
methodology for calculating induced travel demand for capacity increasing transportation projects
on the State Highway System. It is noted that the proposed project does not propose any changes to
the Caltrans owned and operated network.

Caltrans also issued Traffic Safety Bulletin 20-02-R1: Interim Local Development Intergovernmental
Review Safety Review Practitioner Guidance in December 2020, 12 describing the methods with which
Caltrans will assess the safety impacts of projects on the Caltrans owned and operated network. This
guidance states that Caltrans will provide its safety assessment to lead agencies for inclusion in
environmental documents.

Finally, Caltrans has adopted procedures to oversee construction activities on and around its
facilities. The Caltrans Construction Manual 13 describes best practices for construction activities,
including personnel and equipment safety requirements, temporary traffic control, signage, and
other requirements aimed at reducing construction-related hazards and constructing projects safely
and efficiently. Any work proposed on Caltrans facilities would be required to abide by these
requirements.

Senate Bill 743
As noted above, in response to SB 743, the OPR updated the CEQA Guidelines to include new
transportation-related evaluation metrics. In late 2018, updates to the CEQA Guidelines were
finalized and adopted. These changes became effective on December 28, 2018. The updated CEQA
Guidelines address SB 743 and require lead agencies to assess VMT impacts when analyzing
potential environmental impacts of projects. The updated CEQA Guidelines indicate “a development
project that is not exempt and that results in VMT greater than regional average for the land use
type may indicate a significant impact.” The latest direction from OPR also lists new exemptions for

The updated guidelines eliminate the use of automobile delay metrics, such as Level of Service (LOS),
from determining significant environmental impacts from vehicle travel. VMT has been identified as
the most appropriate metric to evaluate a project’s transportation impacts, as projects that result in
lower than average VMT support goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while projects that
result in higher than average levels of vehicle travel contribute to an increasing rate of greenhouse
gas emissions.

Regional
Plan Bay Area 2050-Sustainable Communities Strategy/Regional Transportation Plan
Plan Bay Area, published by the MTC and ABAG, is a long-range integrated transportation and land
use/housing strategy through 2050 for the Bay Area, adopted in 2026, that serves as the Bay Area’s
Sustainable Communities Strategy/Regional Transportation Plan (SCS/RTP). Plan Bay Area 2050+ is a
25-year plan for nine counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa
Clara, Solano, and Sonoma. Plan Bay Area 2050+ aims to improve housing, the economy,
transportation, and the environment through 35 strategies that will make the Bay Area more
affordable, connected, diverse, healthy, and vibrant for all by 2050. The 35 strategies are divided
among four elements—Housing, Economy, Transportation, and the Environment—that lay out vision
for the Bay Area. Serving as an update to the 2021 Plan Bay Area 2050, Plan Bay Area 2050+ is
forecasted to make significant progress in tackling the greatest challenges facing the region, from
housing affordability to the intensifying impacts of global climate change.

Plan Bay Area 2050 includes strategies such as building a Complete Streets network, advancing a
Vision Zero road safety policy, improving the frequency and reliability of local transit, and reducing
climate emissions from vehicles by encouraging Bay Area residents to drive less.

Alameda County Transportation Commission
The Alameda CTC is a joint powers authority governed by a 22-member commission that comprises
elected offices from each of the 14 cities in Alameda County; the Alameda County Board of
Supervisors; and elected representatives for Alameda County Transit and BART. The Alameda CTC
coordinates countywide transportation planning efforts and delivers projects and programs.

Alameda CTC also serves as Alameda County’s congestion management agency. The Alameda CTC
administers a Land Use Analysis Program, which is one of the legislatively required elements of the
Alameda CTC Congestion Management Program. Alameda CTC reviews local land use plans and
projects with the potential to cause countywide or regional impacts. The purpose of the Alameda
CTC’s review is to assess impacts of individual development actions on the regional transportation
system and ensure that significant impacts are appropriately mitigated.

Alameda CTC guidelines state that impacts on all modes of transit should be considered, as follows:

Alameda CTC Countywide Transportation Plan
The Countywide Transportation Plan 14 establishes near-term priorities and guides long-term
decision-making for the Alameda CTC. It establishes a vision for the County’s complex transportation
system that supports vibrant and livable communities. The Countywide Transportation Plan is
updated every 4 years and serves as a key input into the region’s transportation plan, Plan Bay Area
2050. The current Countywide Transportation Plan covers transportation projects, policies, and
programs out to the year 2050 for Alameda County.

The Countywide Transportation Plan includes two companion documents:

        • Community-Based Transportation Plan: An assessment of transportation needs in the
             County’s low-income communities and communities of color with a focus on input collected
             via community engagement activities.
        • New Mobility Roadmap: A document that provides a foundation for agency policy, advocacy,
             and funding decisions to advance new mobility technologies and services for the Alameda CTC
             and partner agencies as well as the private sector. The outcome of the New Mobility Roadmap
             is a set of seven initiatives, each of which has a comprehensive list of potential actions that
             could be taken to address and implement new mobility technologies and services in Alameda
             County.

federal, State, regional, and local funding sources under Alameda CTC’s purview. The expenditure
and revenue assumptions are updated annually and proposals for new programs and projects are

West Berkeley Plan

area between San Pablo Avenue and the Eastshore Highway. It sets forth the City's key land use,
environmental, economic development, transportation, housing and social services, and physical
form (i.e., urban design, historic preservation, and open space) policies for the West Berkeley area.
In conjunction with the Land Use and Environmental Quality Elements, the Transportation Element
presents a strategy for maintaining and improving both the efficiency and environmental soundness
of transportation in West Berkeley. The following goals and policies are applicable to the proposed
project:

Goal 1           Improve traffic flow and air quality by reducing reliance on single occupant
                 automobiles, by encouraging use of alternatives means of transportation.

                 Plan) the amount and location of added development, intensified land use, and
                 added parking in West Berkeley so that development in West Berkeley does not
                 exceed transportation system capacity.

Specific Thresholds of Significance
To analyze the proposed project’s potential environmental impacts under the foregoing significance
thresholds, the City has established standards related to traffic circulation, bicycle and pedestrian
circulation, transit service, VMT, design feature hazards, and emergency access. Relevant standards
can be found in the General Plan, the City of Berkeley VMT Criteria and Thresholds (Thresholds), and
Municipal Code Section 19.48.010. The relevant regulatory framework is provided above. These
specific thresholds of significance are described in more detail below and additional information is
provided in the Transportation Analysis.

Alternative Transportation, Bicycle Facilities, Pedestrian Facilities, and Transit Facilities
Transit Facilities
Generally, a project causes a significant impact to transit facilities and services if an element of it
conflicts with existing or planned transit services. The evaluation of transit facilities shall consider if:

     • A project creates demand for public transit services above the capacity which is provided or
          planned.
     • A project or project-related mitigation disrupts existing transit services or facilities.

     • A project or project-related mitigation conflicts with an existing or planned transit facility.

     • A project or project-related mitigation conflicts with transit policies adopted by the City or AC
          Transit for their respective facilities in the study area.

Bicycle and Pedestrian Facilities
The City of Berkeley Bicycle Plan and 2020 Pedestrian Plan describe objectives necessary to ensure
that bicycle and pedestrian facilities and infrastructure are safe and effective for City residents,
although they do not provide specific significance thresholds. Using the City of Berkeley Bicycle Plan
and 2020 Pedestrian Plan and City input as a guide, the following approach is used to determine
significant impacts to these facilities.

A significant impact would occur when a proposed project:

     • Creates a hazardous condition that currently does not exist for pedestrians and bicyclists or
          otherwise interferes with pedestrian accessibility to the site and adjoining areas.
     • Conflicts with an existing or planned pedestrian or bicycle facility.

     • Conflicts with policies related to bicycle and pedestrian activity adopted by the City.

Vehicle Miles Traveled
The Thresholds define the following thresholds of significance regarding VMT:

        • Residential—If a project exceeds the regional household VMT per capita minus 15 percent;

        • Employment (e.g., office)—If a project exceeds the regional VMT per employee minus 15
             percent;
        • Regional-serving (e.g., retail)—If it exceeds the regional VMT per retail employee minus 15
             percent;
        • Mixed-use projects—Evaluate each land use independently, per the thresholds of significance
             described above.

The Thresholds define a variety of screening thresholds; projects that meet such thresholds may be
exempt from the requirement to include a VMT analysis as the impact to VMT would be presumed
to be less than significant. Such pre-screened projects include those fulfilling at least one of the
following conditions, described in more detail above.

        • Transit Priority Area
        • Low-Income Housing
        • Small Projects
        • Locally Serving Public Facility
        • Projects in Low VMT Areas

Design Feature Hazards
A significant impact would occur if the proposed project violates roadway design policies set forth in
the General Plan or the Municipal Code.

Emergency Access
The General Plan Transportation and Disaster Preparedness and Safety Elements do not provide
significance thresholds for emergency access. The Municipal Code Chapter 9.48 adopts the 2025
California Fire Code as the standard for the City and adopts the amendments prescribed by (Ord.
7791-NS § 1 (part), 2021; Ord. 7680-NS § 1 (part), 2026).

The methodology qualitatively evaluates the potential for the proposed project to result in
inadequate emergency access. The analysis accounts for the ability of facilities on or near the project
site to accommodate emergency service operators and alterations to the public right-of-way that
could result in changes to turning movements or alter the ability of emergency service operators to
access the project site.

Impact Evaluation
Effect on Circulation System
Impact TRANS-1:          The proposed project could conflict with a program plan, ordinance or policy of
                         the circulation system, including transit, roadway, bicycle and pedestrian facilities.

Construction
The construction of the proposed project would require the use of off-road construction equipment
and on-road vehicles associated with worker, vendor, and hauling trips. Equipment and vehicles
would be typical of other construction projects throughout the City. Some construction activities
would occur in City rights-of-way; however, no Caltrans rights-of-way would be impacted.
Construction of the proposed project could impact Harrison Street, Second Street, and Gilman
Streets and result in temporary alterations, closures, or blockages to sidewalks, pedestrian paths,
bicycle facilities, and/or automobile lanes; storage of building materials, dumpsters, debris within
the public right-of-way; provision of exclusive contractor parking on-street; and significant truck
activity. This could result in a significant impact.

Prior to approval of building permits for the proposed project, the City would review the proposed
construction activities and scheduling. The City would require the preparation and approval of a
Construction Transportation Plan (CTP), which would include a series of actions to address the
temporary effects associated with construction, as described in more detail in MM TRANS-1, and
which would reduce construction impacts to a less than significant level. The City would review and
approve the CTP before construction activities are allowed to begin. Implementation of MM TRANS-
1 would ensure connectivity of the circulation system during project construction. Therefore,
construction impacts related to circulation system performance in terms of roadway, transit, bicycle,
and pedestrian facilities would be less than significant with mitigation.

Operation
Circulation System
Following the completion of the project, the Zero Waste Division does not anticipate any increase in
volume of materials, although, given efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed
Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) would be capable of processing an average of 80 to 130 tons of
recyclable material per day (an increase of up to 85 tons per day). The increase in capacity (or future
maximum operating capacity) is due to the enhancement of the facility with components such as
laser sorters, magnets to separate metals, and fans to separate paper, which would allow for more
efficient processing. As the enhanced processing relates entirely to mechanical components, the
increase in potential throughput would not require any increase in employees.

The City and Zero Waste Division would continue to promote diversion of waste materials in
accordance with local and State Law, such that an increased amount of material coming into the
project site is expected to be processed at the MRF rather than at the transfer station portion of the
facility. Accordingly, the number of vehicle trips entering the facility to deliver material generated
within the City is not expected to increase substantially.




3.13-18                                                                                                                                                         FirstCarbon Solutions
                 https://adecinnovations.sharepoint.com/sites/PublicationsSite/Shared Documents/Publications/Client (PN-JN)/2732/27320011/EIR/3 - Draft EIR/27320011 Sec03-13 Transportation.docx
City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Draft EIR                                                                                                                                                                          Transportation


The increase related to diversion of existing throughput from the transfer station to the MRF is not
expected to reach the maximum throughput capacity of 130 tons per day. Accordingly, the Zero
Waste Division acknowledges that, in the future, the excess processing capacity of the MRF may
allow the Zero Waste Division to offer access to the MRF to nearby communities such as El Cerrito
and San Pablo. To that end, overall trips may increase, to the extent that the nearby communities
choose to utilize the MRF for their processing needs. Given the expected total increase in capacity of
up to 85 tons per day, and the anticipated use of commercial trucks for delivery of materials at a rate
of 7 tons per truck, the future maximum operating capacity would result in an estimated 12 trucks
per day above existing conditions if the facility were to operate at its future maximum operating
capacity. Since the site operates from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on typical days, this corresponds to
about 1.5 additional trucks per hour, which is within the daily fluctuation in truck traffic during
typical operations at the site and on the adjacent streets. Therefore, the additional trucks would not
have a noticeable effect on traffic operations or cause a significant impact on related topics such as
noise and air quality.

Although the proposed project would relocate some of the existing services and driveways within
the project site and would modify the internal vehicular circulation within the project site, all trucks
and passenger vehicles would continue to access and leave the site on Gilman Street and/or Second
Street, although the driveway locations along these streets may be modified. Therefore, the
proposed project would not increase traffic congestion in the project vicinity. In addition, the
proposed project would not modify Gilman Street, Second Street, or Harrison Street adjacent to the
project site. Overall, the proposed project would not conflict with an applicable plan, ordinance, or
policy establishing a measure of effectiveness for the performance of the roadway system, including
the applicable CMP.

During construction of the proposed project, materials would be diverted to other processing
facilities. There are several receiving transfer stations in the area that currently serve the City under
existing agreements. Because the total volume of waste handled and the corresponding number of
collection vehicles and trips would not increase, the diversion represents a redistribution of existing
vehicle trips rather than an increase in vehicle activity. In addition, vehicular activities would
continue on roadways that already serve similar vehicle types, such as refuse trucks. Thus, the
diversion would not result in a long-term operational change or conflict with applicable
transportation policies.

The specific facilities utilized for diversion of materials during construction, and the duration of any
diversions, will depend on the final construction phasing plan, contractor requirements, facility
availability, and regulatory considerations. Once the proposed project is in the design phase, the
project applicant will issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) to local processing facilities to solicit
proposals for receiving materials during construction. Although diversion of all materials is unlikely
for the entire construction period, to be conservative the analysis in the EIR assumes full diversion of
all materials for the 15-month construction period.

Bicycle Facilities
The Interchange Project recently replaced the existing Class II 19 bike lanes on Gilman Street with a

facilities. The proposed project would accommodate bicycle parking for 64 bicycles, which would
exceed the 62 bicycle parking spaces required by the Municipal Code. 20

Pedestrian Facilities
Existing pedestrian facilities adjacent to the project site include sidewalks along both sides of Second
Street and Gilman Street along the project frontage. With respect to Gilman Street, the proposed
project would not modify the existing sidewalks. The existing sidewalk on the western side of Second
Street would remain as is. Approximately 11,710 square feet (existing) of the northern portion of
Second Street would be repaved and redeveloped as the main truck entry, while maintaining public
access to the driveway of the adjacent property to the west and relocating the public vehicle
turnaround area to south of its existing location.

The existing sidewalk on the eastern side of Second Street would be redeveloped as part of the
proposed project. The proposed project would also include a publicly accessible pervious pedestrian
access path (Creek Walk) that would be made of permeable pavement and would be approximately
5 feet wide and 95 feet long. The Creek Walk would lead to a small respite (seating) area at the site’s
northwestern corner that would be approximately 20 feet long with a 22-foot 7-inch-wide northern
end and a 12-foot 3-inch-wide southern end that would feature an information podium display
about the Bay Area watershed. Because it would replace the existing sidewalk on the eastern side of
Second Street in compliance with applicable State and local regulations, this sidewalk and Creek
Walk would comply with the 2020 Pedestrian Plan goal of improving safety and comfort for people
