New development projects that include landscape areas of 500 square feet or more are subject to
the Ordinance. This applies to residential, commercial, industrial, and institutional projects that
require a permit, plan check, or design review. The previous landscape size threshold for new
development projects ranged from 2,500 square feet to 5,000 square feet. The size threshold for
existing landscapes that are being rehabilitated has not changed, remaining at 2,500 square feet.
Only rehabilitated landscapes that are associated with a building or landscape permit, plan check, or
design review are subject to the Ordinance.

Senate Bill 407
SB 407, enacted in 2009, mandates that all existing buildings in California come up to current State
plumbing fixture standards within this decade. This law establishes requirements that residential and
commercial property built and available for use on or before January 1, 1994, replace plumbing
fixtures that are not water conserving, defined as “noncompliant plumbing fixtures.” This law also
requires a seller or transferor of single-family residential property show to the purchaser or
transferee, in writing, the specified requirements for replacing plumbing fixtures and whether the
real property includes noncompliant plumbing. Similar disclosure requirements went into effect for
multi-family and commercial transactions on January 1, 2019. SB 837, passed in 2011, reinforces the
disclosure requirement by amending the statutorily required transfer disclosure statement to include
disclosure about whether the property follows SB 407 requirements.

Title 22 of California Code of Regulations
Title 22 regulates the use of reclaimed wastewater (recycled water) and sets forth water quality
standards related thereto. In most cases, only disinfected tertiary water may be used on food crops
where recycled water would encounter the edible portion of a crop. Disinfected secondary
treatment may be used for food crops where the edible portion is produced below ground and will
not encounter secondary effluent. Lesser levels of treatment are required for other types of crops,
such as orchards, vineyards, and fiber crops.

General Waste Discharge Requirement
On May 2, 2006, the State Water Board adopted a General Waste Discharge Requirement (Order No.
2006-0003) for all publicly owned sanitary sewer collection systems in California with more than one
mile of sewer pipe. Order No. 2006-0003 provides a consistent Statewide approach to reducing
sanitary sewer overflows by requiring public sewer system operators to take all feasible steps to
control the volume of waste discharged into the system, to prevent sanitary sewer waste from
entering the storm sewer system, and to develop a SSMP. The General Waste Discharge Requirement
also requires that storm sewer overflows be reported to the State Water Board using an online
reporting system. The State Water Board delegated authority to its nine RWQCBs to enforce these
requirements.

Assembly Bill 341
The purpose of AB 341 is to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by diverting commercial solid
waste to recycling efforts and to expand the opportunity for additional recycling services and
recycling manufacturing facilities in California. In addition to Mandatory Commercial Recycling, AB
341 sets a Statewide goal for 75 percent disposal reduction by the year 2020.

California Integrated Waste Management Act
To minimize the amount of solid waste that must be disposed of by transformation and land
disposal, the State Legislature passed AB 939, the California Integrated Waste Management Act of
1989 (AB 939), effective January 1990. The legislation required each local jurisdiction in the State to
set diversion requirements of 25 percent in 1995 and 50 percent in 2000; established a
comprehensive Statewide system of permitting, inspections, enforcement, and maintenance for
solid waste facilities; and authorized local jurisdictions to impose fees based on the types or
amounts of solid waste generated. In 2007, amendments to the California Integrated Waste
Management Act introduced a new per capita disposal and goal measurement system that moves
the emphasis from an estimated diversion measurement number to using an actual disposal
measurement number as a per capita disposal rate factor. As such, the new disposal-based indicator
(pounds per person per year) uses only two factors: a jurisdiction’s population (or in some cases
employment) and its disposal as reported by disposal facilities.

Senate Bill 1016
SB 1016 builds on AB 939 compliance requirements by requiring that the 50 percent solid waste
diversion be measured in terms of per capita disposal expressed as pounds per person per day. The
new per capita disposal and goal measurement system moves the emphasis from an estimated
diversion measurement number to using an actual disposal measurement number as a factor. Every
year CalRecycle calculates each jurisdiction’s per capita (per resident and per employee) disposal
rates and reviews jurisdiction compliance on a case-by-case basis. Jurisdictions are not compared to
other jurisdictions or the Statewide average but compared to their own 50 percent per capita
disposal target.

Senate Bill 1383
SB 1383 was signed in September 2016 to reduce emissions of short-lived climate pollutants. As it
pertains to CalRecycle, SB 1383 establishes targets to achieve a 50 percent reduction in the level of
the Statewide disposal of organic waste from the 2014 level by 2020 and a 75 percent reduction by
2025. The law grants CalRecycle the regulatory authority required to achieve the organic waste
disposal reduction targets and establishes an additional target that not less than 20 percent of
currently disposed edible food 15 is recovered for human consumption by 2025. 16

California Public Utilities Commission
The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) regulates privately owned telecommunication,
electric, natural gas, water, railroad, rail transit, and passenger transportation companies. It is the
responsibility of the CPUC to (1) assure California utility customers safe, reliable utility service at
reasonable rates; (2) protect utility customers from fraud; and (3) promote a healthy California
economy. The Public Utilities Code, adopted by the legislature, defines the jurisdiction of the CPUC.

California Code of Regulations Title 24
Part 6 (Energy Efficiency Standards for Residential and Nonresidential Buildings)
California Code of Regulations Title 24 Part 6 (California’s Energy Efficiency Standards for Residential
and Nonresidential Buildings) was first adopted in 1978 in response to a legislative mandate to
reduce California’s energy consumption. The standards are updated periodically to allow
consideration and possible incorporation of new energy-efficient technologies and methods and are
now considered some of the most stringent in the nation. Energy-efficient buildings require less
electricity; therefore, increased energy efficiency reduces fossil fuel consumption and decreases
GHG emissions. The 2022 Building Energy Efficiency Standards went into effect on January 1, 2023. 17

Part 11 (California Green Building Standards Code)
California Code of Regulations Title 24, Part 11, is a comprehensive and uniform regulatory code for
all residential, commercial, and school buildings that went into effect January 1, 2011. The code is
updated on a regular basis with requirements that are now considered some of the most stringent in
the nation, with the most recent update consisting of the 2025 California Green Building Standards
Code (CALGreen) that became effective January 1, 2026. 18 Local jurisdictions are permitted to adopt
more stringent requirements, as State law provides methods for local enhancements. The code
recognizes that many jurisdictions have existing C&D ordinances and defers to them as the ruling
guidance if they provide a minimum 50 percent waste diversion requirement. The code also provides
exemptions for areas not served by C&D recycling infrastructure. The California Building Standards
Code (CBC) provides the minimum standard that buildings must meet to be certified for occupancy,
which is enforced by the local building or planning departments with jurisdiction over the building.

CALGreen (California Code of Regulations [CCR] Title 24, Part 11) requires:

          • Short-term bicycle parking. If a commercial project is anticipated to generate visitor traffic,
               provide permanently anchored bicycle racks within 200 feet of the visitors’ entrance, readily
               visible to passers-by, for 5 percent of visitor motorized vehicle parking capacity, with a
               minimum of one two-bike capacity rack (§ 5.106.4.1.1).
          • Long-term bicycle parking. For buildings with over 10 tenant-occupants, provide secure
               bicycle parking for 5 percent of tenant-occupied motorized vehicle parking capacity, with a
               minimum of one space (§ 5.106.4.1.2).
          • Designated parking. Provide designated parking in commercial projects for any combination
               of low-emitting, fuel-efficient and carpool/van pool vehicles as shown in Table 5.106.5.2 (§
               5.106.5.2).
          • Recycling by Occupants. Provide readily accessible areas that serve the entire building and
               are identified for the depositing, storage and collection of nonhazardous materials for
               recycling (§ 5.410.1).

Solid Waste Reuse and Recycling Act
The Solid Waste Reuse and Recycling Access Act requires areas in development projects to be set
aside for collecting and loading recyclable materials. The Solid Waste Reuse and Recycling Access Act
required CalRecycle to develop a model ordinance for adoption by any local agency relating to
adequate areas for collection and loading of recyclable materials as part of development projects.
Local agencies are required to adopt the model or an ordinance of their own to govern adequate
areas in development projects for collection and loading of recyclable materials.

Plan Bay Area 2050 is a long-range plan helping to chart the course for the future of the nine-county
San Francisco Bay Area. Plan Bay Area 2050 focuses on four key elements: housing, the economy,
transportation and the environment, and identifies a path to help make the Bay Area more equitable
for all residents and more resilient in the face of unexpected challenges. The environment chapter
(Chapter 5) specifically references long-term regional strategies and goals surrounding water and
energy, among other topics.

3.15.4 - Project Impacts and Mitigation Measures
Significance Criteria
The City has decided, in its discretion, to utilize Appendix G of the State California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines as thresholds of significance for this project. To determine whether
impacts to utilities and service systems would have significant environmental effects, the following
questions are analyzed and evaluated. The proposed project would have a potentially significant
impact if it would:

        a) Require or result in the relocation or construction of new or expanded water, wastewater
           treatment or stormwater drainage, electric power, natural gas, or telecommunications
           facilities, the construction or relocation of which could cause significant environmental
           effects.
        b) Have sufficient water supplies available to serve the project and reasonably foreseeable
           future development during normal, dry, and multiple dry years.
        c) Result in a determination by the wastewater treatment provider which serves or may serve
           the proposed project that it has adequate capacity to serve the project’s projected demand in
           addition to the provider’s existing commitments.
        d) Generate solid waste in excess of State or local standards, or in excess of the capacity of local
           infrastructure, or otherwise impair the attainment of solid waste reduction goals.
        e) Comply with federal, State, and local statutes and regulations related to solid waste.

Because the proposed project is replacing an outdated facility, it is assumed utility service
connections for domestic water, storm drainage, sanitary sewer, electricity, telephone, and data
would be of similar capacity, if not less than existing conditions.

Water Supply
The existing and proposed land uses are the same and the proposed project would service the same
area as the existing facility; therefore, the proposed project is not expected to increase demand for
water. Furthermore, the proposed project would utilize water conservation methods, including
rainwater harvesting and low water usage fixtures, which is anticipated to reduce water usage on-
site as compared to existing conditions. Therefore, the proposed project is not expected to increase
demand for water and would not have an impact on EBMUD’s ability to supply water to its service
area. Therefore, the proposed project would not trigger the need for new or expanded water supply
and impacts would be less than significant.

Wastewater
Wastewater Treatment
Wastewater from the proposed project would be conveyed to the MWWTP via the 48-inch diameter
wastewater pipeline in Second Street in compliance with applicable requirements and standards
established by the San Francisco Bay RWQCB and under applicable laws and regulations. In a
response to the Notice of Preparation (NOP), EBMUD noted that EBMUD’s MWWTP and interceptor
system are anticipated to have adequate dry weather capacity to accommodate the proposed
wastewater flows from the proposed project and to treat such flows. 24

With respect to wet weather flows, EBMUD noted that the water collection system in the East San
Francisco Bay Area experiences exceptionally high peak flows during storms due to excessive
infiltration and inflow (I/I) that enters the system through cracks and misconnections in both public
and private sewer lines. EBMUD has historically operated three Wet Weather Facilities (WWFs) to
provide primary treatment and disinfection for peak wet weather flows that exceed the treatment
capacity of the MWWTP. Because of reinterpretation of applicable law, EBMUD’s NPDES permit now
prohibits discharges from EBMUD’s WWFs. A federal consent decree requires EBMUD to eliminate
WWF discharges by 2036. Among other requirements, the consent decree requires that EBMUD
continue to implement its Regional Private Sewer Lateral Ordinance and identify key areas of I/I over
a 22-year period. This must result in a certain level of reduction in WWF discharges. As such, to
ensure the proposed project contributes to these legally required I/I reductions the Lead Agency
would ensure that the proposed project complies with EBMUD’s Regional Private Sewer Lateral
Ordinance and support I/I reductions, which would be reviewed during the project approval process
and require a certificate of compliance. The proposed project would include the replacement or
rehabilitation of any existing sanitary sewer collection systems, including sewer lateral lines, to
ensure that such systems and lines are free from defects or, alternatively, disconnected from the
sanitary sewer system pursuant to applicable EBMUD standards and requirements. In addition, as a
condition of approval, the proposed project would include new wastewater collection systems,
including sewer lateral lines, constructed to prevent I/I to the maximum extent feasible while
meeting all requirements contained in the Regional Private Sewer Lateral Ordinance and applicable
municipal codes or Satellite Agency ordinances and in compliance with applicable EBMUD standards
and requirements. Therefore, the proposed project would not trigger the need for new or expanded
wastewater treatment facilities and impacts would be less than significant.

Stormwater Drainage
The proposed project would result in a decrease in on-site impervious surfaces compared with
existing conditions (from approximately 98 to approximately 89 percent). Because the proposed
project would disturb more than 1 acre of land and would replace 10,000 square feet or more of
impervious surfaces, the proposed project would be required to adhere to the applicable provisions
of the Construction General Permit, which would require preparation and implementation of a
SWPPP and the Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit (MRP). The proposed project would
also be required to adhere to applicable policies in the General Plan (including, but not limited to,
Policy EM-24 and Chapters 17.06 and 17.16 of the Municipal Code, which provide regulations with
respect to storm drainage.) In addition, the proposed project would be required to adhere to all
other applicable requirements and standards including the incorporation of Best Management
Practices (BMPs) and Low Impact Development (LID) to comply with applicable C.3 requirements and
the City’s Stormwater Management and Discharge Control Ordinance.

As discussed in Section 3.9 Hydrology and Water Quality, both the Codornices and Gilman Street
Watersheds have stormwater capacity constraints downstream of the project site for flows with a
10-year or greater recurrence. Stormwater runoff from the site is expected to decrease under post-
project conditions, due to enhanced on-site stormwater treatment facilities that will retain
stormwaters and meter off-site flow. Although detailed stormwater routing has not yet been
designed for post-project conditions, the proposed site drainage is expected to remain generally the
same and is not expected to include any rerouting of current drainage patterns. However, if portions
of the project site that previously drained to one watershed are diverted to the other, exceedance of
storm drain capacity may occur despite the overall decrease in stormwater runoff. To address this
potentially significant impact, the proposed project would be required to implement MM HYD-3a to
confirm that final project designs and stormwater plans do not result in increases to peak
stormwater flows or volumes. MM HYD-3b provides standards for final design of the stormwater
infrastructure. Compliance with MM HYD-3a and MM HYD-3b would ensure that the proposed

Energy (Electric Power and Natural Gas)
None of the proposed buildings would include natural gas plumbing or hookups; accordingly, the
project would result in a decrease in reliance on fossil fuels.

The project site is currently served with electric power by Ava, and the proposed project would
continue to be served with electricity service provided by Ava. The proposed project has targeted a
net zero energy approach, maximizing use of renewable energy strategies, including solar. As
described more fully in Section 3.5, Energy, of this Draft EIR, the proposed project would be
developed according to Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED®) standards as
required by the City, which include several sustainable features. As described in the Project
Description, the proposed project would be developed as a net zero energy development that
includes:

        • 38,500 square feet of photovoltaics (PV) equipment mounted on structure rooftops,

        • landscaping would be drought-tolerant and native to minimize maintenance needs once the
             plantings are fully established,
        • a rainwater harvesting system would be installed and used for outdoor watering,

        • Ligh-emitting diode (LED)-type light fixtures would be installed in both indoor and outdoor
             areas,
        • on-site electric vehicle charging stations for staff passenger vehicles, truck parking, and the
             transfer vehicle fleet in compliance with the most up to date regulations

As a result, the proposed project would generate electricity on-site that would supply all or nearly all
of the project’s operational energy demand, with the exception of electric vehicle charging. The
proposed project would utilize rainwater capture systems to water landscaped areas and wash down
exterior paved surfaces instead of using water from the City’s water system. Additionally, the use of
LED-type lighting fixtures would drastically reduce electricity consumption compared to older
lighting fixtures. Therefore, the proposed project would result in less energy usage than existing
conditions and would not result in the need for new or expanded electric power facilities.

The proposed project would not include natural gas plumbing within buildings and instead would
rely on electricity as the primary building energy source. As a project design feature, none of the
proposed buildings would include natural gas plumbing or hookups. Although the existing project
site includes the Trillium, Inc. CNG filling, the proposed project would only remove and replace this
station. The proposed project would not increase the output or storage of this filling station or use of
natural gas. Therefore, the proposed project would not include new natural gas infrastructure and
would not result in the need for new or expanded natural gas facilities. No impact would occur.

As illustrated in Table 3.15-1, EBMUD can meet customer demand out to 2050 during normal years,
single dry years, and two consecutive dry years; however, during the third year of a multi-year
drought, even with customer demand reduction measures in place, EBMUD would need to obtain
supplemental supplies to meet customer demands by the year 2040. 25 Although potential supply
shortages were identified for the multi-year-drought scenario beginning in about 2040, EBMUD
continues to work to diversify its supply portfolio to adapt to these potential constraints, including
investigating potential groundwater recharge/extraction and banking options, water transfer
agreements, and other regional partnerships. By pursuing these projects in tandem, EBMUD
anticipates that the projected shortages would be minimized. Because the existing and proposed
land uses are the same and the proposed project would service the same area as the existing facility,
the proposed project is not expected to increase demand for water. Furthermore, the proposed
project would utilize water conservation methods, including rainwater harvesting and low water
usage fixtures, which is anticipated to reduce water usage on-site as compared to existing
conditions.

the proposed project comply with EBMUD’s Regional Private Sewer Lateral Ordinance and support I/I
reductions, which would be reviewed during the project approval process and require a certificate of
compliance. Therefore, EBMUD would have adequate capacity to serve the proposed project’s
projected demand in addition to the provider’s existing commitments, and impacts would be less
than significant.

Level of Significance
Less than significant impact.

The proposed project could have a significant impact if it would result in insufficient daily capacity or
permitted daily capacity at the Altamont Landfill to serve the proposed project’s waste generation.

For purposes of a conservative analysis, the values in Table 3.15-3 do not consider the mitigating
aspects of applicable laws and regulations that would further reduce the amount of demolition and
construction solid waste that would occur as a part of the proposed project. For example, EM-8 of
the General Plan encourages the rehabilitation and reuse of buildings whenever appropriate and
feasible and California Code of Regulations Title 24, Part 11 requires a minimum of 65 percent
diversion of construction and demolition waste from landfills. Chapter 12.38 of the Municipal Code
outlines the City’s Recycling Policy, which requires the City to recycle at least 50 percent, by weight,
of all waste generated in the City. The proposed project would be required to adhere to the
foregoing applicable federal, State, and local statutes and regulations. For the foregoing reasons, it is
reasonable to assume that the values provided in Table 3.15-3 overstate the recycling and
construction debris and this analysis overstates the solid waste generated during operation; thus this
analysis is considered conservative.

Operation
With respect to solid waste that would be generated by the proposed project during operation, the
following methodology was utilized for purposes of this analysis. Pursuant to State Law SB 1016,
Berkeley targets a disposal rate of 11.2 pounds per employee per day. 32 The 2022 disposal rate for
employment exceeds this target, with the City’s disposal rate being 6.2 pounds per employee per
day. Based on this rate, the proposed project is estimated to generate approximately 143 cubic yards
of solid waste annually at buildout during operation. 33 However, the proposed project would not
increase the number of employees compared to existing operations; therefore, the proposed project
is expected to continue to generate a similar volume of employee-generated solid waste compared
to baseline conditions.

Following implementation of the proposed project, the City does not anticipate any increase in
volume of materials, although given efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed MRF
would be capable of processing an average of 80–130 tons of recyclable materials (an increase of up
to 85 tons per day). The increase in capacity relates to the proposed enhanced components such as
laser sorters, magnets to separate metals, and fans to separate paper, all of which would allow for
more efficient processing. As stated above, because the enhanced processing relates entirely to
mechanical components, the increase in potential throughput would not require any increase in
employees. However, similar to the estimated demolition and construction debris, the foregoing
figures do not consider diversion factors. Therefore, this analysis likely overstates the amount of
operational-related solid waste and is thus considered conservative. Given that the proposed project
would be constructed in phases, this analysis conservatively assumes that construction and
demolition and operation could overlap for a portion of the construction of the proposed project.
Therefore, as a conservative estimate, the total anticipated construction and demolition debris,
approximately 17,738 cubic yards, has been added to the estimated first annual solid waste
generation amount of approximately 143 cubic yards for a total maximum solid waste generation of
approximately 17,881 cubic yards. The 17,881 cubic yards of C&D and operational solid waste is
approximately 0.03 percent of the remaining capacity at Altamont Landfill; thus, the proposed
project would represent only approximately less than 0.03 percent of the remaining capacity.
Therefore, the Altamont Landfill would be able to accommodate the solid waste generated by the
proposed project.

The solid waste transfer station and MRF are inherently equipped to properly separate, recycle, and
dispose of solid waste generated by both construction and operation of the proposed project. Based
on the foregoing, the proposed project would not generate solid waste in excess of State or local
standards, or in excess of the capacity of local infrastructure, or otherwise impair the attainment of

Solid Waste Regulations Consistency
Impact UTIL-5:               The proposed project would comply with federal, State, and local statutes and

For purposes of this analysis, the proposed project would have a potentially significant effect if it
were unable to comply with AB 939 solid waste diversion goals. The proposed project is required to
comply with federal, State, and local statutes and regulations related to solid waste. For example,
EM-8 of the General Plan encourages the rehabilitation and reuse of buildings whenever appropriate
and feasible and California Code of Regulations Title 24, Part 11 requires a minimum of 65 percent
diversion of construction and demolition waste from landfills. Goal 7 and Policies 7.1 and 7.2 of the
Environmental Quality Element of the West Berkeley Plan support the increase of recycling a broad
range of materials. Chapter 12.38 of the Municipal Code outlines the City’s Recycling Policy, which
requires the City to recycle at least 50 percent (similar to AB 939), by weight, of all waste generated
would ensure compliance with the Integrated Waste Management Act by ensuring project
construction waste is transferred to facilities that can adequately recycle solid waste. Regarding
operational-related impacts, the proposed project would also be required to comply with SB 1016.
As of 2022, at a rate of 6.2 pounds per employee per day, the City was exceeding its 11.2 pounds per
employee per day target imposed by state law. 34

The proposed project would be required to comply with applicable federal, State, and local
management and reduction statutes and regulations related to solid waste, including, but not
limited to, the Berkeley’s Recycle Policy, SB 1016, Integrated Waste Management Act, and adherence
to Policy EM-8 of the General Plan; therefore, impacts would be less than significant.

Storm Drainage
Both the Codornices and Gilman Watersheds currently lack sufficient capacity to handle storm
events larger than the 10-year event and face an existing impact from flooding. Codornices Creek is
constrained by the culvert under I-80 and insufficient overbank storage between the Union Pacific
Railroad right-of-way and I-80 that results in overland release to Second Street. In the Gilman Basin,
the storm drain system is undersized such that storm flows back up and flood low-lying areas along
Gilman Street at events greater than a 10-year recurrence. Future cumulative development and
redevelopment along Codornices Creek would continue to add additional overbank storage near the
Creek in compliance with the City of Berkeley Creek Ordinance. Given the existing high level of
urbanization within both watersheds, large-scale cumulative flooding impacts are unlikely, especially
when considering the increased emphasis on LID design and the opportunities to retrofit detention
facilities. With respect to stormwater drainage impacts, implementation of cumulative projects
would result in a less than significant cumulative impact.

Furthermore, the proposed project would not have a cumulatively considerable contribution to the
less than significant cumulative impacts. The proposed project would reduce stormwater runoff to
both watersheds and would provide additional overbank storage along Codornices Creek. Therefore,
the proposed project would not make a cumulatively considerable contribution to the less than
significant cumulative impact and the cumulative impact would be considered less than significant.

CHAPTER 4: EFFECTS FOUND NOT TO BE SIGNIFICANT

4.1 - Introduction
This chapter is based, in part, on the Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project
Environmental Impact Report (EIR) Notice of Preparation (NOP), dated August 31, 2023, and
contained in Appendix A of this EIR. The NOP was prepared to identify the potentially significant
effects of the proposed project and was circulated for public review between August 31, 2023, and
September 30, 2023.

This chapter provides a brief description of effects found not to be significant or less than significant,
based on the NOP, NOP public comments received, or more detailed analysis conducted as part of
the EIR preparation process. No NOP public comments were received related to Agriculture and
Forestry Resources, Mineral Resources, Population and Housing, Recreation, and Wildfire. Note that
a number of impacts that are found to be less than significant are addressed in the various EIR
topical sections (Sections 3.1 through 3.15) to provide more comprehensive discussion of why
impacts are less than significant, in order to better inform decision-makers and the general public.

4.2 - Environmental Effects Found not to be Significant
4.2.1 - Agriculture and Forestry Resources
Important Farmland
The project site is located within an urbanized area and does not support agricultural land use
activities. The California Department of Conservation Farmland Mapping and Monitoring Program
(FMMP) maps the project site as “Urban and Built-up Land,” which is a nonagricultural designation. 1
Urban and Built-up Land is defined as land occupied by structures such as those with residential,
industrial, or commercial uses. As such, implementation of the proposed project would not convert
Prime or Unique Farmland or Farmland of Statewide Importance to nonagricultural uses and no
impact would occur.

Agricultural Zoning and Williamson Act Contracts
The project site does not contain any land zoned for agricultural uses. 2 The project site does not
contain any parcels under a Williamson Act contract. The project site does not support agricultural
land use activities and, therefore, would not be eligible for a Williamson Act contract. This condition
precludes the possibility of conflicts with agricultural zoning or a Williamson Act contract. No impact
would occur.

Forest Land
In accordance with the definition provided in California Public Resources Code Section 12220(g),
“forest land” is land that can support, under natural conditions, 10 percent native tree cover of any
species, including hardwoods, and that allows for the preservation or management of forest-related
resources such as timber, aesthetic value, fish and wildlife, biodiversity, water quality, recreational
facilities, and other public benefits.

The project site is located within an urbanized area and does not support forest land use activities.
As mapped by the United States Department of Agriculture Forest Service, there are no National
Forest lands within the project site or its vicinity. 3

The California Department of Conservation FMMP maps the project site as “Urban and Built-up
Land.” Urban and Built-up Land is defined as land occupied by structures such as residential,
industrial, or commercial uses. As such, the project site does not support forest land use activities
and would not result in the conversion of forest land to non-forest uses. No impact would occur.

Forest Zoning
The project site is not zoned for forest uses or timberland by the City of Berkeley Zoning Ordinance. 4
As such, development of the proposed project would not result in the conversion of agricultural or
forest land uses to urban uses. No impact would occur.

Pressures to Convert Agricultural Land or Forest Land
The project site is located within an urbanized area and does not support agricultural or forest land
use activities. The nearest Important Farmland is over 10 miles east of the project site in Contra
Costa County 5 and the nearest forest land is over 10 miles to the south of the project. 6 As such,
development of the proposed project would not result in the conversion of agricultural or forest land
uses to urban uses. No impact would occur.

4.2.2 - Mineral Resources
Loss of Mineral Resources of Statewide or Local Importance
There are no mineral resources within the City of Berkeley or within the project site or its vicinity. 7
Furthermore, implementation of the proposed project would not result in the loss of a locally

4.2.3 - Population and Housing
Growth Inducement
Direct population growth would result if the proposed project were to include residential units.
Because the proposed project would replace the existing solid waste transfer facility and materials
recovery facility and would not develop residential homes or apartments, no direct population growth
would be expected to occur as a result of construction of the proposed project.

Indirect population growth due to the creation of employment opportunities could occur because of
the proposed project. While construction workers would be required to construct the project, it is
expected they would be from the local labor force and would not move to the area for this project.
Following the implementation of the project, the City does not anticipate any increase in volume of
materials, although given efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed Materials
Recovery Facility (MRF) would be capable of processing an average of 80-130 tons of recyclable
material per day (an increase of up to 85 tons per day). The increase in capacity relates to the
enhancement of the facility with components such as laser sorters, magnets to separate metals, and
fans to separate paper, all of which would allow for more efficient processing. As the enhanced
processing relates entirely to mechanical components, the increase in potential throughput would
not require any increase in employees and would not result in indirect population growth.

Therefore, the proposed project would not result in a significant, unplanned increase in the
population of the City of Berkeley (City), and impacts would be less than significant.

Displacement of Persons or Housing
The proposed project would not require removal of any residential structures. As such, no impact
associated with the displacement of significant numbers of people or housing would occur.

not be expected to result in a significant increase to the population of the City, the quantity of
visitors and total facility usage would not likely increase from the existing baseline. While
construction workers would be required, it is expected they would be from the local labor force and

4.2.5 - Wildfire
The proposed project is in a Local Responsibility Area (LRA), and it is not located in a Very High Fire
Hazard Severity Zone (VHFHSZ). 13 The nearest VHFHSZ is located approximately 1.6 miles northeast
of the project site. The project site is not located in a designated wildland area that would contain
substantial forest fire risks or hazards nor is it within the boundaries of a Wildland-Urban Interface
(WUI).

Factors that may contribute to the risk of wildland fire include dense non-native vegetation, slopes
or inadequate roads, and lack of adequate water pressure and fire service in fire-prone locations.
The project site is flat and located in an urban and developed area that does not contain dense
vegetation and is surrounded by developed properties, access roads, and infrastructure. The
proposed project would not require the installation of infrastructure intended to decrease wildfire
risk. Therefore, the proposed project would have no impact in this regard. 14

CHAPTER 5: OTHER CEQA CONSIDERATIONS

5.1 - Significant Unavoidable Impacts
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15126.2(a),(c) requires an
Environmental Impact Report (EIR) to identify and focus on the significant environmental effects of
the proposed project, including effects that cannot be avoided if the proposed project were
implemented.

Based on analysis contained in this Draft EIR, and the entire administrative record before it, the City
has determined that the proposed project would not result in any significant and unavoidable direct,
indirect or cumulative impacts.

5.2 - Growth-inducing Impacts
There are two types of growth-inducing impacts that a project may have: direct and indirect. To
assess the potential for growth-inducing impacts, the project’s characteristics that may encourage
and facilitate activities that individually or cumulatively may affect the environment must be
evaluated (CEQA Guidelines § 15126.2(e)). CEQA Guidelines, as interpreted by the City, state that a
significant growth-inducing impact may result if the proposed project would:

        • Induce substantial population growth in an area (for example, by proposing new homes and
             commercial or industrial businesses beyond the land use density/intensity envisioned in the
             general plan);
        • Substantially alter the planned location, distribution, density, or growth rate of the population
             of an area; or
        • Include extensions of roads or other infrastructure not assumed in the general plan or
             adopted capital improvements project list when such infrastructure exceeds the needs of the
             project and could accommodate future developments.

This analysis evaluates whether a project could foster economic or population growth, or the
construction of additional housing, either directly or indirectly, in the surrounding environment.

Direct Growth-inducing Impacts
Direct growth-inducing impacts occur when project development imposes new burdens on a
community by directly inducing population growth or by leading to construction of additional
developments in the same area. Increases in the population may tax existing community service
facilities, requiring construction of new facilities that could cause significant environmental effects.
Also included in this category are projects that remove physical obstacles to population growth (such
as a new road into an undeveloped area or a wastewater treatment plant with excess capacity that
could allow additional development in the service area). Construction of these types of infrastructure

                                                                    City of Berkeley—Solid Waste and Recycling Transfer Station Replacement Project

projects cannot be considered isolated from the development they facilitate and serve, and could
significantly affect the environment, either individually or cumulatively.

The proposed project would include demolition and removal of all existing buildings, concrete
foundations, and other paved surfaces. The proposed project would also remove the existing shrubs
and groundcovers on the site, while protecting trees that would not be in conflict with proposed
utilities, grading, stormwater treatment facilities, and architectural improvements. The proposed
project would involve the replacement of the existing transfer station and Materials Recovery Facility
(MRF) with a proposed facility that is designed to enhance recycling and solid waste operations,
address on-site traffic flow, serve existing and future needs of the local community, and replace
outdated buildings. The proposed project does not involve development of new housing or habitable
residences, and the proposed project would not result in the hiring of any new employees (see
Chapter 2, Project Description for additional details regarding employment).

As described in Chapter 4, Effects Found not to be Significant, direct population growth would result
if the proposed project were to include residential units. Because the proposed project is industrial
in nature and would not develop single-family or multi-family residential uses, therefore no direct
population growth would be expected to occur. Removal of any direct barriers to growth would not
occur because the proposed project would be limited to redevelopment of the existing SW&RTS and
would not remove any existing obstacles that currently prevent growth within the City. For example,
the proposed project would not require expansion of existing water, wastewater, and public facilities
and services beyond what was already planned for in the General Plan. Though it would redevelop
the existing transfer station and MRF, the infrastructure installed as part of the proposed project
would be sized and located similar to existing conditions expressly to serve the proposed project and
would not, therefore, induce growth in the project vicinity.

Therefore, because the project does not propose housing, nor would it remove any direct barriers to
growth, the proposed project would not directly increase population.

Indirect Growth-Inducing Impacts
Indirect population growth occurs when a project creates substantial employment opportunities or
provides new, upsized infrastructure that could lead to additional unplanned growth. Following the
implementation of the proposed project, the City does not anticipate any increase in volume of
materials, although given efficiencies in the proposed project design, the proposed MRF would be
capable of processing an average of 80-130 tons of recyclable material per day (an increase of up to
85 tons per day). The increase in capacity relates to the enhancement of the facility with
components such as laser sorters, magnets to separate metals, and fans to separate paper, all of
which would allow for more efficient processing. As the enhanced processing relates entirely to
mechanical components, the increase in potential throughput would not require any increase in
employees.

Therefore, the proposed project would not include upsized infrastructure that could lead to
additional unplanned growth. Because the proposed project is sized to accommodate already
approved and expected growth in areas already developed based on the population projections of

5.3 - Significant Irreversible Environmental Changes
As mandated by CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.2(d), the Draft EIR must address significant
irreversible environmental changes that would result from implementation of the proposed project.
Primary impacts and, particularly, secondary impacts (such as highway improvement which provides
access to a previously inaccessible area) generally commit future generations to similar uses.
Specifically, such an irreversible environmental change would occur if:

        • The proposed project would involve a large commitment of nonrenewable resources, which
             makes removal or nonuse thereafter unlikely;
        • Irreversible damage can result from environmental accidents associated with the proposed
             project; and
        • Any irretrievable commitments of resources are not justified (e.g., the proposed project
             results in the wasteful use of energy). (Refer to Section 3.5, Energy, which addresses this topic
             in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Appendix F)

The proposed project would involve the replacement of the Existing SW&RTS with a proposed facility
that is designed to enhance recycling and solid waste operations, address on-site traffic flow, serve
existing and future needs of the local community, and replace outdated buildings. Chapter 2, Project
Description describes Concept A and Concept B more fully. The proposed project would include
demolition and removal of all existing buildings, concrete foundations, and other paved surfaces. The
proposed project would also remove the existing shrubs and groundcovers on the site, while protecting
trees that would not be in conflict with proposed utilities, grading, stormwater treatment facilities, and
architectural improvements.

Construction would include the use of building materials, such as petroleum-based products and
metals, that cannot reasonably be recreated. Construction would involve significant consumption of
energy, consisting predominantly of petroleum-based fuels that deplete supplies of nonrenewable
resources. Construction of structures, other improvements and infrastructure would also consume
energy and water.

However, construction debris recycling practices would be expected to result in the recovery and reuse
of building materials such as concrete, lumber, and steel; these practices would also limit disposal of
these materials, some of which are nonrenewable. Steel used for structure beams, columns and

features as described in Chapter 2, Project Description. Adherence to CALGreen and the reduction,

and effluent and lessen the severity of corresponding environmental effects. Although the proposed
project would result in an irretrievable commitment of nonrenewable resources and water for

hazardous materials (see Section 3.8, Hazards and Hazardous Materials). The City of Berkely Zero

Alameda County Environmental Health for review and approval if the tenants/operators intend to
store significant amounts of hazardous materials on-site.

According to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE), the proposed
project is in a Local Responsibility Area (LRA), and it is not located in a Very High Fire Hazard Severity
Zone (VHFHSZ).1 The nearest VHFHSZ is located approximately 1.6 miles northeast of the project
site. The project site has not previously experienced wildfire and is not located in or near an area of
steep terrain or historical wildfire burn, nor does it experience consistent high winds; the project
site would not be prone to wildfire risk. In addition, as discussed in Section 3.12, Public Services,
existing fire protection facilities would be adequate to serve the project site, and the proposed
project would not result in a significant impact related to need for new or altered fire protection
facilities. Thus, implementation of the proposed project would not have the potential to result in
significant environmental accidents related to wildfire hazards and would not result in significant
irreversible environmental changes.

CHAPTER 6: ALTERNATIVES TO THE PROPOSED PROJECT

6.1 - Introduction
The following section contains a comparative impact assessment of a reasonable range of potentially
feasible alternatives to the proposed project. The primary purpose of an alternatives analysis under
the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is to provide decision-makers with a reasonable
range of potentially feasible project alternatives that could attain most of the basic project
objectives, while avoiding or reducing any of the proposed project’s significant adverse
environmental effects. Important considerations for this alternatives analysis are described below
and are incorporated herein pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6.

As demonstrated by the administrative record for the proposed project, all impacts are avoided, less
than significant or can be mitigated to below a level of significance; therefore, the proposed project
does not have any significant unavoidable direct, indirect or cumulative impacts.

An Environmental Impact Report (EIR) must describe a reasonable range of alternatives to the
proposed project, or to its location, that would feasibly attain most of the project's basic objectives
while reducing or avoiding any of its significant effects. The discussion of alternatives is subject to a
rule of reason and the scope of alternatives to be analyzed must be evaluated on the facts of each
case. Accordingly, analysis of the following three alternatives to the proposed project is provided to
allow decision-makers to consider the proposed project in light of alternative development options,
thereby promoting CEQA’s purpose as an information disclosure statute. This analysis is guided by
the following considerations set forth under CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6:

        • An EIR need not consider every conceivable alternative to a project;

        • An EIR should identify alternatives that were considered by the lead agency, but rejected as
             infeasible during the scoping process;
        • Reasons for rejecting an alternative include:
             - Failure to meet most of the basic project objectives;
             - Infeasibility; or
             - Inability to avoid significant environmental effects.

that preliminary transfer station and recycling operation designs reflected the desires of the

Guidelines § 15126(f)(2)(A)). The CEQA Guidelines establish that only locations that would
accomplish this objective should be considered as alternative location for the proposed project.

The CEQA Guidelines identify the following factors that may be considered when addressing the
feasibility of an alternative location (CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(f)(1):

        1. Site suitability
        2. Economic viability
        3. Availability of infrastructure
        4. General Plan consistency
        5. Other plans or regulatory limitations
        6. Jurisdictional boundaries
        7. Whether the proponent can reasonably acquire, control, or otherwise have access to the
           alternative site

Thus, an alternative location would need to be at least of comparable size within an industrial area
within the City that is designated and zoned for a manufacturing use, have adequate roadway
access, and utility capacity. To identify an alternative location that might be reasonably considered to
“feasibly accomplish most of the basic purposes” of the project and also reduce significant impacts,
it was assumed that such a location would ideally have the following characteristics:

        • At least 7.48 acres in size
        • Located on an infill site in an industrial area
        • Designated and zoned for manufacturing
        • Served by available infrastructure
        • Available for purchase and development

No potential alternative locations were identified that could satisfy the above-referenced criteria,
given the parameters necessary for this type of facility. Moreover, even if there were such a site,
given the urbanized, already built-up nature of this area of the City, coupled with the nature of the
identified project impacts, it is reasonable to conclude that any such site would have similar
characteristics as the project site and would not result in a reduction or avoidance of impacts at
issue. Furthermore, if an alternate location were pursued that did not meet the above criteria, such
as not being in an urbanized and industrial portion of the City, it is likely that a number of impacts
would actually increase (e.g., biological, cultural, tribal cultural, transportation, land use, air quality,
noise, etc.) if it were not an infill site, lack of proximity to available infrastructure, potential increase
in nearby sensitive receptors, and potential increase in biological and other site-related constraints.

Therefore, because no suitable alternative location is available that could lessen the impacts of the
proposed project, based on CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6, a potential alternative location was
rejected as infeasible.

6.4.2 - Alternative Manufacturing Use
An alternative manufacturing use, consistent with the existing Manufacturing land use and zoning
designations was considered. This alternative was rejected because it would result in the loss of the

City’s existing transfer station and MRF, which are vital public facilities within the City of Berkeley.
This would result in severe disruption to this existing service and existing commercial and public
users would have to travel to further away facilities, which would result in an increase in vehicle
miles traveled, among other potential environmental impacts. In addition, an alternative
manufacturing use may result in other significant unavoidable environmental issues, such as air

Guidelines, alternative manufacturing use of the project site was rejected as impractical and
infeasible and unable to meet the objectives of the proposed project.

6.4.3 - Alternative Configurations
As described in Section 6.1.2, the Zero Waste Division and ZWC conducted an extensive outreach
process to ensure that preliminary transfer station and recycling operation designs reflected the
desires of the community. Nine public meetings were held, three at each stage of the process. From
the design process, a vetting cycle eliminated more than a dozen iterations that were not viable for
technical reasons, including inability to maintain operations during construction, inefficient
circulation, limited capacity, and/or significant cost impacts.

6.4.4 - Reduced Density Alternative
This alternative would provide for additional transitional creek landscaping and would widen the
Codornices Creek channel at the northern end of the site by removing material. Similar to the
proposed project, this alternative includes two buildings (one for the proposed transfer station and
vehicle maintenance activities and one for MRF activities). This alternative could result in greater
impacts because a facility with reduced density would not be able to process as much solid waste as
the proposed project. As such, less solid waste would be diverted from landfills. This alternative
would not meet the project objective to develop a facility that provides a maximum amount of space
for the separation of materials, resulting in maximization of recovery and diversion of reusable and
recyclable materials that would otherwise be transported to the landfill. Furthermore, it would have
greater impacts related to solid waste.

6.5 - Alternatives to the Proposed Project
This Draft EIR presents a reasonable range of potentially feasible alternatives to the proposed project
for analysis and evaluation of their comparative merits, pursuant to criteria for evaluation of
alternatives in CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6. Where a project does not involve any significant
and unavoidable impacts and the potential impacts associated with a project are less than significant
or can all be reduced to below a level of significance with the incorporation of project design
features, compliance with existing regulations and/or mitigation, the analysis properly considers
alternatives that would also reduce or eliminate those impacts that are less than significant with
mitigation. CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(a) states that an EIR need not evaluate every
conceivable alternative to a project.

An EIR must briefly describe the rationale for selection and rejection of alternatives. The lead agency
may make an initial determination as to which alternatives are potentially feasible and, therefore,
merit in-depth consideration, and which are clearly infeasible. Alternatives that are remote or

The two alternatives to the proposed project analyzed in this section are as follows:

        • No Project/No Development Alternative (Alternative 1): Under the No Project/No

             redeveloped. Under this alternative, all buildings and paving on-site would remain and the

             improvements would not occur and no transitional creek landscaping would be planted and

             portion of the project site. An overall conceptual site plan is provided in Exhibit 6-1. This

             sorting and baling area, and administrative offices. The proposed facility would include
             electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure, solar panels, be Leadership in Energy and
             Environmental Design (LEED®) certified, and, similar to the proposed project, would also
             feature a pervious pedestrian access path (referred to herein as Creek Walk). This Alternative
             would provide a creek buffer to protect the adjacent Codornices Creek.

6.6 - Alternative 1—No Project/No Development Alternative
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(e) requires that an EIR evaluate a “No Project Alternative,” which is
intended to allow decision-makers to compare the impacts of approving the project with the impacts
of not approving the project. In cases where the project constitutes a land development project, the
No Project Alternative is the “circumstance under which the project does not proceed.” For many
projects, the No Project Alternative represents a “No Development” scenario, in which the project
site remains in its existing condition and no development occurs for the foreseeable future.
However, CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(e)(3)(B) establishes that “[i]f disapproval of the project
under consideration would result in predictable actions by others such as the proposal of some
other project, this ‘no project’ consequence should be discussed.”

In this case, the project site is currently used as a solid waste transfer facility and MRF. Therefore, the
No Project/No Development Alternative consists of the continuation of these land use activities for
the foreseeable future. This alternative assumes the existing facility would remain in regulatory
compliance and that the Zero Waste Division would implement actions, if any are identified by the
regulatory agencies, to maintain compliance with local, State, and federal standards. In addition, as
part of the No Project/No Development Alternative, some improvements to the existing facilities are
expected to be implemented in the foreseeable future. These include roof repair, added storage, and
installation of an aboveground tank to replace the two underground storage tanks that were
removed in 2025.

6.6.1 - Impact Analysis
Aesthetics
As described in Section 3.1, Aesthetics, the proposed project’s impacts related to scenic vistas, scenic
resources, consistency with regulations, as well as with respect to lighting and glare would be less
than significant.

Under the No Project/No Development Alternative, the site would remain in its current condition.
There would be no change in scenic vistas, scenic resources, consistency with regulations, nighttime
lighting, or daytime glare, as there would be no change to existing on-site and off-site conditions.
Thus, impacts related to aesthetics would be less than significant under this alternative.

The No Project/No Development Alternative would not realize the benefits associated with
redeveloping the site with a modern structure. This alternative would not, for example, include new
project features such as signage that denotes the entrance to the proposed facility that would create
visual interest and establish a sense of place in the City’s Industrial District. This alternative would
not redevelop the site with newer buildings and diversity in building materials that would promote
greater aesthetic appeal. By including these features, the proposed project would be consistent with
Policies UD-17, UD-24, UD-25, and UD-29 of the General Plan and Policies 3.1, 3.2, 3.5, 5.2, and 9.11
of the West Berkeley Plan; however, the No Project/No Development Alternative would not advance
any of these policies to the same degree as the proposed project. Therefore, although aesthetics
impacts were found to be less than significant for both the No Project/No Development Alternative

and the proposed project, the No Project/No Development Alternative would result in greater

Air Quality
As described in Section 3.2, Air Quality, the proposed project’s impacts related to air quality would
be less than significant with respect to exposure to objectionable odors during construction and
operation. The proposed project’s impacts related to consistency with an air quality plan would be
less than significant with mitigation incorporated. Impacts related to criteria pollutant emissions
would be less than significant with mitigation for construction and less than significant for operation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to sensitive receptors’ exposure to toxic air contaminant
concentrations would be less than significant with mitigation. Cumulative impacts would be less than
significant.

Under the No Project/No Development Alternative, there would be no ground disturbance either
within the project site or within the areas proposed for the off-site improvements; therefore, no
impacts to air quality would occur under this alternative during construction. As this alternative
would not result in operational changes to the facility, this alternative’s impacts related to
consistency with an applicable air quality plan, criteria pollutant emissions, sensitive receptors’
exposure to toxic air contaminant concentrations, and exposure to objectionable odors would be
less than significant.

As described in Section 2, Project Description, the new solid waste transfer station and MRF would
be fully enclosed with code-compliant ventilation systems that would include roof-mounted exhaust
fans. These roof-mounted exhaust fans would include Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value (MERV) 8
filtration media that would filter exhaust. Moreover, the buildings would include overhead misting
systems to mitigate airborne dust and include odor neutralizers. Therefore, the proposed project
would include improved air filtering and odor source control as project design features that would
reduce the potential odor impacts to sensitive receptors compared to existing conditions. The No
Project/No Development Alternative would not realize these same benefits.

Because the No Project/No Development alternative would not require the mitigation associated
with construction of the proposed project, this alternative would result in lesser impacts on air
quality as compared to the proposed project. However, the ultimate impact conclusions of less than
significant would be the same under both circumstances.

Biological Resources
As described in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, the proposed project’s impacts related to special-
status species, sensitive natural communities, fish and wildlife movement corridors, and consistency
with local biological resources policies/ordinances would be less than significant with mitigation
incorporated. The proposed project would result in a less cumulative impact and would result in no
impact with respect to wetlands and jurisdictional features or conflicting with an adopted
Habitat/Natural Community Conservation Plan.

Because the No Project/No Development alternative would not require the mitigation associated

Energy
As described in Section 3.5, Energy, the proposed project would result in energy consumption during

less than significant with respect to energy use during construction and at operation, conflicting with
a plan for renewable energy or energy efficiency, and cumulative impacts.

Under the No Project/No Development Alternative, there would be no ground disturbance both
within the project site and within the areas proposed for the off-site improvements; therefore, no
impacts related to energy consumption would occur under this alternative during construction.
During operation, the No Project/No Development alternative would have a lower electricity
demand than the proposed project without the addition of EV charging infrastructure to support the
EV trucks. However, the No Project/No Development alternative would continue to have diesel
trucks which is not consistent with the State’s plan to transition away from reliance on fossil fuels.

In addition, under this Alternative, the existing facility would not realize the same benefits as the

Geology and Soils
As described in Section 3.6, Geology and Soils, the proposed project’s impacts related to exposure of
persons, structures, or improvements to seismic- and soil-related hazards; to soil erosion or the loss of
topsoil; or paleontological resource would be less than significant level with mitigation incorporated.
The proposed project would have no impacts with respect to wastewater disposal systems, and
cumulative impacts would be less than significant.

Because the No Project/No Development Alternative would result in the continuation of the current
land use activities for the foreseeable future, and no ground disturbance associated with
construction would be required, no impacts related to the potential exposure of persons and
property to seismic- and soil-related hazards; soil erosion or the loss of topsoil; wastewater disposal
systems; or paleontological resources, would occur under this alternative, and no mitigation would
be required.

However, the existing facility does not currently meet all seismic requirements due to its age. As
such, this alternative would not realize the same degree of benefit as the proposed project. The
existing facility would be required to fund upgrades to the facility to meet seismic standards.
However, these impacts would be less than significant under both circumstances.

Greenhouse Gas Emissions
As described in Section 3.7, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, the proposed project’s impacts with respect
to GHG emissions generation would be less than significant with mitigation incorporated for

As described in Section 3.8, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, the proposed project’s impacts with
respect to routine transport, use, or disposal of hazardous materials; hazardous emissions proximate

The No Project/No Development Alternative would result in the continuation of the current land use
activities for the foreseeable future. Therefore, this existing less than significant impacts related to
routine transport, use, or disposal of hazardous materials; emergency response and evacuation; and
wildland fires would occur under this alternative. Because the site is not located near a school or
airport, there would be no impacts related to hazardous emissions proximate to a school or
proximity to a public airport safety hazard.

Under the No Project/No Development Alternative, the existing structures, which may contain lead-
based paint (LBP) and asbestos-containing material (ACM), would remain. Because no development
would occur under the No Project/No Development Alternative, none of the existing buildings would
be demolished, and any potential LBP and ACM would not have the opportunity to be released so no
exposure to these materials due to a release would occur. Any exposure for employees or visitors to
the project site to LBP and ACM would be similar to existing conditions.

As discussed in Section 3.8, Hazardous Materials, and analyzed in the Phase I Environmental Site

potentially contaminated soil or groundwater would not be released and exposure to hazardous
materials would be similar to existing conditions. Therefore, no impact would occur with respect to
hazardous materials upset risk.

As part of the Feasibility Study (Appendix B), the City of Berkeley Transfer Station & MRF Site
Conditions Review & Assessment was completed in February of 2019. It concluded that several of
the existing structures, most notably the existing transfer station, are in poor or very poor condition.
Hazardous conditions related to continued degradation of the structures, such as worker safety,
would continue under this alternative. In addition, the existing buildings are out of compliance with
the currently in effect California Building and Fire Codes. As such, this alternative would not realize
the same degree of benefit as the proposed project. The existing facility would be required to fund
upgrades to the facility to meet seismic standards. However, these impacts would be less than
significant under both circumstances.

6.6.2 - Conclusion
This alternative would avoid the proposed project’s less than significant impacts with respect to
biological, cultural, and tribal cultural resources, geology and soils, and transportation, and would
avoid the need for construction-related mitigation associated with those environmental topical
areas. It would result in a less than significant impact with respect to air quality, and would avoid the
need for construction-related mitigation, resulting in a lesser impact in this regard. It would result in
substantially similar impacts to the proposed project’s less than significant impact associated with
energy, GHG emissions, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, land use and planning,
and public services. It would result in a slightly less than significant impact than air quality, biological
resources, cultural resources, hydrology and water quality, noise, transportation, tribal cultural
resources, and utilities and service systems, ultimate impact conclusions of less than significant
would be the same under both circumstances. It would result in a greater impact to aesthetics;
however, these impacts would be less than significant under both circumstances.

The No Project/No Development Alternative would not meet any of the project objectives because
the facilities would not be redeveloped as described in Section 2, Project Description and none of
the improvements would be completed. The existing infrastructure has been in operation for over 35
years, and the transfer station, MRF, and operational facilities have exceeded their service life and
need replacement. In addition, many of the standards and policies in place today in support of GHG
emission reductions were not in place when the facilities were built, and the facilities are not in
compliance with the current California Building Standards Code (CBC) and California Fire Code
(including seismic requirements). Furthermore, the existing solid waste transfer station and

alternative would feature the Creek Walk, providing additional pedestrian facilities. Impacts related

mitigation.

to the proposed project, and therefore the ultimate less than significant conclusions would be the
same under both circumstances.

Tribal Cultural Resources
As described in Section 3.14, Tribal Cultural Resources, the proposed project’s impacts related to
tribal cultural resources would be less than significant with mitigation. Cumulative impacts would be
less than significant.

This alternative would result in grading and other ground disturbance activities on the project site,
as well as removal of existing structures, similar to the proposed project. In addition, this alternative
would be subject to the same applicable laws, regulations, policies, and mitigation measures as the
proposed project. Therefore, similar to the proposed project, impacts related to tribal cultural
resources would be less than significant with mitigation incorporated. This alternative would result
in less than significant impacts with respect to cumulative impacts. Therefore, this alternative would
result in substantially similar impacts on tribal cultural resources as compared to the proposed
project. The ultimate less than significant impact conclusions would be the same under both
circumstances.

Utilities and Service Systems
As described in Section 3.15, Utilities and Service Systems, the proposed project’s impacts related to
water supply or conveyance facilities; wastewater treatment or conveyance facilities; electric power;
telecommunications facilities; landfill capacity; consistency with solid waste regulations; and

cumulative impacts would be less than significant. The proposed project’s impacts related to
stormwater drainage facilities would be less than significant levels with mitigation incorporated.

This alternative would be developed on the same site as the proposed project and would be subject
to the same applicable laws, regulations, and policies. Because this alternative would result in the
continuation of the current land use activities for the foreseeable future and would not result in a
direct or indirect increase in population, similar to the proposed project, this alternative’s impacts
related to water supply or conveyance facilities; wastewater treatment or conveyance facilities;
electric power; telecommunications facilities; landfill capacity; consistency with solid waste
regulations; and cumulative impacts would be less than significant.

With respect to stormwater drainage, and as described in Section 3.9, Hydrology and Water Quality,
both the Codornices and Gilman Street Watersheds have stormwater capacity constraints
downstream of the project site for flows with a 10-year or greater recurrence. Because this
alternative would be on the same site as the proposed project, and subject to the same flooding and
storm drainage issues, this alternative would also include implementation of MM HYD-3a and MM
HYD-3b. Similar to the proposed project, due to enhanced on-site stormwater treatment facilities
that will retain stormwaters and meter off-site flow, stormwater runoff from the site is expected to
decrease under post-project conditions. Because this alternative and the proposed project would
both require mitigation to address storm drainage issues, they would have a similar, less than
significant impact after mitigation. Therefore, this alternative would result in substantially similar
impacts on utilities and service systems as compared to the proposed project. The ultimate less than
significant impact conclusions would be the same under both circumstances. However, unlike the
proposed project, the One Building Alternative would result in the new building being located over
an existing utility easement adjacent to the existing Vehicle Maintenance Building. This configuration
would obstruct or substantially constrain access to the easement for utility maintenance and repair
purposes. Mitigation to ensure utility access would likely require redesign of the One Building
Alternative, relocation of the affected utilities, or dedication of a replacement easement with
equivalent access. As a result, the One Building Alternative would result in greater impacts to utility
system access and maintenance compared to the proposed project, which would preserve
unobstructed access to the easement area.

6.7.2 - Conclusion
This alternative would result in substantially similar impacts to the proposed project’s less than
significant impact associated with aesthetics, energy, and public services. This alternative and the
proposed project would both require mitigation to reduce impacts associated with air quality,
biological resources, cultural resources, geology and soils, GHG emissions, hazards and hazardous
materials, hydrology and water quality, land use and planning, noise, transportation, and tribal
cultural resources. Therefore, they would have a similar, less than significant impact after mitigation
for these impact areas. This alternative would have a greater impact on utility systems compared to
the proposed project because the proposed single building would cover an existing utility easement,
making access needed for utility service, maintenance, repair, and replacement more difficult than
under the proposed project, which would consist of two buildings that would allow for unobstructed
access to the easement area.

The One Building Alternative would include the replacement of the existing solid waste transfer
station with a proposed facility that is designed to enhance recycling and solid waste operations,
address on-site traffic flow, serve existing and future needs of the local community, and replace
outdated buildings. The alternative would also include environmental strategies/sustainability
features similar to the proposed project. The One Building Alternative would also include internal
pedestrian circulation that would clarify pedestrian paths as opposed to existing conditions. This
internal circulation would also improve the safety and comfort of people accessing the site on foot.
As such, although the One Building Alternative would meet many of the project objectives, it would
not meet all objectives to the same degree as the proposed project because its single-building
configuration would constrain access needed for utility service, facility maintenance, repair,
replacement, and future infrastructure needs.

6.8 - Environmentally Superior Alternative
Table 6-2 presents the potential environmental impacts of the proposed project and those of the
two alternatives to the proposed project. As shown in Table 6-2, the No Project/No Development
Alternative would not result in any changes and would not require any mitigation. Accordingly, it
would be the environmentally superior alternative. However, CEQA Guidelines state that if the No
Project Alternative is the environmentally superior alternative, the EIR must also identify “an
environmentally superior alternative” from among the other alternatives (CEQA Guidelines §
15126.6(e)(2)).The remaining alternatives, the proposed project and the One Building Alternative,
would result in similar environmental impacts (Table 6-2). Both the proposed project and the One
Building Alternative would meet all of the project objectives (see Table 6-3). However, the One
Building Alternative would result in greater impacts related to utilities and service systems because
the single-building configuration would cover an existing utility easement, rendering the utilities
within that easement inaccessible for routine maintenance, repair, replacement, and emergency
response purposes. Mitigation to ensure utility access would likely require relocation of the affected
utilities or dedication of a replacement easement with equivalent access. Because such
modifications could alter the alternative’s site plan, cost, and feasibility, the One Building Alternative
would have greater utility-related constraints than the proposed project.

By contrast, the proposed project’s two-building configuration would preserve unobstructed access
to the easement area and allow those utility facilities to remain accessible. For this reason, the
proposed project would be environmentally superior to the One Building Alternative.
